en: The Bhārgava Tantra
The First Chapter.
We worship Lord Hayagrīva, who consists of knowledge and bliss, whose form is like a pure crystal, and who is the foundation of all sciences. 1.1.
Having prostrated before Agastya, that tiger among sages, who was staying on the peak of Mount Mahendra,
those preeminent sages, becoming composed, questioned him.
O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, you who are learned in all the scriptures:
how have we all today crossed over the ocean of existence?
Although the scriptures have been studied and the three Vedas have been thoroughly mastered,
nevertheless, O Lord of Sages, our minds are not at all stainless.
"How shall we cross over the ocean of existence?
Tell us today the means by which we may go to the imperishable state. (1.5)
Having heard this, the highly effulgent sage Svāyambhuva himself began to speak to the seers that which he had himself studied and properly practiced.
In former times, indeed, the Rākṣasa Vātāpi was digested by Agastya during a Śrāddha feast;
afterwards, when Ilvala became enraged, he too was slain by him.
"Aha! Two demons have been destroyed by me while I was performing penance.
Because of them, our own ascetic merit has been lost; what shall we do?"—thus he reflected. (1.8)
Having approached the Himavat, which is frequented by gods and gandharvas,
where the waters of the Gaṅgā flow forth, and which is honored by siddhas and vidyādharas.
It is embraced by the light of Śaṅkara, it brings delight to Pārvatī,
and it is stamped with the lotus-feet of Nārāyaṇa, the great yogi.
Endowed with the bearer of meritorious fragrance, worshipped by Indra and the other gods,
and assuming a supreme form other than his own at the time of the dissolution of the three cities.
It was filled with groves of trees bowed down by the weight of fruits and flowers,
crowded with many hermitages, and was the stainless abode of Hari.
I performed most fierce asceticism, abstaining from food and with senses subdued;
for then, that terrible, wondrous, and sin-destroying penance was increasing in intensity.
I heard a voice from the sky speaking with profound resonance;
it consisted of few syllables yet possessed great meaning, and brought forth happiness in its ultimate result. || 1.14 ||
If Hari is propitiated by austerity, what is the purpose? If Hari is not propitiated by austerity, what is the purpose? (1.15)
If Hari is both within and without, what is the purpose of austerity?
If Hari is neither within nor without, what is the purpose of austerity? (1.16)
"O Brahmin, desist from your asceticism and go to Mount Mahendra;
having approached Rāma there, you shall obtain happiness from him. (1.17)
Having heard this voice from the sky, which bestowed pleasure upon the mind and the ears,
I desisted from my ascetic penance and once again proceeded toward the southern direction.
Then, having reached Mount Mahendra, which is frequented by holy gandharvas,
I beheld Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, together with the sages.
Resembling molten gold, with a reddish-brown beard and matted locks,
he was clothed in bark and deerskin, and bore a blazing axe.
Like the sun scorching, like the moon cooling,
and like the flood of Vāsudeva’s radiance illuminating the entire world.
He shone with an exceeding splendor through his majesty, like Nārāyaṇa with Śrī, like Parameṣṭhin with Bhāratī, and like Śarva with Girijā. || 1.22 ||
Beholding that Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who was beautiful in every limb,
I bowed my head in supreme joy.
O best of sages, my body has been cast down upon the surface of the earth like a felled tree at the lotus feet of Rāma.
Having been permitted, he rose and, approaching with a loud voice, gratified that Lord with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā.
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, whose nature is peaceful bliss and pure consciousness;
salutations to you, the unconquered, and salutations to the treasury of the six divine attributes.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Person, who abide in great majesty;
salutations to you who possess a thousand heads and a thousand feet.
Salutations to you who have a thousand arms; salutations to you who have a thousand eyes;
salutations to you who are formless; salutations to you who possess a single form.
Salutations to you who possess manifold forms, and salutations to you who are the imperishable;
salutations to you, the all-pervading one, known through the Vedas, the Supreme Self.
Salutations to you, whose form is pure consciousness alone, who are the embodiment of the three Vedas;
salutations to you, the most minute, the most massive, and the greatest.
Salutation to you who are nearest and farthest, and to you who are most swift;
salutation to you who are greatest, most excellent, and youngest. (1.32)

Salutations to you, the fivefold self; salutations to the inner witness of all; salutations to the one whose form encompasses all conceptual constructs, and who is the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
Salutations to you, whose form consists of the qualities, who conforms to the forms of those qualities,
who is both differentiated and undifferentiated, and whose nature is both the whole and the parts.
Salutations again and again to Him who is empty of beginning, middle, and end, and who possesses those [attributes];
salutations to Him who is expressed by the Praṇava and whose form is the Praṇava.
Salutations to You, Viṣṇu, who assumes the forms of Brahmā and others for the sake of establishing the course of the world, and who manifests through various distinct forms such as Nṛsiṃha.
Homage to him whose body is untouched by the ripening of karmas or by afflictions;
homage to the god who is the friend of Brahman, the treasury of splendors. 1.37.
Salutations again and again to the most excellent one, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who possesses the eternal, unique, and manifold equipment for protecting the world.
Salutations again and again to the sacrificer, to the sacrifice, and to that which is to be sacrificed;
salutations to you, whose self is the fruit of the sacrifice, and who are endowed with sacred study.
Salutations to the Supreme Swan; salutations to you who possess all virtues;
salutations again and again to him who abides in the supreme ether.
Thus praised, the lotus-eyed Lord Rāma,
the deity and sovereign of the world, looked upon me with compassion and spoke.
"O son of Kumbha, for what purpose has Rāma approached Mahendra?
O lord of yogins, you appear as if afraid; from where has this fear come upon you? (1.42)
Neither from Indra nor from Varuṇa, nor even from Brahmā or the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva),
nor even directly from Nārāyaṇa himself, shall you have any fear hereafter.
Whether they be the sons of Vivasvat, or Rākṣasas, or Dānavas along with the serpents—
if they should do anything disagreeable, their fate shall be the battle-axe.
Therefore, remaining as if fearless, speak your business with all haste;
I shall accomplish it this very day, for my vision of you has brought auspicious results.
Thus addressed by the son of Jamadagni, the pot-born sage, filled with fear,
began to speak duly to Rāma of immeasurable splendor.
O God, there is no fear for Brahmā, nor for Viṣṇu, nor for Śaṅkara;
nor even from Jiṣṇu, nor from Yama, nor from Varuṇa, nor even from a Rākṣasa. 1.47.
I have no fear even of the Rākṣasas, nor of the gods, nor of the Asuras;
nor do I have fear from any others today, for I have come here terrified by sin.
Both Vātāpi and Ilvala were Rākṣasas who acted as thorns to the sages;
they were requested by the gods and the great-souled ṛṣis to be slain.
"I have granted them immunity from being slain by those two Rākṣasas;
my mind was already resolved, even though I was subsequently invited by the Rākṣasa. (1.50)
At the śrāddha ceremony for his father, the rākṣasa asked whether it had been successful; I replied, "It was successful," though I myself had become a ball of food within his belly.
Vātāpi was digested by me; then Ilvala became enraged and began to strike me with his fist, but I let out a roar of defiance.
By him the Rākṣasa was consumed, and by him all my ascetic merit was taken away;
distressed by this, I went to the snow-adorned mountain for the sake of penance.
"I was performing most intense austerities when an incorporeal voice said:
'What will you gain by this penance? Be devoted to Rāma. (1.54)
Therefore, rising from my ascetic practice, I have today come to you for refuge; O Blessed One, look upon me with favor, for I am innocent.
Having heard these words, the divine and venerable sage Bhārgava,
the lord, then replied with pleasure to the son of Mitrāvaruṇa.
O Rāma,
for the pleasure of the sages who are like fire and of the gods,
both Vātāpi and Ilvala were destroyed by you through the power of your asceticism.
O sinless one, it was through you that the sages and the gods became free from the thorn of sorrow;
for that purpose, you performed austerities on the slopes of the Himalayas.
O bull among sages, by this very sight of you I have become purified;
you shall not experience the terrible fear of the depletion of your ascetic merit. (59)
And that doubt which existed in your heart, born from the cause of the thunderbolt and the Rākṣasa—
that too, O Pot-born One, dispel by hearing the ritual procedure for the worship of Hari.
What is that system for the worship of Hari by Agastya, and how did that system come to be?
You ought to instruct me on all of this in its entirety, without omission.
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious Bhārgavatantra.
The Second Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said: The Lord Brahmā received that Tantra of inexhaustible extent, which resides in the Supreme Brahman,
measuring one and a half crores [of verses].
The sage Nārada also took half a crore from Brahmā,
and the sage Kapila offered five hundred thousand.
Vainateya also received from Janārdana one hundred thousand verses concerning the feet [of the Lord],
while the serpent [Śeṣa] received twenty thousand verses on the ritual system for the worship of Hari.
The sage Vikhanas accepted forty thousand [girls];
Lakṣmī took sixty thousand, and Vasundharā one hundred thousand.
Śuka [composed] five thousand [verses], Hara one thousand,
and the blessed Parāśara fourteen thousand.
Viṣvaksena also took up two hundred thousand verses of Hari’s work,
and many other eminent sages likewise took as much as they desired.
This scripture of Hari, which is incalculable and filled his belly, I shall now tell to you in brief; by this, you will become purified.
Worship the Lord of Ramā according to that scriptural injunction;
by that, O Pot-born One, all impurity goes to its dissolution.
The remembrance, the chanting of the praises, the worship, the salutation of the feet, the circumambulation, and the sight of Viṣṇu destroy the entire multitude of sins.
Even a single one of these is sufficient for the removal of all sins;
how much more so many? That man who possesses them is indeed Lord Hari himself.
Whatever one desires, if one serves Viṣṇu with devotion and a focused mind, all that comes into the palm of one's hand; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
He who constructs a temple for Viṣṇu shall have Vaikuṇṭha as his abode;
and he who fashions an image of Hari shall attain absorption into Viṣṇu.
He by whom thrones are fashioned moves in a celestial vehicle in heaven;
likewise, he who provides the parasol, the fly-whisk, the throne, the footstool, and the garment [attains that state]. (2.13)
He performs various services for the Lord of Kamalā;
yet he [remains] in that very way in the pure sky, frequented by the immortals.
He who constructs ponds, oblong lakes, wells, tanks, and the like, is attended by the gods and is not defiled by sin. (2.15)
May he who provides armor, weapons, ornaments, garlands, crowns, and the like, be ever peaceful; he is not touched by suffering. (2.16)
And his delightful gardens, the earth garlanded with crops, the assembly hall,
and the beautiful pavilion— all were situated in the highest sky.
He produces various kinds of food offerings— edibles, soft foods, lickables, and drinks— and thereafter he certainly becomes an eater of nectar.
He who performs his duties with joy, without desiring any worldly enjoyment,
shall be dissolved in that very supreme, stainless abode.
O Agastya, he who always sits joyfully meditating on Hari in the abode of the gods shall never again dwell within a mother’s womb.
O Pot-born One, he who, free from desire, gives water to the God of gods,
shall never again drink his mother’s milk.
"He who, full of devotion, fans the Lord of Gods with a palm-leaf fan, shall not be tainted by the three types of suffering; such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures. (2.22)
He who offers incense with devotion does not sink into hell;
he who perfumes the dwelling is not deprived of heaven. (2.23)
And he who gives a garment to Viṣṇu, for him nakedness is no longer spoken of;
he who, having beheld Viṣṇu with joy, attains the state of being in the same world as Him (sālokya). || 2.24 ||
Hari is the object of that meditation for one who lights lamps;
through sweeping and smearing [the temple], sins certainly go to destruction.
Adorning the temple of the Lord with archways, painted friezes, and other decorations,
may he always be adorned in Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Lord.
If one pleases the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and hymns of praise,
He shall always be pleased by all [these means] in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Whoever causes song, dance, and instrumental music— which are dear to Hari— to be performed,
becomes fully satisfied by each of those [acts] in the supreme state.
He whose supreme devotion is unwavering toward the Lord who reclines on the infinite [serpent], whose form is the highest bliss, is a vessel for Brahman.
That man who possesses devotion toward those endowed with devotion to the Blessed One shall become the very life-breath of the Blessed One, and Hari shall become his abode.
Therefore, constantly meditate in your mind upon Vāsudeva, the eternal wielder of the Śārṅga bow; by that, imperishable perfection shall be yours.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Third Chapter.
O venerable Agastya, descendant of Bhṛgu, illustrious one whose form is composed of all auspiciousness! O Lord of the universe, how may one construct the temple of Hari? (3.1)
Śrī Rāma,
having provided abundant water and established groves,
should construct a temple for the deities for the increase of his fame and merit.
Adorning those worlds which are attained through sacrifices and charitable works, one should construct a dwelling for the gods; for both purposes are seen here. (3.3)
In these places— whether natural or man-made, and provided with water and gardens— the deities manifest their presence.
In the lakes, where the sun's rays were warded off by the parasols of lotuses, and where the pure waters were rippled by waves upon which white lilies rested on the shoulders of swans; || 3.5 ||
Resounding with the cries of swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, cranes, and ruddy geese,
where water-fowl rested in the shade of the nicula thickets at the edges.
There, flocks of male and female curlews warbled melodiously, while the sweet notes of kalahamsa geese resounded;
the trees were adorned with blossoming nīra flowers, and the auspicious rows of river confluences graced the landscape.
The rivers, with their banks rising high like sandbanks and laughing with swans,
[shone] upon the grounds at the edges of forests, by the rivers, and near the mountain cascades.
The deities always take delight in cities provided with gardens,
on auspicious mountains, and on the shores of the ocean.
In those hermitages of the sages where Brāhmaṇas always reside,
the gods, headed by Hari, always desire to dwell.
O Pot-born One, wherever the ground may be excellent and pleasing to the gods on earth,
it shall be dear to the deities as well.
A temple of the deity should always be constructed with sixty-four squares;
therein, a central door situated in the middle of the cardinal directions is recommended.
Whatever the width may be, its height should be double that;
the hip should be equal to one-third of the height.
The inner sanctum (garbha) shall be half the width [of the temple], and the other walls shall surround it on all sides. The door shall be one-fourth the width of the sanctum and twice as high.
The branch of the udumbara tree is one-quarter of its height in width;
likewise, the thickness of the two branches is recorded as being equal to the span of the tree.
It is praised for having three, five, seven, or nine branches;
one should place the two *pratihāra* sections at the fourth part from the bottom of the branches.
The remainder [of the ground] one should adorn with auspicious birds, śrīvṛkṣa trees, svastikas, water-jars, pairs of figures, leafy creepers, and images. (3.17)
The image, together with its pedestal (piṇḍikā), shall be eight parts less than the measurement of the door;
there, two parts shall be the image and the third part shall be the pedestal.
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Vimānacchanda, and Nandana;
Samudra, Padma, Garuḍa, Nadīvardhana, and Kuñjara. || 3.19 ||
The Guharāja, the bull, the lion, the sarvatobhadra, and the pitcher;
likewise the swan, the circle, the quadrangle, and the sixteen- and eight-cornered [mandalas]. (3.20)
Thus these twenty temples of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow have been described;
their characteristics are now stated according to the sequence previously mentioned.
Having halved the length and width mentioned previously according to one's wealth, or by means of a fourth part, one should construct everything in accordance with one's resources. || 3.22 ||

The half-maṇḍapa is said to have a length equal to that of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), or increased by one-quarter, or by one-and-a-half [parts], or joined with an increase of three-quarters. || 3.23 ||
The dance-hall (nṛttārdhamaṇḍapa) should be half the size of the [main] pavilion,
equal in width, or twice as large, according to one's desire.
O bull among sages, they know that the first enclosure between these two pavilions, extending thus in length, is named the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala). || 3.25 ||
One should enclose this with a vimāna, or else it may be a half-maṇḍapa;
immediately after that, one should cause a rampart called antarhāra to be constructed.
The third enclosure, called the boundary (maryādā), is described by the Creator;
having installed the primary image within the womb-chamber at the station of Brahmā, it should be consecrated.
Alternatively, one should perform the installation of the *dhruva* (fixed) image in either a temple for the gods (*daiva*) or a human dwelling;
having installed Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the entrance of the sanctum (*garbha*) in their proper order.

At the entrance of the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa), on both sides of the door of the area known as the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala), [one should place] those who have the conch and discus as their preeminent marks.
O bull among sages, both Jaya and Vijaya should be fashioned at the gateway in the abode called Antarhāra, bearing lotuses and maces.
Durjaya and Prabala should be stationed at the two sides of the boundary gate;
now hear of these attendants in the single-walled abode.
The king of birds (Garuḍa) should be fashioned in front of the half-maṇḍapa of the dance hall;
Ravi (the Sun) is [to be placed] in the northern hall of the gate, facing the temple.
On the southern pillar of that very [mandala], Candramas is assigned;
Kāma is in the southeast, Brahmā in the south, and Gajānana should be in the southwest.
One should assign Ṣaṇmukha to the west, Durgā to the northwest, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) to the north, and Śaṅkara along with Kṣetrapāla to the northeast. (3.34)
One should visualize Viṣvaksena in the space between Someśa and [the other deity];
the seven Mothers in the southern courtyard, and Śrī in the southwest (nairṛta).
Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas) are to be worshipped in their respective directions within the courtyard;
there should be an altar for offerings (balipīṭhikā) either inside or outside the gate-tower (gopura).
A distinction is described regarding the abode called Antarhara;
in the places of the sun and the moon, there are the two special forms, Puruṣa and Acyuta.
Likewise, Sūrya and Candramas are to be placed in the second enclosure;
Hayagrīva is to be established in the place of Smara, and Saṅkarṣaṇa in the place of Vidhi.
Varāha is in the place of Vighnarāja; Pradyumna is in the place of Ṣaṇmukha; Ananta should be in the place of Kātyāyanī; and Aniruddha is in the Narāsana seat.
If there is a man-lion (Nṛkesarī) in the courtyard of Śaṃkara or on the pedestals,
Indra and the other deities are to be worshipped in their respective places according to order.

The wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, the wielder of the conch, the wielder of the sword, the bearer of the club, the wielder of the horn-bow, the wielder of the lotus, and likewise the wielder of the thunderbolt— these bearers of divine weapons are to be worshipped.
Those positions which have been proclaimed for the first enclosure should all be known as the retinue in the second enclosure, respectively. (3.42)
In the enclosure of the boundary wall, on both sides of the gateway,
one should install the conch and the discus, the two supreme weapons of the God of gods.
Having installed Upendra at the top of the gateway (gopura),
one should thereafter arrange the Prākṛta and other deities in the sequence beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Upendra, Prākṛta, Puṇya, Puṣkara, Viśvabhāvana, Asuraghna, Kṛtānta, and Bhūtanātha is remembered as the eighth. || 3.45 ||
In the courtyard, at the location of the pedestal, one should arrange Kumuda and the others:
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana. (3.46)
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, Supratiṣṭhita,
Viṣvaksena, Kṣetrapāla, and Khageśvara are then [to be worshipped] in the south-eastern direction.
O Agastya, one should imagine the great pedestal facing the primary object of knowledge,
and right there, the flagstaff of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should designate the place for cooking either in the first enclosure, or in the second enclosure, or even in the third enclosure. || 3.49 ||
The well may be located in the western (Vāruṇa), northern (Saumya), or even the northeastern (Śārva) direction;
or rather, one should construct the well wherever the essence of water is present.
The temple of the God of gods is considered to be of three types: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara;
it is known as the pure Vaiṣṇava Vimāna.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Fourth Chapter.
O Agastya, how is it that an image of Vāsudeva, of Hari, can be fashioned? O Lord, please tell me out of compassion: how many varieties of images (bimba) are there? 4.1.
Having reached the path of the window, those sunbeams which shine—
within them, subtle particles of dust, the ultimate atoms, are drifting.
From eight [successive measures]—an atom, a mote of dust, a hair-tip, a nit, a louse, and a barleycorn—the *mānāṅgula* is obtained; three grains of rice constitute the *mānāntarāṅgula*.
The long interval between the two middle joints of the middle finger of the teacher’s right hand is declared to be a *mātrāṅgula*.
A fist is formed by the remaining fingers excluding the thumb;
one should divide this into four parts, and one such part is known as a *muṣṭyaṅguli*.
Whatever measure of the image there may be, having divided it again into ten parts,
that which is obtained by dividing one part into twelve shall be the *dehalabdha-aṅgula* (the finger-breadth obtained from the body).
The image is of seven kinds: made of jewels, made of stone, made of wood, made of metal, as well as made of clay, made of cloth, and made of painting. (4.7)
The images of Vāsudeva are being described, O Agastya;
therein, first, the representation of his form and its constituent limbs is explained.
He grew in height from head to foot in regular succession,
until he had attained a stature of one hundred finger-breadths from his body.
One should fashion the image according to the measurement of twenty-four [finger-breadths].
The uṣṇīṣa is considered to be one aṅgula, and the hairline (keśānta) is held to be three aṅgulas.
From that [point] to the end of the line of sight, it measures thirty-six *yava*s;
likewise, it should extend to the end of the nostrils, and similarly to the chin. (4.11)
O Lord of Sages, from the hairline to the chin,
the measurement of the face is one hundred and eight barleycorns.
The neck is desired to be one and a half aṅgulas, and the throat three aṅgulas;
this is declared by the mouth, starting from the line of the *hikkā* and ending at the heart. (4.13)
From that point up to the navel, the height is desired to be three and a half finger-breadths;
from that point up to the penis, the height is likewise desired to be the same.
From that base down to the knee, it is three less than thirty finger-breadths (twenty-seven);
the height of the knee-circle is desired to be four finger-breadths. || 4.15 ||
The measurement of the thigh is said to extend from below the knee to the end of the armpit;
its height from there [to the top] is four finger-breadths, ending at the *tāla* [mark].
Whatever measurements are obtained for the body when the ten-tāla system is fully worshipped, those same proportions,
having been divided accordingly, are prescribed for the medium-sized image-ritual.
The face is thirteen finger-breadths [in length], four finger-breadths at three places [the eyes, nose, and mouth],
and the measurement of the thigh is declared to be twenty-six finger-breadths in height.
Likewise, the height of the shanks is equal to the other [thigh];
however, in the case of the inferior ten-tāla measurement, the face is considered to be one hundred yavas.
In the three places [of measurement], it should be exactly that; the thigh is two hundred and sixty-four yavas, and the shank is of equal height; by the primary rule, the rest is considered equal.
The length of the Lord of Kamalā is one hundred and twenty yavas; the big toe (aṅguṣṭha) shall be four [yavas] in measure, and the index finger (tarjanī) shall be equal in length to that.
The middle finger is held to be thirty-one barley-corns in length;
the ring finger should be thirty barley-corns, and the little finger consists of three finger-breadths.
The heels are five *yava*s in length and four *aṅgula*s in width;
from the end of the *hikkā* downward, the upper arm is twenty-seven *aṅgula*s.
Then, from the wrist to the end [of the forearm], it is twenty-six finger-breadths in length;
and from the wrist, the palm is further increased by two barley-corns.
The distance from the middle finger to the end [of the hand] is said to be seven finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
the thumb is five finger-breadths long, and the index finger is likewise extended.
The middle finger is six finger-breadths long;
the index and ring fingers are equal in length, each being six barley-corns longer than [the base of the hand].
The nail is known to be equal in size to the little finger and the thumb, with its fleshy part attached;
the length of the nail is one finger-breadth, while the remaining portion is measured at six barley-corns.
The upabāhu should be like the bāhu, four finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length;
the neck should be four barley-corns (yava) high, and the stalk (nāla) five finger-breadths long.
The penis is five finger-breadths in length, while the scrotum is four finger-breadths;
immediately following that, the forehead has a width of eight and a half finger-breadths.
It is twelve finger-breadths in width and shaped like the crescent moon;
from there, the distance between the two ears is thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
The width of the chin below that [neck] should be ten finger-breadths;
it should be full, measuring two and a quarter finger-breadths, and its shape should be like a bow.
The expansion of the neck should gradually be nine finger-breadths, then one less [eight], and likewise seven and a half finger-breadths at the base, middle, and tip. || 4.32 ||
The distance from the end of the clavicle down to the base of the arms should be forty finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length, and it should be four barley-corns (yava) in width. || 4.33 ||
The width between the armpits is three finger-breadths and twenty-five;
the measurement for the distance between the breasts is eighteen finger-breadths. (4.34)
The middle of the belly is declared to have a width of sixteen finger-breadths;
the hips are eighteen finger-breadths, and the lower abdomen is desired to be [the same]. (4.35)
The width of the hip region is three finger-breadths; the width of the root of the thigh is twenty-five and a half finger-breadths. (4.36)
The tip is desired to be one and a half finger-breadths; the middle is held to be two finger-breadths;
and the width at the base of the liṅga is declared to be two finger-breadths. (4.37)
The base of the scrotum is three finger-breadths wide; the middle part is again one and a half [finger-breadths] wider;
and the tip of the scrotum is measured at thirty-two barley-corns in width.
O Pot-born One, the middle of the thigh should be eleven finger-breadths in width,
and its tip should be ten finger-breadths wide.
The kneecap should be nine finger-breadths [in width], resembling a half-moon together with its base;
the middle part should be nine or eight [finger-breadths], and the top of the shank seven and a half.
The portion of the stalk is broad by four and a half finger-breadths;
the width at the base of the foot is three finger-breadths plus four barley-corns.
The tip of the middle finger is five and a half finger-breadths; the base is six and a half finger-breadths;
and the two arms are seven finger-breadths each.
In the middle and at the tip, it has an equal width; furthermore, the forearm portion is seven and a half [units] wide at the base and five and a half [units] wide at the top.
In the middle, it should be four [finger-breadths] wide; at the tip, it is said to be at the wrist-joint.
Likewise, the palm is recorded as being five finger-breadths plus a half.
The width at the base of the thumb is two finger-breadths; the middle finger is six barley-corns [in thickness]; its tip is considered to be equal to one finger-breadth.
The width at the base of the index finger is measured by nine barleycorns;
the middle [width] is one finger-breadth, and the tip is said to be seven barleycorns.
The base of the middle finger is ten barley-corns; its middle is nine barley-corns;
its tip is said to be one finger-breadth; the other [fingers] are equal to the index finger.
The base [of the ring finger] is eight barley-corns; for the middle [finger], it is exactly seven;
at the tip of the fingers, it is six barley-corns; and the width of the nail is three-quarters of a barley-corn less than the tips of the fingers.
In the center of the palm, there is a line situated at the base of the middle finger;
starting from the base of the little finger, a line extends toward the middle finger.
The middle finger should be measured by the wise starting from the base of the thumb and ending at the tip of the index finger; thus is the middle finger [determined]. 4.50.
And between those two lines,
a line leading to the base of the index finger should be drawn according to the scriptures by a craftsman skilled in the treatises.
The width of the forehead should be three and a quarter finger-breadths;
below that, the two eyebrows should be fashioned, forty barley-corns in length.
In the middle, it is as broad as a barley grain; at the tip of a nit, it is like a bow. The space between those two is nine barley grains wide and eighteen barley grains long.
The length and breadth of the pupil of the eye is said to be one barleycorn (yava);
the white circle (śvetabimba) is one finger-breadth (aṅgula), and the black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) is likewise.
The light is one barley-corn in measure; in its center is a space the size of a barley-corn;
in that center is the measure of a louse, and there again is the sight and the row of eyelashes.
There are eighty eyelashes on the front of the face, which are black;
the distance between the two eyes is two finger-breadths, as is the distance from the middle of the eye to the outer corner. (4.56)
The width of the ear should be forty barley-corns, and its thickness two finger-breadths;
the length of the upper ear shall be three and a half finger-breadths.
The stalk should be five finger-breadths in length, while its width is six barley-corns; subsequently, the rim (pālī) should be four barley-corns wide, fashioned equal to the stalk.
The hollow between Śravaṇa and Pippalī is four barley-corns deep;
it is curved in three places, like the cheek-bowl of a Pippalī-elephant.
The binding consists of a three-finger-width opening, elevated to the level of the eye-thread;
the widths at the base, middle, and tip of the nose are stated in sequence as follows. (4.60)
The base [of the stūpa] should be one finger-breadth, one and a half finger-breadths, two finger-breadths, or two finger-breadths plus four barley-corns high;
the middle part should be raised by one finger-breadth plus that same amount.
The root [of the tube] should be two barley-corns wide, while the tip is excellent at two finger-breadths;
its hollow should be six barley-corns in length, and the middle of its cavity four barley-corns.
The width of the side of the nostril is proclaimed to be two barley-corns;
its height is half a finger-breadth, and the nose [opening] is like a sesame flower.
The upper lip is desired to be four and a half finger-breadths in length;
its width is half a finger-breadth, and its lower part is one and a half finger-breadths in length.
His cheek was broad, and its ridge was as long as a single barleycorn;
his chin measured eighteen barleycorns in both width and length.
The ankle is as high as the toes of the foot and resembles the surface of a mirror;
the two broad parts [of the feet] are equal, like the two canine teeth, measuring four barley-corns.
The thirty-two teeth should be fashioned by the wise according to the scriptures;
the tongue should be six finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths in width.
The neck is marked by three lines; from the line of the hiccups, the position of the breasts is determined.
The circumference [of each breast] is eleven finger-breadths, and the circle of the breast itself is two finger-breadths.
The nipple, situated in the center of the breast-circle, should be four barley-corns [in height];
the navel-cavity is desired to be four barley-corns [deep] and spiraling to the right. (4.69)
The axle is one and a half finger-breadths in circumference and half a finger-breadth in height;
from the crown of the head to the end of the hair at the back is eleven finger-breadths.
From the crown of the head to the edge of the hair on the side, the measurement is twelve finger-breadths;
one should know that the distance between the two ears is fifteen and a half finger-breadths.
At its base, middle, and top parts, the back of the neck is respectively nine and a half finger-breadths wide, and likewise nine finger-breadths.
And below that, there should be the placement of the *kakuda* (the hump), measuring eight [units] in length, height, and width; the end of the *kakuda* should be four *yava*s.
The distance between the two arms at the back should be thirty-six finger-breadths in width,
and the distance between the two armpits should be twenty-six finger-breadths.
O Brahmin, the width of the middle of the back is seventeen finger-breadths;
likewise, the two sides of the hips are twenty-five finger-breadths wide.
The width of the hip region should be twenty-six finger-breadths;
likewise, the middle of the hump at the waist should be thirty-six finger-breadths.
Its height is two finger-breadths; its fullness is one finger-breadth at the middle; the base of the breast is eight finger-breadths, and the middle should be seven finger-breadths. (4.77)
The width at the three points beginning from the base of the thighs should be, in order, the maximum of three finger-breadths,
and then [the next two] should be one and a half and thirteen finger-breadths respectively.
It should be twelve finger-breadths [in height], and likewise twelve finger-breadths [in width];
the knee should have an extent of eight finger-breadths, and [the other part] should be eight and a half finger-breadths.
The width of the middle of the shank is four finger-breadths;
the ankle bone is likewise four finger-breadths, increased by four barley-corns; and the ankle itself is four finger-breadths.
The measurement for the width of all [the hands] is considered to be threefold;
the right hand [of the deity] is either granting fearlessness or bestowing boons. (4.81)
The tip of the hand should be made equal to the line of the breasts;
the distance between those two should measure twelve finger-breadths.
Between the thumb and the forefinger, there should be a lotus with its stalk;
on the palm of the hand, one should draw the shape of a lotus in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
In the primary left hand, which is turned downwards, one should fashion an auspicious mace;
in the two secondary hands, however, one should place the conch and the discus.
An expert in the treatises on the arts may, according to his desire, place various weapons upon the eight arms of the deity.
The crown, earrings, necklaces, the sacrificial thread, the finger-rings, the Kaustubha gem, the forest garland, and the Śrīvatsa on his right breast. (4.86)
One should place upon her lovely armlets and bracelets, a girdle and anklets, as well as fine linen for the lower garment along with an upper robe.
One should apply the ornaments that are appropriate to the place and time, whether he is sitting, lying down, or standing, according to his pleasure. (4.88)
Or one may conceive of the form of Viṣṇu as mounted upon the king of birds;
thus one should install the deity in the inner sanctum at the station of Brahmā.
Alternatively, one should place [the deity] within the divine or human door-line;
thus the wise man should install the deity at the time of consecration.
One should place the eight goddesses, beginning with Śrī, on both sides;
one should arrange the two goddesses, Śrī on the right and Dharā on the left, of the god.
The goddesses Rati, Sarasvatī, and Tuṣṭi are to the right of the god;
Kīrti, Prīti, and Śānti are stationed to his left. (4.92)
One should install [the image] with eight, four, two, or even just one [deity], or perhaps without [any other deities], except for the Lord of the gods of gods, who should be accompanied by Śrīvatsa.
Furthermore, this is the specific distinction in the visualization of the goddesses, Śrī and the others:
their necks are marked with three lines, and the position of their breasts is determined from the line of the *hikkā*.

The circular breast-mound should be eleven finger-breadths in circumference; the nipple, situated in the center of the breast-mound, should be four barley-corns in size and two finger-breadths [in diameter].
The circle of the chest between the breasts is eighteen finger-breadths in extent,
measured exactly as it is with fifteen finger-breadths.
The width and the height [of the shoulders] should be nine finger-breadths;
the distance between the breasts is desired to be twelve finger-breadths.
The extent of the black circle is proclaimed to be two finger-breadths;
the vulva is six finger-breadths in width, and the birth canal is three and a half finger-breadths.
She should adorn her with other garments and ornaments suited to her strength,
or else she may arrange a crown or a braided hair-knot.
When the goddesses are not independent, they have two arms on their respective sides;
when they are independent, they have four arms, or two arms according to one's preference.
The goddess stationed on the right side holds a flower in her right hand;
the goddess stationed on the left side holds a lotus in her left hand.

One who is skilled in the treatises on craftsmanship should fashion the festival image and the *kautuka* image from another [material], having made them equal to one-third of the size of the primary image (*mūlabimba*). 4.102.
The bathing image is also prescribed to be of that same height; likewise the image for the offering of oblations, the portrait for the occasion of lying down and rising, and the festive image.
The ritual image to be fashioned should be the size of a palm tree;
when it is fixed upon the Brahma-section at the Pole Star, there is no further need for the conceptualization of its limbs.
A wise man should fashion the occasional image using the very same proportions as the mundane image;
the mobile image made of metal should be half the size of the permanent image.
With that [disc], the wise one should perform all worldly rites for the gods;
with the disc, there should be the offering of bali and likewise immersion in sacred waters.
In the ritual for worshipping the root-mantra (mūlārcanā) during the Brahma-period, the bed should be prepared with a tuft of grass (kūrca).
Whether it be a divine or human [image] to be installed, one should assign the ritual acts to the Brahma-period.
By that alone, all rites—daily, occasional, and optional—are fulfilled;
likewise, in the practice of standing, walking, or sitting, the fixed image [of the deity] is employed in due order. (4.108)

The ritual image and so forth should be treated in the same manner; however, when the [deity] has gone to sleep in the permanent [image], one may either remain standing or sit as desired, according to one's inclination, regarding the ritual image and the rest.
The image for the perpetual festival should be established everywhere;
and there should be the sixfold images of the ritual actions and so forth, together with Śrī and Bhūmi.

Alternatively, having divided the measurement of the image into three parts, one may fashion the pedestal with one part, [the other two being for the deity] together with Śrī and Bhūmi, or for a single festive marriage-thread ceremony.
The enclosure, provided with the five components such as shoes and so forth, brings comfort;
it may be circular or square, with its length equal to its width.
Having divided the height of the pedestal into three parts, one should fashion a lotus with one part,
provided with twelve or eight petals according to one's preference.
O Agastya, one should fashion either a lotus with petals measuring one-fourth [of the total], or a lotus alone,
or even a pedestal alone.
Whether the image is seated, one should make the pedestal either as wide as it is long, or longer than it is wide;
likewise, the pedestal may be half the size of the image or one-third its size.
One should imagine there a lotus with many petals, endowed with a pericarp and filaments, serving as a support for the hanging feet.
With one leg contracted and the other extended, he should cause the latter to hang downward;
it may be made with three-quarters, or half, of the size of the principal image (mūlabera). || 4.117 ||
Such is the height of the attendants as spoken by Vaikuṇṭha;
the goddess Brahmādyā is equal to the shoulder of Hari, like his own retinue.

Having thus fashioned all the offering pedestals according to the measurement of the *piṇḍikā*, one should arrange the images in the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and perform the ritual placement of the stakes (*kīla*).
Then follows the placement of the jars (kalaśanyāsa), and immediately after that, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Fifth Chapter.
O Blessed One, how indeed should the wise Agastya perform the installation of Viṣṇu? What materials are to be gathered there that are appropriate? Please tell me this. (5.1)
Śrī Rāma should construct the pavilion for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in front of the Prasāda,
either in the first enclosure or even in the second enclosure.
In the third enclosure, or in a suitable location within the site,
one should construct a beautiful square measuring ten *bāhudaṇḍas*.
The most skilled artisan should fashion it with four doors;
in its center, five cubits in size, there shall be a beautiful square.
Or else, it may be built with bricks in a square shape, half the height of a cubit;
one should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) outside of that [altar] at a distance of three palm-lengths.
It should be quadrangular in the east, shaped like a bow in the south,
circular in the west, and possessed of three corners in the north.
A cord measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in both width and length is prepared;
the pit fashioned in the eastern part is prescribed to be square.
The bow should be sixty finger-breadths long, and the bowstring thirty-six finger-breadths;
this shall be the bow-shaped pit (cāpakuṇḍa) on the southern side of the altar-ground.
One should prepare a thirty-two finger-breadth thread tripled [in length];
clearly, a triangle exists to the north of the ground of the altar. || 5.9 ||

If one rotates a cord from the center, the length of which is equal to the number of fingers of the side, this becomes a circular kuṇḍa; in the western quarter, it is the ground for the altar (vedikā).
Having first laid out the lines with twenty-four finger-breadths [of space],
one should dig the ground deeply, leaving a depth of two finger-breadths outside that footprint.
The wise one should construct three Mekhalās with firm bricks;
alternatively, they may be outside the Prakṛti at a measurement of four aṅgulas.
One should construct three tiers for the girdle (mekhalā) using well-baked bricks and make them firm;
the first tier should be one palm (tāla) in measure, and the middle one eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) high.
The final girdle should be exactly four finger-breadths in measure;
one should fashion the yoni on the western or the southern side.
It should be as long as the number of fingers in a fortnight, resembling the shape of a trumpet,
narrow at the base and broad at the top, depressed in the middle, with its head resting on the ground.
One should fashion [the sacrificial ground] so that it appears like the leaf of an aśvattha tree for each pit;
however, for one seeking liberation, there should be no womb [altar], nor should the pit have only a single girdle.
One should construct a water-shed provided with four gates,
enriched with a central altar and sacrificial pits, and a bathing pavilion in the northeast.
One should prepare a well-guarded plot of ground for planting the sprouts,
and solid curtains should be hung according to the prescribed rule.
In the bathing pavilion, there should be an altar measuring two or three cubits,
and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be fashioned with faces made of plantain leaves and flowers.
On the tip of the needle was the face of a boar, a stream of ghee was its dwelling place, and its mouth held a vessel of clarified butter;
yet the face of the boar was not upon the sacrificial ladle.
Below the mouth, one should fashion the throat and both extended arm-staffs;
at the base of these two, one should likewise fashion either a bulbous root (kanda) or a lotus.
O Agastya, one should fashion four archways provided with three spikes each, and devoid of branches at the bottom.
One should fashion it with a length of twenty-two finger-breadths, a width of half that,
and a thickness of half again, making it eight finger-breadths thick.
One should prepare a bathing pedestal proportionate to the size of the image,
as well as seats for the officiating priests, the worshippers, and the preceptor.
The two sandals should be shaped like feet; everything should be made from sacrificial wood.
[One should depict] the Śrīvatsa, the full pitcher, the kettledrum, and the circular mirror.
O son of Kaśyapa, one should likewise draw a pair of fish, a conch, and a discus—
each of these eight being drawn individually— in the diagram of the eight auspicious signs.
One should draw the shape of a tortoise upon those respective seats for the officiants;
these eight banners are white, red, yellow, and blue.
The great jars, the subsidiary jars, the water-pots, and likewise the water-vessels; the pitchers also should be brought together, as well as the lamp-stands and clarified butter.
Oil and lamp-vessels, wicks of excellent quality,
fragrant sandalwood, and sweet-smelling flowers.
And garments of fine silk, woolen blankets, and beautiful tiger skins and black antelope skins, all unworn. 5.30.
Fuel-sticks, *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, grains, bedding and seating, a pillow for the head, mouthfuls of water, a cotton mattress, and a jeweled blanket. (5.31)
Various kinds of grain and various kinds of jewels,
the seven metals beginning with gold, and beautiful cows together with their calves.
Incense substances such as camphor, ghanasāra, and guggulu; betel, areca nut, garlands, and necklaces made of flowers. || 5.33 ||
Fruits, nectar, milk, curd, sugar, molasses, and two golden probes—this was the complete collection of materials for the eyes. (5.34)
An image of a water-pot, five ornaments, a bracelet,
a frying pan, a water-tub, and golden lotuses.
There were also threads, as well as pots, bowls, jars, and the like;
common shallow dishes and even auspicious earthenware vessels.
There were also beautiful maidens, lovely and well-adorned,
along with incense burners, lamp vessels, bells, camphor, and lotuses.

The vessel for water for the feet and the vessel for sipping water are called *arghya*; there is the vessel for invocation, the vessel for the food offering (*naivedya*), the vessel for drinking water, and the receiving vessel. (5.38)
The sandals, the mirror, the golden comb, the vessel for the lamp, and the containers for the waving of lights, the collyrium, and the offering of oblations. || 5.39 ||
A fan, a parasol, a chowrie, a flower-basket, baskets, a spade, dried cow-dung, and a heap of wood. || 5.40 ||
Today, the sacrificial vessel, the stirring-ladle, the bellows, and the fans;
the vessel for clarified butter, the cooking-pot, the *praṇītā* water-vessel, and likewise the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel. || 5.41 ||
The eight articles for the binding ceremony included a plow made of gold,
a full amount of wealth as a sacrificial fee, and various kinds of musical instruments.
There were beautiful courtesans skilled in dance and song,
and Brahmins proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who were absorbed in the Blessed One.
The sacred seat for the deity’s procession and various vehicles as well;
diverse torches held in the hands, and the auspicious, rutting elephant.
The ritual threads and the sacrificial pins must also be prepared for the performance of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Bhārgava-tantra.
The Sixth Chapter.
What is the nature of the consecration, O Brahmin, and what is the nature of one who has been consecrated?
What indeed is the auspicious time for the consecration of all embodied beings? (6.1)
O Lord, what kind of qualified person is required, or how is this concluded?
Please tell me out of compassion, O Master, regarding the supreme abode of Jamadagni.
Śrī Rāma,
endowed with supreme faith, possessed of a virtuous heart,
a believer in the Lord of the gods of gods, and himself a sovereign, has fixed his mind [upon Him]. (6.3)
Immeasurable wealth, grain, and energy—these three dwell there incessantly; he shall be the one who establishes them.
One who is pure, skillful, grateful toward the lineages of gurus,
and does not delay in performing duties— he alone should undertake the ritual action.
Whether he belongs to one of the four castes or is of mixed origin, accompanied by all his kinsmen and placing the preceptor at the forefront, he should accomplish the consecration through him.
One who knows the Pāñcarātra, who is tranquil, skilled in all philosophical systems, free from desire, having conquered the pairs of opposites, and devoid of all defects. (6.7)
He was of upright intellect, always devoted solely to the meditation on Brahman, auspicious,
belonging to the first caste, a devotee of the Lord, and entirely dedicated to Nārāyaṇa.
A wise person should first carefully choose a preceptor for the office of Ācārya in rites such as the installation festival and the performance of expiatory ceremonies.
Then, that wise man should choose sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij), or eight, or four, or three, or two, from among those very same gurus.
In the absence of officiating priests,
the preceptor alone should complete the sacrifice according to the rules of a single-day ritual, O Pot-born One.
The forest-dweller and the ascetic, as well as the other three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa—
all these are not entitled [to this], being devoid of the five purificatory rites.
Neither the Kuṇḍas nor the Golakas shall be considered born in the natural order;
they are not entitled to perform sacred rites, for by birth alone they do not possess the status of being born from the Brahmin womb.
Even one who is physically impaired may be qualified for the status of a Guru, provided he possesses weightiness through knowledge;
having thus reflected upon everything, one should first choose a teacher.
At the commencement of the rite, the patron should cause a cow, land, gold,
and a coconut to be given to the preceptor.
Now I shall speak of the time for consecration; listen, O lord of sages!
The northern solstice is declared the primary [time], while the southern solstice is the inferior.
In the consecration of a permanent image (dhruvabera), the primary method of installation is best;
that of the ritual images (karmabimba) is inferior and never leads to any fault.
In performing a consecration ceremony, one should avoid the four months of the ancestors;
in all other months, however, one may have it performed without hesitation.
One should avoid, in every respect, the month during which there is an eclipse, as well as the childhood of Mercury and the infatuation of Jupiter and Venus.
Or else, one should avoid the fortnight, as well as the period before and after it; a cloudy day, the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti), and the intercalary month known as *mala*.
One should avoid in every way the Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa yogas;
one should also avoid Sundays, Tuesdays, Saturdays, and the Viṣṭi karana.
The days of the new moon, the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī), Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, and all the constellations associated with fierce deities should be avoided with great effort.
One should avoid the first three asterisms, as well as Maghā, which are censured by the ancestors; and Āśleṣā, Svātī, Citrā, Śraviṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj. (6.23)
The wise should select a site that is neither too high nor too low, but level;
it should be free from conjunctions with malefic aspects and not occupied by a planet in the eighth house.
If that ascendant in the tenth house is conjoined with malefic planets,
the preceptor, having thoroughly examined this together with the astrologers, should avoid it.
Having observed the abundance of virtues and the collection of qualities through the scriptures,
one should act in accordance with the inclinations of the patron, the village, and the local inhabitants.
Having determined such an auspicious day with the best of the twice-born,
the preceptor, who knows the essence of the scriptures, should begin the installation.
For that purpose, the sacrificer, the officiating priests, and the supreme preceptor should bathe and undergo the rite of shaving at an auspicious and favorable time.
Having bathed, wearing clean garments, and adorned with all ornaments,
they summoned the chariot-maker, the potter, and other artisans.
Having gratified those teachers and dismissed them, as well as the artisans,
he had the artisans open the eyes of the ritual images according to the prescribed rule.
Having gratified them with wealth, garments, and things that gladden the mind,
one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited for the sake of complete purification.
On ground smeared with cow dung and adorned with colored powders and offerings,
one should place a water-pot filled with grain, wrapped with thread, upon a pedestal of grain.
Having invoked the Lord of Śrī there, [upon a seat] rich with reeds, kusha grass, and leaves,
he should worship Him with unbroken rice and other offerings, using both the Gāyatrī and the Vaiṣṇavī mantras.
The officiating priests, having recited the *abliṅga* purificatory mantras, the *pavamāna* verses, the purifying formulas,
and the peace-mantras, as well as the *vyāhṛti-vidyā*, [performed the rite].
Having washed the pedestal with auspicious waters brought for the image, one should sprinkle it for the sake of the sprouts and then perform the collection of the earth.
Having washed his feet up to the knees and his hands up to the wrists,
and having sipped water three times, he should adorn himself with tilaka marks made of clay and wear the sacred grass ring.
Having purified both the basket and the spade with auspicious waters,
he first adorned the spade with garments, perfumes, and garlands.
Then either the officiating priest or the attendant should carry him on his head, while Brāhmaṇas recite the Śākuna Sūkta and auspicious musical instruments are played. || 6.38 ||
Accompanied by the lamps of his arms and the pure requisites for worship,
he took refuge in an auspicious spot in either the eastern or the northern direction.
Seated and facing the east, the preceptor,
having restrained his breath and purified the collection of elements, should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited.
One should sprinkle the ground, as well as the spade and the basket, with the *vyāhṛtis*;
one should have the officiating priests consecrate the earth with the *Bhūmisūkta*.
The Guru should meditate upon the Goddess Earth, who is clothed by the ocean, adorned with mountains for breasts, pregnant with jewels, and rich with crops. (6.42)

Having invoked the Earth with the Earth-mantra, one should worship the Earth upon the ground with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), as well as with perfumes and various kinds of flowers.
With incense, lamps, and various food offerings pleasing to the palate,
one should praise with hymns the Goddess Earth, who is adorned with jewels.
O bearer of all beings, O beloved, O you who are saluted by all the worlds;
O wife of Viṣṇu, O sustainer of the universe, O Earth, O you who are garlanded with crops!
O Goddess, rich with the hair of the forest of merit, adorned with the breasts of mountains, clothed by the ocean, and dwelling in the region of rivers! 6.46
O Goddess who dwells in the anthill, who speaks the Vedas, who is served by the sacred scriptures, whose eyes are like blooming lotuses—be gracious, O beloved of Hari! 6.47
Salutations to you, O Mistress of the World; salutations to you, who are worshipped by all the gods.
Salutations to you, O Bhārgavī, my mother; I am prostrate before you, O Vasundharā.
O Maheśvarī, O Earth, who have arisen from the power of Viṣṇu, who are conch-white in color and strewn with many jewels, salutations, salutations to you!
Having thus praised, bowed, and meditated with a pure mind,
the supreme teacher [used] the mantra "Aśvakrāntā" and a spade.
Facing the east, he should take up all the clay with the *kroḍa-vidyā* mantra;
he should place that clay in a basket made of bamboo using the root mantra.
Having covered it with a new cloth while reciting the Astra-mantra, the preceptor himself,
together with Brahmins who recite auspicious prayers, takes it upon his own head.
Accompanied by various other auspicious rites, the preceptor should enter the temple;
having circumambulated the sacred abode, he proceeds to the pavilion for the offering of sprouts.
Thereafter, the patron should likewise honor that clay,
as well as the preceptor and the officiating priests, with garments, perfumes, flowers, and ornaments for the five limbs.
O Lotus-born One, this fivefold ornament consisting of the necklace, the sacred thread, the bracelets, the armlets, and the finger-rings has thus been described.

Then, having properly adorned them on the ground where the seedlings are to be planted and having had the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited, one should sprinkle the *pālikā* vessels and the other items.
Having taken twelve small pots and tied their necks with grass and other materials,
he then filled them with clay and placed them on the ground prepared for sowing seeds.
Having approached a seat that has been smeared with cow dung and adorned with colored garlands,
one should prepare a pedestal there filled with grain.
One should likewise lay down five threads extending eastward and five extending crosswise, forming sixteen squares; in the center of this, there are four squares.
Having swept the area around the site of the *pālikās* with a water-pot, one should perform the installation of the *pālikās* using the very mantra of the *puruṣasūkta*. (6.60)
Having adorned the water-pot with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice,
and in due order with threads, cloths, a shallow dish, and a tuft of grass.
Having arranged the sprouting grains— wheat, rice, *sāḍhakī*,
mung beans along with chickpeas, kidney beans, and likewise sesame seeds— (6.62).
One should bring these nine grains— black gram and horse gram—
and having washed them, one should bathe them with cow’s milk while reciting the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī.
Having invoked Brahmā with the mantra "Ṛtaṃ satya," one should worship him;
then, having filled the Soma-vessel with scented water and precious gems, [one should proceed].
One should invoke and worship Soma with the mantra "sante payāṃsi";
one should perform the invocation of Viṣṇu in twelve *pālikā* vessels. (6.65)
"His vastness," "Pratadviṣṇu," "Whose vastness," and both the following [verses], "He strode across," "The firm ones are his," "Three times the god," and "He has pervaded. (6.66)
Then, with the mantras "ato devā" and "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should [place the vessels] in order within the earthen bowls containing kuśa grass,
starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Having invoked [the deity] and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should thereafter prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the eastern side of the altar of the earthen vessels (pālikā).

Having properly prepared the fire according to the rules, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the mantra "sante payāṃsi," and then collect the residual drops (sampāta).
Having offered the final oblation with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," the preceptor should sprinkle the seed-vessel and the small pots with the residual clarified butter.
Having again worshipped the Moon in the water-pot and offered oblations,
one should perform the sowing of the seed with the twelve-syllable mantra.
The preceptor or the other officiating priests should sow the seed silently;
thereafter, he should cover it with earth while reciting the mantra beginning with "mūrdhānam."
"May Varuṇa sprinkle this for me with milk," he thought;
thus, he joyfully kept the lamp burning day and night without extinguishing it. (6.73)
One should perform the daily worship of the water-jar until the ritual is completed;
one should carry out the propitiation of the *pālikās* and offer oblations morning and evening.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Seventh Chapter.
Having thus offered the sprouts, Rāma should perform the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) for the purification of the palaces, pavilions, and the surrounding walls. || 7.1 ||
For the pacification of all defects and for the sake of completing the rite being performed without obstacles, the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) is highly recommended.
Having fashioned an image of the Lord of the Site out of kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and other blades of grass, complete in all its limbs, and having adorned it with cloth and ornaments. || 7.3 ||
Having also adorned [the deity] with flowers on the ground to the south of the pavilion,
one should prepare a seat made of seven blades of darbha grass and place it upon the chest.

Having sprinkled [the site] with the waters of the Puṇyāha rite, the preceptor should invoke the Lord of the Site (Vāstvīśa) upon the sacrificial mound using the eight-syllable mantra of the Lord of the Site, and then worship the Master of the Site.
With the mantra "asunīte," one should establish the vital breath (prāṇa),
[honoring it] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), as well as fragrances, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having worshipped according to the scriptures with incenses, lamps, food offerings, and betel-leaf accompanied by perfumes, and having gratified [the deity] according to one's wealth.
In the western direction, one should offer oblations into the fire for the Lord of the Site;
with the five Upaniṣadic mantras, one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter.
With fuel-sticks of *śamī*, *apāmārga*, and *khadira* wood, respectively,
he should offer eight oblations each, separately, with the root mantra of the Lord of the Site (*vāstvīśa*).
One should also offer oblations into the fire with the four *ṛc* verses beginning with "vāstospate pratīhi," using sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and then [offer] from the root-mantra of Vāstvīśa.
One should again offer oblations with clarified butter one hundred and eight times;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Vedic verse "idaṃ viṣṇu," [the rite is complete].

Having burned the effigy of the site with the verse beginning "parivāja," and having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire, [he should abandon] that dwelling, such as the pavilion and so forth.
One should set aside the remaining portion of the site in the northeast direction of the village;
then, having bathed according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the sprinkling with the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) mantra.
For the sake of removing the sins associated with the decrease or increase of measures such as the māna, unmāna, and māṇa,
one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the images, the rows [of deities], and the pedestals.
Having placed the images upon the pedestal and washed them with auspicious waters,
one should likewise smear the pedestals and the sanctuaries with cow dung and other substances.
Having established a fire in front of the images with *samī* leaves,
he performed one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*) accompanied by unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
At the conclusion of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the ritual attendance upon the fire (vahnyupasthāna):
"Salutations to you, the Blessed One, whose nature is Jātavedas."
To Nārāyaṇa, the priest of the sacrificial offerings for gods and ancestors respectively,
the one to whom the deities are to be sacrificed, the Self, the Supreme Self.
"O Lord, remain for a long time within this image for our welfare.
Having thus offered worship, the wise one should perform the ritual of pure bathing. 7.19.
In front of the images, one should place a water-pot upon a seat made of grain,
its entire body wrapped with thread and adorned with perfumes, garments, and other ornaments.
Filled with two āḍhakas of cow’s ghee, provided with a tuft of hair and a sprout, and covered with a shallow earthen bowl (śarāva). || 7.21 ||
Having established [the image], performed the rite for an auspicious day, and sprinkled it according to the rules,
he should invoke Vāsudeva with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, up to the offering of food (naivedya) in due order,
one should perform the ceremonial bath with ghee while reciting the mantra "ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe."
One should bathe [the deity] with warm water while reciting the mantra "mānastoke";
then, one should adorn all the images with new garments.
Adorned with ornaments, perfumes, and garlands, according to the rules and according to his wealth,
he should perform the ritual immersion in water in a river or similar body of auspicious water.

For those [images] that are unfit for immersion in water—namely those made of the three substances (wood, clay, or cloth), or those that are painted, or those on cloth, or those that are heavy such as stone and so forth—[one should perform the preliminary consecration]. 7.26.

One who knows the essence of the *Pratiṣṭhā-tantra* should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) in the shade, having drawn out a large quantity of water into a wooden trough or a cauldron. (7.27)
Having cast it into a heap of grain and perfumed it with fragrances,
one should invoke the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā there and worship them.
One should place a seat (kūrca) made of twenty-eight blades of darbha grass there;
having invoked the deity therein and worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
There, the master who knows the tantra should recollect the sequence of withdrawal;
having displayed the wheel-mudrā, he should perform the worship of the protection-vase.
Then, at the side of that granary, he placed nine jars filled with water,
adorned with ornaments, containing water-pots, gems, and iron.
Having installed Brahmā in the center and Āyudheśvara in the water-pot (karaka),
the wise man should worship the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, in the other jars.
One should wrap all the limbs of the image with a new cloth;
then, the wise man should scatter white mustard seeds while reciting the mantra beginning with "rakṣohaṇa."
For the goddesses, Śrī and the others, [the seat is made] with twenty-three *kuśa* blades;
for Rudra Parameṣṭhin, it is with twenty-five *darbha* blades.
One should prepare a seat of kuśa grass with twenty-two blades for those who subsist on other nectars;
then, having placed the images upon a vehicle accompanied by Vedic musical instruments, [one proceeds].
Accompanied by all auspicious rites, he should lead [the image] to the riverbank;
having set it down on the bank of the river or similar water and sprinkled it with the water of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), [he should proceed]. || 7.36 ||
One should dry it with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, burn it with the mantra of Fire,
flood it with the syllable of Amṛta, and having invoked Gaṅgā, one should worship her.
In this way, having cast the seat into the pure river water and having prepared the yoga-seat, one should place the image there with its head facing east.
Having worshipped [the deity], one should cause [the image] to lie down; then one should contemplate the withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Having displayed the wheel-mudrā (cakramudrā), one should then proceed as before on the riverbank.
One should perform the worship of the protective jars and scatter white mustard seeds in the cardinal directions;
one should also set up radiant lamps that do not go out.
One should cause the three Vedas to be recited by Brahmins who have mastered them;
however, one should not perform actions such as bathing or drinking in that water.
And they should cause various musical instruments to resound on all sides,
for three nights, or one night, or even for a watch or a moment.

In the absence of a river or similar body of water, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in a cauldron or a wooden water-tub; this is the method for the preliminary consecration of the images.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Eighth Chapter.
Having prepared the sacrificial pavilion, the preceptor, together with the patron,
should wrap the pillars in that pavilion with new cloths.
One should spread out canopies of beautiful cloths and adorn [the area] with banners,
strings of pearls, and other items such as plantain trees and betel-nut trees.
One should adorn the entire pavilion with garlands of *darbha* grass accompanied by fruits, and with ornaments of jewels and gold, and one should fasten archways (*toraṇas*) all around.
Having dug the ground to a depth of two *tālas* at each gate, one should establish fourteen [objects] and also fasten banners starting from the east.
Having fashioned [seats] from the aśvattha, udumbara, vaṭa, and plakṣa trees respectively,
and having decorated them as they appeared, he lit lamps on all sides.
When the afternoon had arrived and the appointed time had passed,
he raised the images from the water, as well as from the jars and the pitchers.
Having dismissed all the deities from the images onto a seat by the bank,
the preceptor should place them facing eastward and wash them with pure waters.
The wise man, having adorned metal images with garments, ornaments, flowers, and other offerings, [should bathe them] with water from tamarind fruits. || 8.8 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon a vehicle, accompanied by the foremost of Brahmins and auspicious sounds such as the chanting of the Vedas,
one should lead [the deity] around the temple in a clockwise direction toward the sacrificial pavilion.
One should place the image upon the northern seat facing the east;
then, having lifted the grass-bushes (kūrca), one should transfer that power into the image.
One should dismiss all the deities from the jars as before;
then, one should perform the opening of the eyes of the images according to the prescribed rule.
One should place a pair of vessels, one golden and one silver, along with a pair of rods— one of silver and one of gold— upon a heap of grain.
One should place a golden vessel in the eastern direction and a silver one in the west;
and all around, eight jars filled with chickpeas.
One should establish [the image], recite [the scriptures] afterwards, perform the *puṇyāha* rite, and also sprinkle it with water;
one should invoke [the deity] into the honey-pitcher with the verse beginning "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari. (8.14)

The others [the officiants] should worship the Sun and the Moon with the mantra "Somo dhenuḥ," using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; they should prepare two vessels, each equipped with a stirring rod.
With the "three honeys," honey indeed, and ghee with the words "O Sovereign," and eight beautiful, charming cows with their calves; || 8.16 ||
Then, having placed it at his side, the Guru should cause the sound of the Three Vedas to resound,
using a golden rod with its tip smeared with honey.
Having opened the right eye with a ghee-soaked wick, the sage [prescribes] the opening of the left eye with a wick held from the south to the north. 8.18.
The two mantras "citraṃ devā" and "tac cakṣuḥ" are prescribed;
having thus opened both eyes, one should discard the covering cloth. (8.19)
The best of guides should present to the deity makaranda, clarified butter, chickpeas, young girls, and cows with their calves. (8.20)
In this manner, the eyes of all the images are opened;
however, during the bathing, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), and the ritual washing, the *kautuka* thread must be held in the hand.
I shall now describe the procedure for the consecration of images, as well as for the preceptor and the officiating priests; listen to this, O Pot-born One (Agastya). 8.22.
The protective cord (pratisara) should be made of gold, silk, or cotton, according to one's means, and should consist of seven or five threads.
One should fashion the marriage-thread (kautuka) with gold weighing one niṣka,
[placing it] upon a lotus filled with rice grains and adorned with betel leaves.
Adorned with fruits such as plantains and coconuts,
one should lay out the lines there and sprinkle them with water from the *puṇyāha* rite.
Having invoked Sudarśana, the king of weapons, there, one should worship him;
[this is done] by consecrating [the object] seven times with the six-syllable mantra of Sudarśana.
With the thumb and ring finger, one should properly smear the protective amulet with sandalwood powder and water while reciting the Aparājita-vidyā.
With the root mantra, one should tie the auspicious marriage-thread on the right hand of the god;
for the goddesses, such as Śrī and others, it should be tied on the left hand.

In the rite of offering the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), the teacher and the guardians of the image should place the marriage-thread (kautuka) on the right hand, by which the initiation (dīkṣā) is successfully accomplished.
O Lord of Sages, for the binding of the gods and goddesses, or others,
one's own respective vidyā-mantra alone is used for the consecration of the wheel-mantras.
The binding of the Guru's wrist-ornament is performed with the mantra "viśvetātā," as is the consecration of all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) by the one who acts as the Brahmā priest.
With the mantra "vṛhatsāma," one should protect them with incense and ashes;
having prostrated before the lotus-eyed Lord with the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Having placed the images upon the bathing pedestal, the supreme guru should then set down seventeen water-pots upon a pedestal of grain.
A jar of ghee at the Brahma-pada, warm water when the lord of heaven (Indra) is presiding;
fruit-water at the Yama-pada, and bathing water in the direction of Varuṇa.
In the north (Saumya) there is Akṣatāmbu; in the southeast (Vahni), Maṇijīvana;
in the southwest (Yātudhāna), Lohatīrtha; and in the northwest (Māruta), Gandhatīrtha.
In the northeast, one should place unbroken grains and barley; in the east, the water for the feet;
in the southern quarter, the water for the guest-offering (arghya);
in the western direction, the water for sipping (ācamana); in the north, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); and in the southeast and southwest, curd and milk respectively.
In Māruta, Madhu, and Bhūteśa, the preparation is with water mixed with ochre dye. || 8.37 ||
Having performed the invocation of the deities eight times with their respective names,
one should offer oblations into the fire and sprinkle the residue (sampāta) there.
The mantra for the Vaiṣṇava rite is the Puruṣasūkta, and the consecration is performed with the Puṃsūkta;
the mantra for the jar of clarified butter is considered to be the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī.
One should cause [the deity] to lie down in the center of the altar, which is prepared with rice grains;
having placed [the image] upon a couch strewn with sesame seeds and adorned with a black antelope skin.
Having placed there a mattress adorned with a jeweled blanket,
one should arrange linen, variegated cloth, and bolsters.
And likewise, one should perfume the pillow with fragrant substances,
using the most purifying mantras beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
The preceptor should cause the Lord of the gods, together with his limbs, to lie down with his head toward the south;
he should cover the image with blankets and fine silk cloths.
In each of the eight directions, one should place eight jars wrapped in thread and cloth,
provided with tufts of grass and sprouts, containing gems and mixed with gold.
Wrapped in two pieces of cloth, or else in a single one together,
and filled with scented water, they should be placed upon a pedestal of grain.
Above the rice grains of the śālī variety, there should be sesame;
this grain-pedestal, enriched with cloth interspersed between the layers, is so described.
One should place a golden image of each respective [deity] there;
one should arrange auspicious objects in the spaces between the jars.
