Having covered it with a reed-mat and decorated the great jar in the west with coconuts and other fruits as appropriate, [he should proceed].
It should be joined with a golden handle, endowed with the nine gems,
provided with all metals, furnished with all perfumes, and accompanied by a tuft of grass.
It should be joined with a leaf-covering, provided with a primary image,
its entire body wrapped in thread, and containing a citron fruit within.
One should place [the vessel] with its bowl upon a grain-seat on the altar;
one should adorn it especially and wrap it with a pair of cloths.
On its right side, one should place a water-pot (karaka) of the same kind;
on both sides of the archways, one should set down two door-jars (dvārakumbha).
One should decorate [the site] as appropriate and fill it with scented water;
one should also fill the great pitcher (mahākumbha) and the small vessel (karaka) with scented waters.
Having thus made his arrangements, the wise king, while the sound of the Vedas was being intoned and the clamor of musical instruments rose up in great excitement, [proceeded].
One should invoke the eternal Vāsudeva into the great pitcher.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma [was present] amidst the quarters of the sky adorned with the sounds of musical instruments emitting deep resonant notes,
while the flocks of birds were endowed with cheerful countenances.
While the women were joyful and skilled in uttering auspicious greetings, and while the lunar orb was auspicious with its moonlight in the cloudless sky; (9.2)

One should perform the invocation of the pitcher at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction, when the mind of the preceptor is pure, free from impurity, and pleasant to touch like a fragrant breeze.
He should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited together with Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas;
he should sprinkle all the jars, the sacrificial materials, and the archways.
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga).
On the eastern archway (toraṇa), Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka, is to be worshipped.
There, between the two banners, the preceptor should wrap [the thread] around both sides;
he should worship Kumuda and Kumudākṣa in their respective order from east to west.
There, one should worship the two jars with full water-vessels;
likewise, one should worship Dharmarāja at the southern archway and at the two banners.
Puṇḍarīka and Vāmana are on both the jars;
Ānanda and Nandana are both to be worshipped in their respective order.
At the western archway, one should also worship the god Varuṇa;
on the two sides of the banner, the two deities Śaṅku and Śrutisunetraka.
One should worship Vīrasena and Suṣeṇa at the two jars,
and Soma at the northern archway, upon those two tied-up banners.
One should worship the two deities Sumukha and Supratiṣṭha, as well as Sambhava and Prabhava, upon the two jars; there are three banners starting from the south.
O Agastya, they were fashioned as yellow, blue, and white;
the Ṛgveda was placed in the east, the Yajurveda in the south, and that named Sāmaveda in the west.
Likewise, the best of Brahmins should cause the Atharvaveda to be recited in the north;
however, in every case, the invocation must be preceded by the Yogapīṭha.
One should perform the invocation (āvāhana) for the images that have been laid down, even though jars have been placed all around them, proceeding in the direction starting from the east.
With the eight verses beginning with "tadasya," which constitute the Viṣṇu-sūkta, the worship of the eight forms of Viṣṇu and the others is performed in their respective order.
Then, having invoked the eternal Supreme Self, Vāsudeva,
into the great pitcher by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, || 9.16 ||
And having invoked Sudarśana, who resembles a thousand suns,
into the water-pot, the wise one should worship him with the arghya and other offerings using his respective mantra.
The water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), as well as the water for sipping (ācamana), the bath-water, the garment, and the sacred thread;
perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, worship, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and hymns of praise. || 9.18 ||
The food offering consists of excellent rice and other delicacies, along with betel leaf and fragrant substances;
at the conclusion, there is the waving of lights (nīrājana), hymns of praise, prostration, and circumambulation.
Having thus completed that worship, one should then honor the fire in the sacrificial pit;
one should perform oblations with fuel-sticks, sacrificial porridges, clarified butter, and seed-syllables.
Agastya said:
O Rāma, Rāma, Lord of the World, Vāsudeva, Eternal One!
Tell me, O All-pervading Lord, out of your compassion, how one should meditate upon Vāsudeva.
Śrī Rāma [beheld] Vāsudeva— the unborn, the peaceful, resembling ten million suns, moons, and fires;
possessing many hands and feet, and many eyes, heads, and faces.
Transcending the senses and beyond all bounds, bearing a most wondrous form,
he illuminated all directions with masses of radiance streaming forth from his body.
The god was endowed with many ornaments, adorned with various weapons,
composed of diverse colors, and possessed a naturally fragrant form.
He, whose majesty is inconceivable, is praised by the sages beginning with Marīci, by the deities beginning with Brahmā, and by Lakṣmī and others.
Who in this world is capable of meditating upon him, or who on earth is capable of praising him?
Nevertheless, [I shall praise] the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Four-armed and of noble form, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, he was adorned with a crown, necklaces, bracelets, a girdle, and earrings. 9.27
Bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, a pure sacrificial thread, and finger-rings;
wearing divine yellow garments and jingling anklets.
It was also attended by eight goddesses with palms joined in reverence,
and served by Viṣvaksena, the lord of birds, along with their retinues.
With a most serene countenance, the child, radiant with a tilaka mark,
sits bestowing fearlessness upon the auspicious seat of Śeṣa’s coils.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with various garlands;
with a smile that surpassed the moonlight, his eyes were like blue lotuses.
He was a great being with a neck like a conch shell, adorned by full and elevated shoulders, and possessed of a broad,
smooth, and very glossy chest that was high, full, and expansive.
With a full belly and a sunken navel, her broad hips were bent under their weight;
she was marked by the beauty of her thighs, which formed a pair that surpassed the splendor of a column of light.
His pair of feet surpassed the blooming lotuses,
and with the rays emanating from his big-toe nails, they outshone the sun.
Having thus meditated upon Vāsudeva, who holds weapons in his broad hands that reach down to his knees, one should perform the rite of invocation.
Having sprinkled with clarified butter either fire churned from wood or ordinary fire while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra, [one should proceed]. 9.36.

One should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) around the sacrificial pits using handfuls of darbha grass, having properly kindled the flame with the verse beginning, "He who goes around. (9.37)
One should consecrate the blazing fire of Jātavedas in the western pit;
then, one should bring it from the western pit into the pits starting from the east.
One should arrange the yoga-pīṭha within the fire-pits in the midst of the fire;
Vāsudeva in the northeast, and likewise Saṅkarṣaṇa in the south.
Having thus invoked Pradyumna in the Varuṇa-pitcher and Aniruddha in the northern spot,
one should then worship the Lord of Gods with clarified butter.
Four sacrificial fuels (samidh) are prescribed in order, starting from the east:
the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Bilva, Udumbara, and Bhūruha trees.
If [the specific wood] is unavailable, the *pālāśa* alone is recommended for all sacrificial pits;
likewise, milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, and food with jaggery are prescribed in their respective order.
The sacrificial oblations (carus) in the fire-pits starting from the east are prescribed as being made with turmeric-rice;
alternatively, one may prepare them with milk-rice (pāyasa) or even with pure (śuddha) rice.
Sesame, rice, barley, bamboo, and seeds [are used] in the fire-oblation in their respective order;
or, if seeds are unavailable, one should perform the rite with sesame seeds in all the sacrificial pits.

The homa offerings in the fires of the east and other directions should be performed by the guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ) with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva, using sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice (caru), and seeds.
O Pot-born One, there shall be one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity];
thus, while the officiating priests are offering oblations, the image-oblation (mūrtihoma) shall be performed in due order.
The most excellent guru himself should perform the fire-oblation of the principles (tattvahoma) in the Brahma-kuṇḍa;
he should meditate upon the image of the God of gods, composed of the elements, situated in front of him.
Then, having served with the arghya and other offerings, one should perform the withdrawal of the principles (tattvasaṃhāra).
One should dissolve earth into water, that [water] into fire, and that [fire] into air.

One should dissolve that [mind] into space, and that [space] into the mind; that [mind], together with the subtle elements (tanmātras) and their respective principles (tattvas), one should dissolve into the ego (ahaṃkāra). (9.49)

Then the Guru should withdraw that sense of ego from the intellect into primordial nature (prakṛti); having honored that [nature] within the individual soul (jīva), he should then cause it to arise once more.

One should offer the principles (tattvas) into the eastern pit with the ghee of a tawny cow; having first sprinkled [the area] with the armor-mantra (varman), one should stand upon the path of emanation.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations for each of the Tattva-mantras and Vyāhṛti-mantras separately;
or there may be twenty-eight or eight oblations for each individual mantra.

The letter *ma* is the mantra of the individual soul (*jīva*); the letter *bha* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*). The letter *ba* is the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), and the letter *pha* is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*). || 9.53 ||
The letter *pa* would be the principle of the mind (*manastattva*), situated in the heart of the image;
the letter *na* would be the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), which has the ear as its sole object. (9.54)
The letter *dha* is the subtle element of touch, eternally established in the skin;
the letter *da* is the subtle element of form, which becomes the object of the two eyes. (9.55)
The letter *tha* is the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) and resides in the tongue alone;
the letter *ta* is the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) and resides at the tip of the nose.
The letter ṇa is the principle of hearing; it should eternally reside in the two ears.
The letter ḍha, however, is the essence of the skin; it exists everywhere upon the skin. (9.57)
The syllable ḌA is the essence of the eye principle; it should eternally reside in the two eyes.
The syllable ṬHA, however, is the essence of the tongue, for the three worlds take the form of the tongue. (9.58)
The letter *ṭa* is the essence of the sense of smell, placed at the tip of the nose;
the letter *ña* is the nature of speech, eternally established in the voice. || 9.59 ||
The syllable *jhakāra* is the principle (*tattva*) of the hands, fashioned by the Creator for the two hands;
the syllable *jakāra* is the phoneme of the principle of the feet, eternally situated on the soles of the feet.
The letter *cha* is the essence of the principle of the anus; it rests at the root of the anus.
The letter *ca* is the essence of the organ of generation; it is situated in the organ of generation. (9.61)

The syllable *ṅa* is the earth element (*pṛthivītattva*), which extends from the feet to the knees; the water element (*aptattva*) is the syllable *dha*, situated from the knees down to the secret place. || 9.62 ||
The letter *ga* is the fire element (*tejastattva*); it extends from the secret place to the navel.
The letter *kha*, whose nature is the wind element (*vāyutattva*), is situated from the navel to the tip of the nose.
The letter *ka* is the essence of the element of space (*ākāśa-tattva*), extending from there up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-bila*).
Thus, the "knower of the principles" (*tattvākṣaka*) has been described; one should extract [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava.
The preeminent teacher should extract the Praṇava, the essential mantra, the salutation, and the name of the location ending in the dative case, followed by the wife of Fire (svāhā). || 9.65 ||
Having offered the oblation and brought the remnants (sampāta), one should sprinkle them upon the respective limbs.
Having thus performed the fire-offering, one should then perform the oblation of the vital breaths (prāṇavāyuhoma).
Having offered the prāṇa into the Suṣumnā immediately thereafter,
one should offer the apāna into the Piṅgalā, and the samāna into the one known as Gandhā.
One should establish the udāna breath in the hastijihvā channel, the vyāna wind in the pūṣā, the lord of serpents (nāgendra) in the yaśasvinī, and the tortoise (kacchapa) in the [yaśasvinī]. 9.68.
Having repeatedly abducted Kṛkara from Alambuṣā, Devadatta at the feet of Kuhū, and Dhanañjaya from Kaiśinī by means of his own magical power, [he departed]. (9.69)
One should sprinkle the falling drops upon the image and there install the [divine] power (śakti),
[visualizing] the conch, discus, mace, lotus, Śārṅga bow, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem.
Having offered the forest garland and the lord of birds with the pouring of the remnants of the oblation,
one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra "asunīte."
Having extracted [the mantra], one should perform the sprinkling of clarified butter with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* syllables at the head;
at the time of the final sprinkling, one should install the respective power (*śakti*) therein.
And for Caṇḍā and the other [deities] of the sacred seats (pīṭha), as well as for the retinue of attendants and all others, the consecration (adhivāsana) takes place at Dhānyapīṭha.

Having performed each respective rite and offered one hundred and eight oblations with clarified butter, he should take the residue of the offerings (sampāta) and sprinkle it upon each of those images.
When the homa has been thus performed in its entirety according to the rules,
one should then perform a śānti-homa for the removal of all defects.
Reciting "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā" one thousand and eight times,
or one hundred and eight times, [he should offer oblations] with clarified butter upon the previously prepared sacrificial grass.

O Lord of Sages, having taken the *sampāta* [remnants] from the oblation, one should sprinkle them over all the limbs; then the [deity] is to be established in the *dhruvabera* at the station of Brahmā.

Then, one should sprinkle [the area] with the waters from the jars beginning with the *vedikā* using mantras addressed to the waters; thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling with the waters from the jars beginning with the *āgneya* while reciting the *Viṣṇu-gāyatrī*.
But at Bahubera, having entered the temple, there should be a sprinkling with water;
thereafter, one should offer the fourfold food to Hari.
One should perform all those services with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om);
then, the radiant one, having raised the image and established it facing the east, [should proceed].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should perform the offering of the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule for all beings, using black-gram rice.
On a surface of the ground smeared with cow dung and properly adorned,
the primordial beings as well as those born of karma are situated in the east and the other directions.
Those who dwell upon mountains, in forests, on the tops of trees, in abodes, at sacred fords, and in the hermitages of seers; 9.83.
Those who dwell in wells, ponds, houses, and so forth—whether they be of the highest, middling, passionate (rājasa), or dark (tāmasa) natures—[should be honored]. 9.84.
"May those who seek offerings come; I shall perform worship for them.
Here is the water for the guest-offering (arghya), here is the water for washing the feet (pādya), and here is the water for sipping (ācamanīya)."
This is the bath with scented water; this is the perfectly pure garment;
this is the fragrance, this the flower, and this the incense together with the lamp.
"May the deities of the bali offering accept this priceless and unblemished [oblation]:
rice mixed with black gram, accompanied by ghee, curd, and molasses. (9.87)
It was provided with various kinds of edible foods mixed with milk-rice (pāyasa), accompanied by betel leaves and areca nuts, and endowed with flowing honey. || 9.88 ||
The wise man should mix with cow’s milk that which is fit to be eaten by the three ancestors; having divided it into three parts, he should perform the offering of the bali.
To those beings on earth who create obstacles to religious duties and who steal away merits— to each and every one of them, this offering is made.

And those who, having employed others in tasks for the sake of their own fruit, obtain it themselves—they are of the quality of passion (rājasa) and middling nature; this tribute is for them from each and every one. 9.91.
To those beings of superior qualities who, seeing [the sacrifice] when sacrifices and other rites have commenced, obtain satisfaction—to each of them, this offering (bali) is given. 9.92.
Having offered the bali-oblation, the preceptor should pray to the deities of the bali:
"The installation of the God of gods, the Supreme Self, is being performed."
"From this point forward, this earth is no longer fit for you to dwell upon;
therefore, depart elsewhere, satisfied by the offering of tribute."
The guide, being humble, should thus entreat the deities of the offering;
they, being pleased by the gift of the offering and having been thus petitioned, reach a state of certainty.
One should consecrate the pedestal of the God of gods upon a seat of grain;
one may likewise consecrate gems, metals, and grains.
One should wrap [the images] individually in new cloths within separate vessels;
then, an oblation of clarified butter accompanied by the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra should be performed one hundred and eight times.
For the purpose of consecration, the supreme guru should bind the golden thread and the protective amulet upon the hand of the God of Gods, preceded by the rite of the auspicious day.
Then they should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in each sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in due order;
the smoke shall carry a holy fragrance, and the flame shall form a circle to the right.
The fire has the luster of gold or resembles a lotus;
the satisfaction of the preceptor’s mind—these are indicators of auspiciousness.
The officiating priests, the sacrificer, and the preeminent teachers should pass that night with the sounds of singing and musical instruments, Vedic chants, and auspicious hymns.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Tenth Chapter.
When the night had turned to dawn and the sun had risen in its stainless splendor, Śrī Rāma,
having reached an auspicious moment, caused Hari to rise from the couch.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and especially adorn [the site];
having entered the inner sanctum, one should place the foundation stone there.
Having made it firm with lime, one should perform the setting of jewels upon that [structure], which is equal in length and breadth, or circular and captivating to the mind. (10.3)
One should place eight items— barley, rice, beans, millet, sesame, mung beans, wild rice, and śāli rice— in the pit, starting from the east.
In the first enclosure, and likewise in the second enclosure,
there were diamonds, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, and crystal as well.
One should place a topaz, a moonstone, and a sapphire in sequence;
and in the third enclosure, gold, silver, copper, and lead.
One should place copper, lead, and bell-metal, as well as a tortoise made of gold,
in sequence into the pit, and finally cast them into the central pit.
Having thus deposited rice seeds, mercury, the nine gems, and gold, the wise one [should perform the rite] with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.
Having covered it firmly with a woman-stone while reciting the Śrīsūkta,
and having made it stable with lime, one should perform the sprinkling with the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
One should invoke Lakṣmī, who dwells in the lotus, upon the pedestal;
one should worship Śrī, who is seated upon the pedestal, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should fashion the image with a male stone, and the pedestal shall be made from a female stone;
the installation of the jewels, however, must be performed upon a neuter stone.
Having covered the pedestal in the sacrificial hall with a new cloth and having worshipped Hari according to the rules, one should also dismiss the sacred fires.
Having first dismissed the deities stationed at the door-arches and the water-jars, as well as those presiding over the offering-pots, and subsequently the deity residing in the Soma-vessel; 10.13.
The image-protectors (mūrtipās) should carry the great water-jars (mahākumbha) and the subsidiary jars (upakumbha),
while the preceptor (ācārya) should proceed at the front, holding an auspicious ritual pitcher (karaka).
One should sprinkle the path ahead with a flowing stream of water;
having led [the image] to the inner sanctum of the temple, one should install it there.
The preceptor, the officiating priests, and others, having raised the deity amidst auspicious rites,
should proceed toward the temple accompanied by the Vedas and various musical instruments.
One should cause the deity to enter within and install him upon the pedestal when an auspicious moment has arrived, while observing the Brahma-thread.
"May I draw you forth; you are the foundation," and "Firm art thou, O Heaven"—with this knowledge, the teacher, standing before him, should establish him with the entire Vidyā. 10.18.
Having observed the Brahma-thread and beheld the state of equanimity,
one should bind [the mind] firmly with the eightfold bond, as if with a plough.
One part of the powder together with one part of guggulu, half a part of lac, and half of that [half] of kuruvinda. || 10.20 ||
The wise man should combine beeswax with half as much cotton, clarified butter, and red ochre, adding them as desired so that the mixture becomes soft.

Afterwards, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and also sprinkle the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) and the image of Vāsudeva; thereafter, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*).
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who is higher than the highest, within the lotus of the heart above the pericarp;
thereafter, one should invoke him into the image, preceded by the ritual of the Yoga-pīṭha.
Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, one should sprinkle [it] with water from the *vardhanī* vessel and then sprinkle it with the water from the jar using the six-syllable mantra.
While the officiating priests were reciting the peace-mantras and the Brahmins were chanting the Vedic hymns amidst the auspicious sounds of instrumental music, dance, and other festive performances.
One should perform the sprinkling with the water of the *brahmakūrca* using the twelve-syllable mantra,
and likewise with the waters from the eight subsidiary jars using their respective vidyās.
One should join each respective power residing in its corresponding pitcher with its respective mantra;
one should then fashion the retinue [of deities] with the remaining water from the pitchers.
The best of preceptors should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the eight-syllable mantra upon the image and always pray for the presence [of the deity] therein.
Having thus invoked the Lord of Gods, sprinkled him with water, and established the Śakti,
one should install the attendants in their respective places according to the prescribed rite.
Having completed all the rites, beginning with the invocation and the sprinkling, and having worshipped the Lord of the Gods with various kinds of offerings; 10.30.

Then, having offered the great oblation (mahāhavis) and having established [the deities] in their proper order, one should present the bali offering according to the scriptures; this is the procedure for the single-liṅga (ekabera) form.
In this Bahuberapratiṣṭhā, there is a certain distinction:
the installation of the Dhruva-bimba at the junction of the divine and the human realms. (10.32)
The worship-pedestal is in the Brahma-square; the ritual image is in the middle square;
the sacrificial image is in that same [middle] square; and the bathing and festive [image] is in the north. (10.33)

One should install the image of the Tīrtha in the south, along with the bed, the offerings, and the ritual objects; furthermore, one should place the worldly image and any other [images] on the outer ground.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable lagna, one should establish the fixed marriage-thread (kautuka),
as well as perform the rites such as the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) for the generation through the dissolution of the principles.
One should perform all rites up to the final propitiation (*śāntyanta*) within the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*);
for all other subsidiary images, one should perform them in the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*).
When the time for the consecration has arrived, the preceptor, having raised the ritual jars,
should subsequently circumambulate the temple clockwise along with the images of its constituent parts.
Having entered within and having placed the water-pots according to the prescribed rite,
one should invoke the imperishable Supreme Self into the primary image (mūlabera).
Listen now to the manner of doing so by means of the five Upaniṣadic mantras:
one should always dissolve Sadāviṣṇu into Mahāviṣṇu, and him into Viṣṇu.

One should place that Viṣṇu within the lotus of the heart, and likewise [place] him in one's own lotus-like hands joined in añjali; then, from the aperture of Brahmā at the fixed orb [of the crown], one should cause him to enter the [divine] image.
Then one should sprinkle the image with water from the *vardhanī* vessel,
and perform the sprinkling of the great jar (*mahākumbha*) with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Thereafter, one should sprinkle [the deities] with water from the secondary jars using their respective vidyās;
one should then install the śaktis, residing in their respective jars, into the primary image (mūlabera).
Having sealed the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) with the Praṇava through meditative absorption,
one who knows the rites of emanation and creation should then perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
The invocation of all the ritual images is considered to be performed from the very beginning;
one should then perform the sprinkling with the water remaining in the ritual pitcher.

For Brahmā and the others who are in the courtyard as his retinue, as well as for Caṇḍa and the others together with Śrī and the rest, [the offering] concludes at the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha). 10.45.
Having brought a large water-pot, the preceptor, together with the Brahmins,
should sprinkle it with their respective mantras and thus complete the entire web of ritual acts.
One should worship the Lord of the gods of gods, up to the offering of food (naivedya), as before;
and at the time of the installation, the patron should also worship the preceptor.
With golden flowers, garments, armlets, finger-rings, earrings,
bracelets, and most enchanting sacred threads.
One should adorn [the image] with silk cloths, fine linen garments, upper robes adorned with gold, turbans, perfumes, flowers, and various other ornaments.
The Lord himself would grant him cows with udders as large as jars and yielding milk, the earth abounding in grain,
and a thousand gold coins.

If he is unable, the master should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of three-quarters, or half, or even one-quarter [of his wealth], or otherwise, a hundred gold coins (niṣkas). || 10.51 ||
One should give half of that to the officiating priests and half of that to the attendants;
furthermore, upon the installation of the deity, one should feed many Brāhmaṇas.
Whether a hundred thousand, ten thousand, or a thousand, according to one's capacity; or, if unable to do all this, one should feed a hundred Brahmins for the successful completion of the sacrifice.
Having daily fed the twice-born on the day of the consecration,
the Lord should bestow upon them sacrificial fees adorned with betel leaves.

The sacrificial fee for the twice-born must indeed be given to those learned in the three Vedas, to those learned in the scriptures, especially to the chanters of hymns, and to other twice-born men as well. 10.55.
A sacrifice devoid of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) does not yield fruit for the patron;
therefore, the lord should bestow sacrificial fees upon all the twice-born.
Having thus established the Lord of Gods, who is endowed with all auspiciousness,
together with the officiating priests, he gratified him with food and wealth.
To the accompaniment of the sound of singing and musical instruments, with the waving of umbrellas and chowries,
and with Brahmins pronouncing benedictions, one should lead the preceptor to his home.
Thus, the sacrificer who installs the deity upon the surface of the earth shall possess incomparable prosperity for his lineage and become like Kubera in wealth. (10.59)
May the lord of the earth become possessed of knowledge, strength, and wisdom;
may obstacles perish, and may the wicked surely go to their destruction.
He shall possess incomparable glory and will enjoy a long life;
he is constantly praised by the immortals and honored by those who perform meritorious deeds.
The merit of those mortals who provide assistance cannot be calculated;
what need is there for much more? They dwell in the celestial realm like gods in heaven.
For those who study the three Vedas and the Shastras, let there be residence in heaven; likewise for those capable of playing musical instruments and performing song, dance, and the like. || 10.63 ||
Those who provide food, drink, and other necessities dwell in the world of the Gandharvas;
likewise, those who hold [their] vehicles, umbrellas, and so forth do not undergo rebirth.
The gods who have authority over vehicles [reside] in the world of the gods, without a doubt;
likewise for teachers, officiating priests, and attendants. (10.65)
Rebirth does not exist for those performers of action by whom Janārdana has been established [as their goal],
and by which men action has been performed free from desire.
Their residence in the third heaven is free from rebirth;
it is the mere sight of Viṣṇu that bestows the fruit of all desires.
How much more so for those desiring fruit, especially at the time of sacrifice?
Having thus established the eternal Vāsudeva, the wise man [should proceed].
Having performed the bathing at the conclusion of the installation, one should hold a great festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner;
this shall bring supreme satisfaction to the Supreme Self, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Eleventh Chapter.
O illustrious Bhārgava, you who are compassionate toward your devotees, please tell me how the great festival of the Supreme Soul should be performed by one who has no wealth. (11.1)
Śrī Rāma said: Listen, O tiger among sages, to the great festival of the God of gods,
by worshipping Hari through which Śakra was liberated from the sin of slaying Vṛtra.
I shall tell you that today; listen with humility. One should perform the auspicious rite for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow within twelve days.
Alternatively, the festival of the Garuda-bannered deity shall take place nine days, or seven, or five days prior to the day of its commencement. (11.4)
Having performed the ritual placement of the seed-syllables (aṅkuranyāsa) for that purpose according to the injunctions of the scriptures,
one should depict on the cloth the god Vainateya, the lord of birds.
He was nine palm trees in height, resembling molten gold;
the Lord had two arms, wore a bodice, and held a trailing flower in his hand.
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with serpent ornaments,
he has placed one foot upon his back while the other is drawn up in a curve.
One should perform the opening of the eyes upon the Lord, whose blue tip of the nose is directed upward as He prepares to fly into the sky with a wide-spread wing.
All other rites for the artisan should be performed according to the prescribed rules for consecration;
having performed the preliminary dwelling of the shadow and having bathed [the image], one should [reflect it] in a mirror.
Having worshipped Vainateya according to the rules with the Gāyatrī mantra,
the preceptor then places him upon a very spacious seat of rice.
To the south of that, upon a heap of grain, one should place the kumbha together with its secondary vessel (upakuṃbha), endowed with the proper characteristics,
along with the vardhanī, and adorned with all ornaments.

One should worship Vainateya in the great pitcher (mahākumbha) and Sudarśana in the vardhanī; in the other eight [pitchers], Indra and the others are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the Mūrti-homa in a single fire-altar, or in the kitchen, using either the Bṛhat Sāman or the Gāyatrī mantra, according to one's preference.
After performing the dissolution and generation of the principles (tattva), as well as the fire-oblation of the principles and so forth as before,
the Guru then spreads out the cloth facing the temple.
Having shown [the image] to the God of gods, he then performed the invocation:
"O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, Lord of all, you who pervade the universe! (11.15)
However, what you have described cannot be accomplished because of a lack of self-reliance, incapacity, and the absence of faith and other such qualities. || 11.16 ||
Today, for the sake of pacifying the deficiency and excess of all beings through your very self,
behold with your two cool eyes that which is depicted upon the cloth.
"Propitiate Vainateya with [mantras] that remove all defects.
Having thus instructed [the disciple], the teacher should perform the invocation after showing [him the deity].
O one of great strength, O mighty-armed Vainateya, lord of birds, manifest yourself upon this cloth; salutations to you, whose form is the Praṇava.
Having thus prayed for her presence with that very Gāyatrī mantra of hers,
and having worshipped her with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, he offered the four kinds of food.
And for Kumbha, one should recite the Gāruḍa mantra according to the scriptures;
one should pass the night in vigil with the chanting of the Vedas and the sounding of musical instruments.
Then, at the clear dawn, having propitiated the Lord of Birds and having adorned him appropriately, he placed him upon a vehicle amidst auspicious rites.
One should lead [the image] clockwise onto the ground in front of the flagstaff,
having spread out the deity situated upon the cloth facing the temple.
Thereafter, he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkle [the area] with water from the pitcher;
he should perform the consecration (*pariṣecana*) around the *vardhanī* vessel using the *Gāruḍa* mantra alone.
One should perform the sprinkling of the jars of Indra and the others with their respective mantras;
having applied the *Gāruḍa* mantra, one should perform the prayer for the presence [of the deity]. (11.25)
At the conclusion of the festival, place [the deity] within the folds of the cloth of the supreme abode;
O Blessed One, King of Birds, protect us and look upon us! 11.26
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Birds during an auspicious moment,
at a favorable conjunction that gladdens the mind, one should perform the hoisting of the banner.
Having placed the festival image upon a vehicle there,
one should bring it with a triple-stranded noose that is as thick as a thumb.
And one should bind it with a woven cord using the mantra "Puruṣātmanā";
the mounting of the banner is said to be performed with the mantra "Suparṇo 'si. (11.29)
Having thus placed the bird upon it and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
[he offered] milk-rice, cakes, and various kinds of fruits.
Having offered [the oblation] to Vainateya, one should worship Indra and the others around him;
having worshipped them according to the rule, the wise man should present the bali offering.
Having arrived at the festival of the sacrifice, the preceptor, having prostrated and performed worship,
and having obtained permission, took up flowers for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Having become cheerful of countenance and having gazed upon the Lord of Birds, [he said:
"From this day forth until the day of the pilgrimage. (11.33)
"O Lord of Birds, establish your residence for the king, the kingdom, the village, the sacrificer, and indeed for the high-souled Vaiṣṇavas. (11.34)
For the sake of contentment and nourishment, for victory over all enemies, and for the purpose of removing untimely death—O Vainateya, be gracious! Om.
Thus, he should properly scatter a handful of flowers over the bird;
then the lord should give cows, land, gold, and other gifts to the Brahmins.
Thereafter, one should lead the festival image into another pavilion and worship it according to the prescribed rule; then one should bring it into the inner sanctum.
For the purpose of summoning all the worlds,
the supreme guide should strike the kettledrum for the sake of all the gods as well.
One should cleanse the ground near the base of the banner with cow dung,
and there one should place the pedestal adorned with various creepers.
Having taken the image of the deity and placed it there, one should worship it;
in front of that image, one should prepare a pedestal of grain.
There, having first placed the drum and the drumstick, [he should then place] one who has bathed, wears clean garments, bears the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and is well-adorned. || 11.41 ||
One should station courtesans wearing the sacred thread on the right side,
and those who are experts in the art of dance in the direction of Indra (the east).
The wise man should station those skilled in singing and instrumental music in the northern quarter,
as well as the drummers and those who play the *pāraśava* drums and other instruments, with the waters of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).
Having sprinkled the great drum, one should worship it as the embodiment of Bhāratī;
one should wrap the drum, which is the form of sound, with a new cloth.
One should adorn [the image] with flowers and various perfumes;
one should worship the Goddess, who consists of the three qualities and is composed of the Veda (Bhāratī), in the center of the drum.
One should worship Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī in the south and north;
O one born from a water-jar, one should worship the god Vāyu in the corner.
Then, meditating upon the three forms with the knowledge of the subtle element of sound,
he should strike the drum with the corner [of his hand] while proclaiming the names of the deities.
Those who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha and those who reside in Satyaloka, those situated in the world of Rudra as well as those dwelling in the world of Svar; || 11.48 ||
One should perform the invocation everywhere for those who dwell in the worlds such as Pātāla and on the surface of the earth, as well as for others who exist in all the worlds.
The invocation of all the sages who are like fire, the gods born of Diti, and others, accompanied by their respective retinues.
During the great festival, the wise one should cause the invocation of the weapons, the goddesses, and the mounts for the service of the Enemy of Madhu.
One should perform the three strikes of the great drum as a call to respond;
therein one should manifest their dance, tone, and rhythm—these three.
Having summoned all the deities preceded by the bali offering and the image,
and having reached the center of the village, one should establish Brahmā there.
One should arrange those guardians of the world, beginning with Indra, in due order upon the sacrificial mounds on the street surrounding the village, for the purpose of offering oblations.
Having thus addressed [the officiants], the wise man should then strive for the festival of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, in accordance with the requirements of place and time.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Twelve
One should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) either on the day prior to the commencement of the festival,
or on the third day, or even on the preceding day.
There were ramparts and palaces, as well as moats and streets, surrounded on all sides by water-stations, archways, and other floral garlands.
One should cleanse [the ground] with cow-dung and water, and adorn the houses as well with colored powders, offerings, unbroken rice grains, and various other beautiful objects.
The sacrificial materials required for the festival, especially those for the purpose of the rite, should be gathered;
and one should construct the sacrificial pavilion within the eastern direction.
With seven pillar-like arms on all sides, it should be square;
in its center there shall be an altar one cubit in height.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) surrounding it are two cubits wide;
or else, there may be a single pit in the eastern part, which is quadrangular and beautiful.
The Āhavanīya fire should be in the east, the Dakṣiṇa fire in the south, and the Gārhapatya fire in the west; one should arrange the Sabhya fire elsewhere.
All activities such as the construction of the archway and so forth are distinguished by what was previously established;
this applies likewise to the teachers, the officiating priests, and the attendants. (12.8)
First, the master should choose four priests;
he should previously honor them with ornaments, garments, perfumes, garlands, and other such offerings.
On the previous day, at night, one should perform the ritual of formal acceptance (adhivāsa);
then, having bathed Hari together with the two goddesses, one should have him lie down upon the bed.
For that purpose, having tied the auspicious thread (kautuka), the most excellent preceptor (deśikottama) should subsequently prepare the bed and place lamps in the corners of the bed.
O best of sages, one should perform eight oblations with fuel-sticks using the Nṛsūkta,
and then again offer eight oblations of sacrificial rice (caru) with clarified butter while reciting the root mantra.
Then, having praised the Lord of the Gods with the Vedas, musical instruments, and auspicious hymns,
one should pass the night in vigil with the recitation of the root mantra.
Then, at the clear dawn when the orb of the sun has appeared,
the preceptor should raise Hari with the mantra "Arise."
With the Vedic mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," one should place [the body] upon the palanquin;
the brāhmaṇas should carry the vehicle while meditating upon the Lord of Birds.
Having performed various dances, songs, and instrumental music,
as well as Vedic chants and hymns, they completed a circumambulation of the village.
Having caused the deity to descend onto an auspicious seat within the decorated pavilion,
the preceptor, having performed the appropriate services, gathered the collected ritual materials.
He should show all those who had been brought there to the god in the assembly of people; then, having bathed the Lord of Gods, having worshipped him, and having offered [the gifts] to him... (12.18)
Having completed the daily fire oblation, the preceptor should lead [the image] into the inner sanctum;
having entered the residence in the evening, he should do so together with the patron.
Having bowed to him and obtained his permission, and having bound the auspicious marriage-thread,
they immediately performed the festive bathing, offerings, and worship for the images as well.
Having tied the protective amulet (pratisara) upon their hands according to the prescribed rite,
he then raised that image of the Lord and circumambulated the temple clockwise.
Having brought Hari to the sacrificial pavilion, one should place him upon a seat;
on the altar, upon a pedestal of grain, one should place the water-pot in the center and [another] to the south.
One should place the ritual vessel and eight jars in order, starting from the east;
the worship is performed as in the consecration of the door-arches and the jars.
One should worship the primary form in the central jar, and the deity of the weapon in the *vardhanī* jar;
Vāsudeva and the others are prescribed for the jars in the directions starting from the east.
One should worship Puruṣa and the others in the corners beginning with the southeast:
namely, these—Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Ananta.
And one should worship according to the rules and present the sacrificial oblations;
likewise, having worshipped the image of Bala and offered it according to the prescribed rite.
Having caused those who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as those learned in the Atharvāṅgirasa, to study in all directions beginning with the east, in due order; || 12.27 ||
When the quarters of the sky have been filled with the sound of musical instruments such as the *tūrya*,
one should worship Vāsudeva and the other deities in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) located in the directions beginning with the east.
There, one should also pray for the presence [of the deity] at the conclusion of the pilgrimage site;
thus is the jar worshipped when the Blessed One, the Lord of All, is present within it.
The oblation should be performed with clarified butter and other substances, using their respective mantras in due order,
along with ghee, flowers, incense materials, and sacrificial fuel sticks.
With milk and curd, as well as with sesame, rice, and barley,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately for each deity presiding over the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), using the appropriate mantras.
The oblation (homa) should be performed twenty-eight or eight times, starting from the east as before;
having thus offered the sacrifice according to the rule, one should again offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Nṛsūkta.
O Pot-born One, at each pit— and specifically at the Brahma-pit— one should offer oblations of milk-rice or clarified butter,
dedicating them to the gods beginning with Brahmā.
And likewise to Brahmā, to Rudra, and to Prajāpati;
to Indra, to Mahendra, to Bhānu, and to Jātavedas.
To Dharmarāja, Maruta, Kubera, and Yama;
to Varuṇa, to the Ṛṣis, to the Vedas, and to the flower-bowed god (Kāmadeva).
And also to all the gods, to the Vedic meters, to the embodiment of Time, to the Earth, to the King of Mountains, to the rivers, and to the forest as a living form. || 12.36 ||
And for the elements, for the animals, for the plants, and likewise for Śrī;
for the Apsarases, for the worlds, for the oceans, and for the sky. || 12.37 ||
And to the Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, and the attendants; to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu);
to Caṇḍa and the other gatekeepers; and to Viṣṇu in all his forms.
Having uttered [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the wife of Agni (Svāhā), one should perform the oblation;
then, having offered with the root mantra and with the Ṛgvedic verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," || 12.39 ||
Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should perform the offering of the *bali*;
the attendants, taking black gram food sprinkled with clarified butter, [should proceed]. (12.40)
Incense, lamps, as well as perfumes and fragrant flowers, and other articles of worship, preceded by Vedic musical instruments. || 12.41 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon the vehicle, one should perform the bali offering together with that [deity];
first, one should cast the bali at each door within the sacrificial hall.
One should offer [oblations] to the gatekeepers, Caṇḍa and the others, as in the daily festival;
having reached the center of the village, one should present the bali offering to Brahmā.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Indra and the other deities starting from the east and ending at the northeast;
the remains of the bali should be cast upon the top of the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
O one born from a water-pot, one should offer the bali-oblation preceded by water;
having worshipped the deity there, one should lead him to the sacrificial hall.

Having propitiated the deities with festive offerings, and having placed [the image] upon a chariot or a palanquin and the like, well-adorned and accompanied by Brahmins reciting benedictions; || 12.46 ||
Having emerged from that temple, he should circumambulate the courtyards and the grounds of all the enclosures, accompanied by learned men who recite the Vedas.
And by those learned in the scriptures, by poets, as well as by those versed in the Purāṇas,
by astrologers, and by physicians, [it was composed] in a mixture of prose and verse.
By those reciting and intent on praise, skilled in various languages;
and by those dancing and singing, and by the company of dancers performing their art.
And by Vedāntins, ascetics, and yogis who were absorbed in the Blessed One,
as they repeatedly proclaimed the scripture of the Blessed One and his majesty.
Accompanied by men delighted in various musical instruments and by women who captivate the eyes and mind,
and adorned with every ornament, he should lead Hari along the path.
An umbrella, yak-tail fans, and beautiful palm-leaf fans;
banners, lamps, pillars, and especially oil-lamps. || 12.52 ||
Incense emitting fragrant scents, arched gateways, and lattice windows;
banners, elephants, horses, and various musical instruments.
Having circumambulated [the shrine] clockwise along with other auspicious rites,
he descended from the vehicle into the interior of the temple and [seated him] upon an auspicious throne.
Having seated the God facing the east and honored him with various kinds of ritual services,
he then bathed him and offered the great sacrificial oblation.
Having performed the lustration ceremony for the Supreme Lord, he should pour out the water upon the auspicious ground;
then, having placed the God upon his bed, he should worship him as is appropriate.
One should cause Puruṣottama to sleep upon the entire bed-chamber arrangement, together with dance, song, and so forth, accompanied by both Śrī and Dharaṇī.
Then at dawn, the preceptor, having raised that deity from his bed and having worshipped him according to the scriptures, [placed] the jar and other items in the sacrificial hall.
Having worshipped the image of Bali and offered oblations into the fire as before,
and having presented the sacrificial offering (bali) as previously done, one should undertake the journey just as at night.
Every day, in the evening and in the morning, worship, fire-offerings,
and ritual oblations must be performed according to the rules, as well as the ceremonial bath in due order.
Day after day, one should perform a festival for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—
whether for the two goddesses, or for Śrī alone, or even for Hari alone without them.
O great sage, when such a great festival of Viṣṇu is increasing,
one should perform the auspicious celebration together with his two goddesses or with Lakṣmī.
Having performed the ritual according to the rules, ending with the offerings of worship and oblations,
and having adorned [the image] and placed it upon a vehicle together with the two goddesses, he brought it to the pavilion.
Then, having led another [image] and placed it upon an auspicious golden lion-throne,
one should bathe the deity, seated facing the east, with auspicious waters.
Having thoroughly washed the pestle and the mortar in pure water in front of the Dhānyapṛṣṭha [deity], while reciting the root mantra.
Having placed it there, wrapped it with new cloths and sprouts,
and adorned it beautifully with flowers, sandalwood, and various fragrant substances.
Having placed turmeric there, one should worship Śrī, the mother of the three worlds,
while meditating upon her, with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, in due order.
Then, well-adorned female servants of the gods, uttering auspicious words,
passed the entire night with subtle and appropriate music.
Having placed a jar made of gold or other materials, wrapped with thread, cloth, and so forth,
upon a heap of grain, one should fill it with the powder of turmeric.
One should place an image of Lakṣmī made of gold and various jewels;
one should also provide a tuft of grass and a sprout, and have them covered with a shallow bowl.
There, having invoked Śrī, one should perform the worship complete with its ancillaries;
according to the rule, one should consecrate [the image] with those powders while reciting the root mantra.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites and as before with the Śrīsūkta-vidyā,
at the conclusion of the offering of the great oblation, the preeminent teacher and the officiating priests [performed the rites].
Having circumambulated Hari, one should scatter handfuls of flowers and praise him with various hymns that gladden the mind.
On a certain day, after a festive celebration has been performed,
one should bathe the Teacher of the World together with his two consorts in a large wooden vat filled with water.
When the afternoon has arrived, the preceptor, having placed the Teacher of the World upon a palanquin together with Śrī and Bhūmi, should lead him to the riverbank.
In a pavilion or a water-shed, adorned with every ornament, and with the quarters of the sky filled by the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and other instruments; (12.76)
It was adorned on all sides by the resonance of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas,
and filled with the sound of the singing of dancing female attendants.
It was filled with the sounds of mutual abuse and harshness cast forth by those intent on hearing the scriptures, as they vied with one another for victory.
It was resplendent with visible lamp-stands and mirrors,
and was beautifully adorned all around with pillars made of plantain and areca trees bearing fruit.
It was adorned with hanging garlands of flowers and strings of pearls,
and featured a beautiful canopy made of an exceedingly pure cloth.
There, having prepared a beautiful pedestal of grain in the center,
one should place a water-vessel made of either gold or silver.
One should fill [the vessel] with water mixed with powdered saffron, camphor, and musk,
and saturated with powdered sandalwood.
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite with Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
one should sprinkle that water-vat (*jaladroṇī*) and contemplate its foundation and other parts.
One should invoke the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, there into the water with mantras,
and worship all those deities of the sacred fords (tīrtha) until the offering of food (naivedya).
They should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn and the *vāruṇa* Sāman;
then, having raised the god up along with the two goddesses, one should place him in a wooden vat filled with water.
There, having worshipped the deity, one should scatter golden unbroken grains (akṣata) in all directions, consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
Then, having raised the Lord of Gods from the lion-throne together with the two goddesses, and having seated him there,
he worshipped him according to the rules and offered the great sacrificial oblation.
Having mounted him upon a vehicle according to the prescribed rites, he should bring him to the auspicious ground;
on another day, he should engage in the hunt of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
O bull among sages, hunting by night is recommended for the god [the king],
after he has performed all the concluding rites of the sacrifice, whether on horseback or even on an elephant.
Having mounted the deity and adorned him beautifully with ornaments and other finery,
one should place the Śārṅga bow, the arrow, and the quiver in their respective positions.
One should also fashion a turban and armor, as well as golden garments;
everything should be most beautiful, including the vehicle and the equipment.
Accompanied by his armed attendants and all auspicious objects,
he led him through the entire forest region and there, at the site of a water-shed (prapā).
One should worship the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) according to the prescribed rule, ending with the offering of food (naivedya);
then, having circumambulated him, one should place [the deity] as before.
When midnight has arrived, the preceptor, having gone to the inner sanctum and bowed down, should entreat Puruṣottama on behalf of the patron.
"O best of gods, you must undertake a pilgrimage tomorrow at dawn;
there, you ought to grant permission for the commencement of the *pratisarā*."
Having made this request, one should tie the protective thread (kautuka) on the hand of the image at the sacred site;
then, having laid it down and worshipped it, one should raise it again in the morning.
Having worshipped everything according to the prescribed rules, one should perform all the rites up to the offering of the bali-oblation;
then, taking the image of the Tīrtha deity and placing it in the pavilion at the entrance, [one should proceed].
Having placed a grain-seat before him,
the preceptor should take the jars that have been set out in the sacrificial hall.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the vardhanī vessel, one should perform the consecration with those jars;
the sprinkling is done with the root mantra, and the consecration with the Nṛsūkta.
One should consecrate the root-vessel with those jars in a single session;
this is recorded as the sequence of consecration, beginning from the east and ending with the central jar.
Having worshipped everything from the garments down to the lamps and having offered them,
he fastened the marriage-thread (maṅgalasūtra), which was accompanied by all auspicious rites.
Or [he may go] by elephant or other vehicle, or by chariot, preceded by the image of the Tīrtha, to the bank of a river, or to the ocean, or to a lake, or to a pond. || 12.102 ||
Having passed through the festive procession, he was brought into the prepared pavilion and,
having been set down from his vehicle, took his seat upon the throne, attended by the curiosity of the holy places.
One should bathe [the deity] with nine consecrated jars according to the prescribed rite,
and perform the invocation of the Gaṅgā and other rivers from sacred bathing sites.
If a sacred image is not available, one should instead immerse the discus three times;
when the rite at a sacred site must be performed with a discus, it should be done with the waters of a river or similar body of water.
The wise one, having sprinkled the auspicious marriage-thread with water falling from the tips of the *kūrca* grass,
should take the discus into the rivers and immerse it with the *cakramantra*.
And even when the discus is not available, one should perform the rite with the tuft of hair alone;
those men who bathe with the God of gods are liberated from all taints.
They certainly go to the eternal abode of the Lord of Kamalā, which is so difficult to attain;
then, having brought them to the pavilion, he worshipped them according to the prescribed rite.
He performed circumambulation of the grove of auspiciousness,
traveling around it a thousand, a hundred, or even a hundred thousand times, according to his wealth.
The Brahmins should be fed daily during the great festival;
on that night, one should perform the ceremonial bathing in the sequence appropriate for the conclusion of the festival.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites up to the offering of the oblation,
and having reached the sacrificial pavilion, he performed the fire-oblation as before.
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma), but one must not take the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya).
For the sake of expiation, one should offer a hundred oblations with the five Upaniṣads.
Thereafter, one should dismiss the fires situated at the *pālikās* and the arches;
having mounted the deity onto the vehicle, one should bring it to the flagstaff.
Having worshipped Vainateya and offered the great oblation, one should,
following the sequence of withdrawal, dissolve that Tārkṣya from the cloth.
But when the image is present, one should lower that banner;
then, [one should dismiss] the deities who were invoked, even though they remain stationed in their respective places.
Having offered the bali-oblation with the *tūrya* alone, the supreme guru dismissed [the deities] with their respective names, together with the silent attendants.
Having entered the abode of the deity, one should place the festival-bath, the offering-cake, the worship, the sacred ford, and the image within the inner sanctum as before.
Then, having recited the eight-syllable mantra a thousand times or at least a hundred times,
and having bowed to the Lord of Gods and obtained his permission, one should return.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the glorious Bhārgavatantra.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
When the night had turned to dawn and the sun had risen, the venerable Śrī Rāma,
having performed his own religious observances together with his devoted Bhāgavatas, [proceeded].
Having entered the interior of the ālaya and performed worship according to the rules,
the preceptor, having completed everything up to the offering of the bali oblation, remains within the pavilion.
The wise one should fashion the lotus-wheel according to the method that will be described;
he should construct an altar-platform with a width equal to its length.
With five or four hands, one should smear a beautiful, visible surface with cow-dung and make it resemble a mirror. (13.4)
One should draw ten and seven lines extending eastward and crosswise;
there are six, five, and two squares in the middle, and then six and three.
Having fixed a stake in the center and then rotated it fivefold,
one should divide the ground with a cord, making the central position the pericarp.
The second is the pericarp and petals for the calculation of the nābhis;
the third and the fourth are said to be the two fields of movement (cārakṣetra).
One should clear the outer compartments for those [lines] whose fifth is the rim;
one should divide that field into three parts by means of the path of rotating the cord.
One should mark the corners and the sūtra-line for the face in the four directions;
when this is done, the area for the doors will be established in the four directions.
One should arrange twelve lotuses on the area of the inner enclosure:
one in each corner, and two on each side of the gate-pavilions (valaja).
And in all four corners, outside the three enclosures,
the one most skilled in the scriptures should fashion the beautiful conch Pāñcajanya.
The wise one should fashion twelve dots within the area of the pericarp;
he should then divide the second [circle] threefold by means of the path of rotating the thread.
The first is the position of the filaments, the second shall be the ground of the petals, and the third is the navel-circle; there are nine filaments plus six.
One should fashion twelve lotus-line drawings upon the surface of the petals;
four are placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and likewise twenty.
Having unified the two, one should fashion the field-lines;
there should be two radii in the intermediate directions and one each in the cardinal directions. (13.15)
One should beautify the mandala with five kinds of colors in their proper order, [colors] resembling lotus petals and like those of the blue water-lily.
A white complexion is produced by flour of śāli rice and fragrant powders;
a yellow complexion by turmeric; and a blue complexion is said to result from the charcoal of sacrificial wood.
A dark complexion is said to result from sacrificial leaves and powders;
it becomes red by means of saffron alone. Thus, it is remembered as being of five kinds.
One should fashion the pericarp with yellow color and the filaments with white;
the lines of the pericarp with pale-red and the surface of the filaments with black.
Having divided the eastern portion into two parts, [one] with white [lines] and the northern part with yellow;
[one should place] white dots at the tips and red dots on the edges of the petals.
At the beginning and end of the petals, it is beautiful with white and red [pigments];
one should then adorn the rim at the edge of the petals with red or white [pigments].
One should adorn the navel with dark blue, the ground of the hub with black,
the spokes with red color, and the inner rim surrounding them with white.
With black [stones] he made the dwelling for the rim, and with white [stones] the ground at the edge of the rim;
the first enclosure was made with black stones, and the second enclosure with white ones.
The third enclosure consists of red lotuses as before;
the gates are red, yellow, black, and white, in the order of the directions starting from Indra.
With the color of a conch shell or Arjuna flowers, it is considered to have a reddish central line;
it is composed of five colors: white, red, yellow, brown, and black. || 13.25 ||
Or one may color the maṇḍala with black flowers;
having thus painted the maṇḍala, one should sprinkle it with water from an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
One should place the auspicious seat upon this [altar], and upon that [seat] one should install the deity;
having worshipped the deity with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, one should bow down before him.
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed Lord of all worlds, Master!
This great festival preceded by the raising of the banner has been performed today for Your pleasure.
And if, by me as the patron, by the officiating priests, or even by the practitioners, any evil deed should arise there through deficiencies or excesses, [may it be averted]. (13.29)
"To pacify those faults, I now wish to worship with flowers;
grant me permission, O Lord, and fulfill this rite as well."
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, one should begin the worship with flowers,
[placing them] upon the twelve points of the vowels of the "twelve-syllable" mantra.
Then, having invoked Vāsudeva into the pericarp, one should perform his worship:
offering water for the guest-reception (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), bathing water, as well as garments and a sacred thread.
Fragrance, flowers, and ornaments—these nine services are prescribed.
O Pot-born One, one should worship with flowers for every syllable.
With flowers held in his joined palms, reciting "Namaḥ" at the end, let there be for me the fruit [of my merit] through these flowers offered to the limbs, beginning with the heart. (13.34)
Then, with reference to the ornaments beginning with the Śrīvatsa,
and the weapons beginning with the Sudarśana, one should perform worship with flowers.
One should worship the eight Śris on the filaments with flowers;
then, one should worship the twelve Śaktis on the spaces between the petals.
On the circle at the edge of the petals, one should worship those powers, Vyāpti and the others;
in the region of the navel, the wise one should invoke Viṣṇu and worship him with flowers.
One should worship Viṣṇu and the others upon the twelve spokes with flowers;
on the circle between the spokes, the gods beginning with Matsya; and on the surface of the rim, [the remaining incarnations].
The eight weapons, beginning with the conch, are in the first enclosure on the outside;
the twelve [deities] beginning with Keśava are in the lotuses of the second enclosure.
Likewise, Vāsudeva and the others are to be worshipped in the third enclosure;
and the twelve Ādityas are to be adored in all twelve lotuses.
One should worship Khageśāna at the eastern gate, Sudarśana at the southern,
the mace (Gadā) at the gate of Apāmpati, and the conch (Śaṅkha) at the northern gate.
Then, with the *Puruṣasūkta*, as well as the *Nārāyaṇa* [sūkta],
and with the mantras of the five Upaniṣads, [he worshipped] at the lotus-feet of the God.
One should perform worship with flowers and present incense and lamps;
likewise, one should praise the Lord of the World with the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
One should offer him food of four kinds, such as milk-rice and other delicacies;
the oblation should be performed in a fire-pit dedicated to Agni, or on a sacrificial mound, or in the kitchen.

With fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice as the primary materials, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations into the fire with the root mantra, concluding with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 13.45 ||
Having performed circumambulation and prostration, and having offered praise to the Lord of Śrī,
one should dismiss those stationed in the mandala and lead them to the first enclosure.
One should dismiss the gods who have come for the sake of service,
as well as all other humans, after circumambulating them clockwise.
The best of preceptors should lead the deity into the interior of the temple, together with the permanent internal attendants who serve him constantly.
Having thus held a great festival and honored the preceptor and the officiating priests,
he adorned them especially with wealth that gladdens the mind.
Having placed that preceptor upon a vehicle accompanied by all auspicious rites,
the lord [the disciple] should circumambulate the village and lead him to his home.
Thus, celebrating this great festival, one rejoices everywhere in this world, and especially in the next; what more could there be beyond this? (13.51)
Whatever fruit arises for men from performing thousands of horse-sacrifices, tens of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices, and a hundred million Aptoryāma sacrifices; || 13.52 ||
By this sacrifice of the god, everything becomes certain;
let them simply serve that God of gods during the great festival.
The desired fruit indeed comes into the palm of the hand; of this there is no doubt.
How much more so for those who are disciplined and whose souls are devoted to service?
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
"O Bhārgava, tell me: after Agastya has caused this auspicious marriage ceremony for the God of gods to be performed, what will he do next?"
Śrī Rāma said:
"One should not perform the marriage rite upon a bed prepared for the gods along with the goddesses; if one were to do it otherwise," (14.2).
The attainment of all auspicious perfections and the increase of longevity arise;
for those who perform auspicious rites for the Goddess, there shall be the fulfillment of their desired aims.
All sufferings perish and one is no longer stained by sins;
the performer of the marriage rite obtains wealth and grain.
Before the day of the wedding, one should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa);
on an auspicious day, a separate auspicious ceremony for the bridegroom's turban (kaustuka-maṅgala) should be performed.
Having adorned the god and the goddess with ornaments, garments, flowers, and other offerings,
he placed them upon a palanquin and brought them to his home.
Having circumambulated the two deities, one should lead them to the auspicious pavilion;
having propitiated Viṣvaksena for the sake of pacifying obstacles to the ritual.
With a serene mind, having propitiated the gods beginning with Brahmā, one should immediately offer sprouts into five *pālikā* vessels on the occasion of a wedding.
"Taking up the seed-vessel, I pay homage to the lords of the directions";
having thus prayed and sat down, [he performed the rite] with the mantra "yā jātā".
Having thus consecrated the seeds with mantras, one should perform the sowing of the seeds;
in the center, however, [one should recite] "brahmajajñānam" and "yata indraḥ purandaraḥ."
That which is his abdominal [portion] in the direction of Yama, there should be "imaṃ me varuṇa";
likewise, Soma [should be placed] for the cow, and the sowing of seeds for Soma should occur once.
The other officiating priests remain silent while the placement is performed twice in silence;
then the preceptor covers [the site] with earth while reciting the mantra beginning with "mūrdhānam. || 14.12 ||
One should sprinkle [the image] with pure water while reciting "imaṃ me varuṇa";
having thus performed the rite preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should then perform the binding of the protective thread (kautuka).
Having consecrated it seven times with the *pratisarā* weapon-mantra,
he should smear it with sandalwood powder mixed with water while reciting the *tryambaka* verse.
With the mantra "viśvettā te," one should bind [the thread] on the right hand of the deity;
for the goddesses, one should bind it on their other hands with their respective mantras.
Having touched it with the right hand, one should consecrate it with the mantra "yo brahmā";
protection shall be afforded by incense and ashes with the mantra "bṛhatsāma."
One should bow three times to the Lord with the *Puṇḍarīkākṣa* mantra; having drawn the fire-altar and established the fire with the verse beginning "O auspicious one, [place] the head. (14.17)
One should tie auspicious [threads] upon the heads of the couple in due order;
with the verse beginning "yāmāharat," one should tie a garland of flowers.
One should perform the washing of Viṣṇu’s feet with the verse beginning "tathā trīṇi padā" and touch oneself with the mantra "mayi te". (14.19)
Then, having filled an earthen vessel with water for the offering, along with unbroken grains and flowers, he should take it in both hands.
Having first prayed to the deity with the words, "The waters are worthy of honor," the preceptor should then mutter the mantra "Āmāgann" over the water in the vessel.
Into the hand of the God of gods, he poured the water that had been brought while reciting the verse "virojo doha," and saying, "samudraṃ va" (to the ocean, you). || 14.22 ||
Taking a bunch of kuśa grass, he should sprinkle [the image] and then give a cow to Hari;
with the mantra "yuvaṃ vastrā," he should clothe Hari with a garment.
One should fashion the sacrificial thread with the *yajñopavīta* mantra; one should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) at the feet with the mantra beginning "irāvatī. (14.24)
Taking the madhuparka in a golden vessel,
he should consecrate it with two mantras, reciting "trayyai" and "āmāgannita" three times each.
The ritual rinsing of the mouth (āpośana) is traditionally remembered with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer for immortality" (amṛtopastaraṇam asi).
Then, reciting the mantra, "That which is honey" (yan madhu), he should present the honey-mixture (madhuparka). || 14.26 ||
The second *āpośana* is prescribed with the *amṛtādhāna* mantra;
then, having shown a cow to Hari, one should do so with the knowledge-mantra "gaurgau" asi.
The preceptor should consecrate the cow with the mantra, "praṇavo caṃ cikituṣe," and having said, "Oṃ, release her," he should then let the cow go.
Saying "It is real," the wise one should offer food to him;
the best of preceptors should loudly say, "Oṃ, prepare [it]. (14.29)
Then, having clothed her in a new garment with the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," and having adorned Śrī, the goddess of the earth, with divine ornaments and garlands.
Having restrained his breath and made the formal resolve, the donor, preceded by the offering of water, [gives] the goddess adorned with ornaments, having announced her own lineage and name.
One should give to Viṣṇu, who is self-existent, the earth together with gold,
as well as a maiden endowed with gold and adorned with all ornaments.
"I shall give [myself] to you, Viṣṇu, out of a desire to conquer the world of Brahmā.
Having said this, with his right hand amidst the sounds of singing and musical instruments, [he offered himself]. (14.33)
With the mantra "devasya tvā," the preceptor should place that hand, together with gold and water, into the right hand of the Supreme Self.
O Lord, one should join the Praṇava with the god Kamala and the earth;
then, [one should place it] upon the head of the goddess who has been taken by the hand of the god.
"May you be firm," saying this, flowers and unbroken grains are scattered;
then, having recited the *ṛc* verse beginning with "abhrātṛghnīm," [the offering is made] to Svayambhū.
"O Agastya, one should show the Goddess with a non-terrifying gaze;
likewise, the ritual duties must be performed and the subjects must be protected. (14.37)
One should contemplate that resolve of theirs as "by us two," and then, taking hold of a blade of darbha grass, one should mutter: "I [perform] this. (14.38)
Having touched [the body] between the eyebrows, he should release it toward the eastern direction;
then, having caused the twice-born who know the Vedas to recite the mantra "O Jīvas, do not weep," [he should proceed]. (14.39)
With the śruti mantra "vyukṣakrūram," one should apply the bathing substances;
with the mantra "aryamṇe," one should fashion a circle of darbha grass for Śrī.
Having placed [the gold] with the mantra "khena sa," one should insert it into the joint;
then, having said "śaṃ te hiraṇyam," one should cover the joint with gold. (14.41)

Having bathed the Goddess with five verses containing the word "water" (abliṅga) and with petals gathered by the twice-born, one should wipe her with a cloth using the mantra beginning with "agnimūr dha".
The covering of Śrī with two garments is performed with the two [mantras] "paritvā" and "gīrvaṇā";
[the offering] is made with the twelve-syllable mantra and the knowledge of the syllable Om (praṇava). || 14.43 ||
One should fasten gold upon his neck, accompanied by all auspicious things; one should bind him with the yoking-cord while reciting, "May he desire favor. (14.44)
The preceptor, facing the northern direction, should perform the marriage oblation;
having strewn the sacrificial grass according to rule, he should carry out the ritual procedure as prescribed.
In the marriage rite, the oblation is performed with fuel-sticks, sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter;
one should offer sixteen oblations with fuel-sticks and clarified butter, reciting the "Hymn to the Goddess."
With the *caru* offering and the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, there should be twenty-four oblations;
with the *Śrīsūkta*, there is the goddess Śrī, and with the *Bhūsūkta*, there is Bhuvaḥ.
If there are other goddesses, [one should perform] sixteen [offerings] with their root-mantras;
thereafter, one should perform the oblation of parched grain (*lājahoma*) with the *Puruṣasūkta*.
