Having circumambulated the fire three times, the preceptor should offer the remaining parched grain into the fire once with the *praṇava*, and again with the five *vāruṇika* mantras.
Having offered the expiatory oblation with the twelve-syllable vidyā,
the rite of the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be performed, and one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Having gratified the Lord of Gods and having worshipped the Goddess,
the preceptor should thereafter cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Then one should perform the lustration (nīrājana) of the deity and likewise the casting of the pedestal;
every day one should feed Brahmins and bathe [the deity] according to the prescribed rule.
One should perform the festival every day, morning and evening, according to the prescribed rule;
and one should constantly offer oblations into the fire at both twilights.
The preceptor should worship all the deities of the sacrificial ladles every day;
when the fourth day arrives, he should do so according to the rule during the fourth watch of the night.
He should have the concluding oblation of the wedding performed for the Lord of Kamalā;
with clarified butter and the mantras of the couple, he should perform one hundred and eight offerings.
The preceptor should again perform the expiatory oblation with the "Five Upaniṣads," and thereafter he should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Root Mantra.
One should offer betel leaves along with areca nuts and other ingredients with the syllable Om (praṇava);
one should also cause betel and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
On the fifth day, there shall be an oil massage for the two of them;
then, having offered the great sacrificial oblation, one should perform a grand festival.
Immediately after the wedding, one should worship the god together with the goddess;
such is the marriage rite for the other goddesses as well.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Fifteenth Chapter.
Agastya is the foremost among the creators, Rudras, Arka, Sutrāman, Kubera, and other nectar-eaters;
and among Tārkṣya, Vighneśa, the Serpent-King, Indra, Caṇḍa, and the stainless sages.
Of the celestial palaces, pavilions, and so forth, as well as the sacrificial pedestals and the like, of the bells, rosaries, vehicles, and especially of the goddesses. || 15.2 ||
O Bhārgava, O Lord, what is the nature of the consecration for radiant objects, lotus-thrones, and so forth, as well as for sandals, and for ponds, wells, and tanks? (15.3)
Śrī Rāma said: Listen, O best of sages, I shall describe the various types of consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
beginning with the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), exactly as they were performed previously.
If there is independence [of the ritual], there should be nine jars; if it is otherwise, there should be one jar.
In all rites, the installation of the great jar is performed with the *vardhanī* jar alone.
One should perform the invocation and installation in the great central jar;
one should perform the worship of Indra and the other deities in the eight subsidiary jars.
The oblation should be performed in a single vessel and not otherwise;
one should perform the extraction of the mantra using the respective name in the dative case. (15.7)
In rites such as the invocation of the vehicle and other offerings, the mantra should begin with the syllable Om and end with Namaḥ;
in the acts of oblation (havana), installation, and festivals, the mantra should end with Svāhā.
The ritual bathing (snapana) should be performed with nine jars and not otherwise conceived;
for images made of clay, stone, or cloth, the bathing should take place upon a mirror.
Now, a brief distinction regarding the goddesses, Śrī and the others, is stated:
having invoked Śrī into a lotus-shaped vessel in the eastern quarter, one should worship her.
At the door, the wise one should install Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī; then, at the station of Viṣvaksena, he should place Sumukhī; and in the nine jars, he should install them in successive order.
Having installed the Goddess in the great pitcher (mahākuṃbha), he should worship her by her own name;
and he should worship Sudarśana in the water-vessel (karaka), and in the eight [vessels] starting from the east, in due order.
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi,
as well as Prahvī, Satyā, and Brāhmī— these are to be worshipped in the pitchers.
Everything else is as before; there is no difference whatsoever.
The laying down of weapons and the sacrifice are proclaimed for Viṣṇu alone. 15.14.
Ascertain the specific characteristics of the celestial palaces, pavilions, and so forth,
after meditating upon Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, who is the very embodiment of the Nṛsūkta.
One should arrange the shadow-bath with a mirror and a kūrca-grass mat;
and one should perform the ritual of the bed upon the great altar by means of the kūrca.

Having touched the *kūrca* grass with the mantra "agnirme vāci," the preceptor should consecrate it; and over the great jar and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he should do so with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī. (15.17)
Having invoked [the deity], one should perform worship and likewise the fire-oblation (homa), O Jar-born One;
having offered sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and sesame seeds in the proper sequence.
Having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, one should sprinkle [the area] with the residual ghee;
all else, as well as for the pavilion, is exactly as before.
One should consecrate all the sacrificial pedestals directly in water,
bathe them according to the prescribed rule, and then place them upon heaps of grain.
Meditation, invocation, and the fire-oblation should also be performed as in the case of the celestial chariot.
"Oṃ, obeisance to the beings" is the mantra of the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha). || 15.21 ||
In the conceptualization of other such seats (pīṭhas),
the deity for the installation of the flagstaff (dhvajastaṃbha) is Khageśvara.
In that case, there is no release of the gaze from the palace and the pedestal;
however, when the ritual of placement (nyāsa) and the fire-oblation (homa) have been completed, one should proceed here as in the case of a celestial chariot (vimāna).
The bed upon the altar is likewise prepared, as is the bath and the consecration with water;
everything else regarding the arrangement of the offering altar is to be done as previously described.
The ritual for the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) shall be performed for both the sandal (pādukā) and the bell (ghaṇṭā).
Śeṣa is the presiding deity of the sandal, and Kamalālayā is the deity of the bell.
Upon the establishment of the kitchen, one should install Lakṣmī there;
Dhātṛ in the middle of the hearth, and Vidhātṛ behind it.
Having established Dharma and Adharma on the right and on the left respectively, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are likewise at that door; the remaining ritual is like that of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Varuṇa is the presiding deity of large oblong ponds, wells, and tanks.
Having first offered the ritual of germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should perform the installation of the water-pot (kumbhasthāpana).
One should tie the auspicious thread (kautuka) upon the pitcher with a tuft of grass (kūrca), and there should be a bed.
There should be the consecration by the principles (tattva-abhimantraṇa), the fire-oblation (homa), and the ritual according to the procedure for the celestial chariot (vimāna-vidhi).

At the time of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the Guru should perform everything else—the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana), as well as the leading forth and the release of the eyes—but not so [the other rites]. 15.30.
One should invoke the rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, there into the water with mantras;
one should employ the water from the great pitcher there by means of the Varuṇa hymn.
For the consecration of a rosary, one should perform the preliminary ritual (adhivāsana) with cow urine;
having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place it upon a lotus leaf.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the waters of the Puṇyāha rite, one should anoint it with saffron;
having placed it upon a seat of śāli rice, one should consecrate it with the mantra "Agnir me".
The Goddess shall be the power of Viṣṇu, and the mantra shall be the eight-syllabled one;
one should perform all the rites, such as the sprinkling of water, according to the prescribed rule.
Fire is the deity of incense, and the sun is the deity of the lamp;
for the parasol, the fly-whisk, and musical instruments, there should be the sprinkling with water consecrated on an auspicious day.
Between the deities such as Caṇḍa, the weapons of the Teacher of the World, and those of Indra and the other gods, there is no distinction whatsoever. (15.36)
In the consecration of an image made of clay, one should perform the rite with sprouts of *pratisarā*;
according to the procedure prescribed for marriage, one should worship a single water-pot.
One should perform the fire-oblation and other rites as before in a single pit (kuṇḍa).
There is no fire-oblation, no offering of bali, no pilgrimage site, and no rite of raising a banner. (15.38)
The hunt is for the water-trough, not for the rites of a festive meal;
and among the various vehicles such as chariots, the deity is the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa). || 15.39 ||
Having worshipped a single pitcher, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
and having performed the fire-oblation to the deity’s form (mūrtihoma), one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the water from the pitcher.

In the installation of the domestic image, the entire rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is performed as before; Hari, when established in the home, brings prosperity to the lineage of the household. (15.41)
"The deity installed in the temple shall protect the three worlds.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Sixteen
Having bathed and performed his morning rites, Śrī Rāma, the teacher, washed his feet and hands outside the temple, sipped water for purification three times, and entered the abode. (16.1)
Having gone to the first enclosure, having bowed to and addressed the Lord of Śrī,
one should then perform the opening of the door after clapping the hands three times.
Then one should awaken the eternal Lord Vāsudeva:
"Awaken, O Lord of the Universe! Awaken, O Consort of Kamalā! (16.3)
O awakened one, lotus-eyed; O awakened one, together with Ramā;
O ocean of infinite auspiciousness, awakened; O ocean of compassion! 16.4
O you with the face of the full moon and the lotus-feet of Kamalā,
the four Vedas praise you, and Druhiṇa and the other gods bow before you.
The moon has gone to the western mountain, and the sun is rising;
open your pair of eyes—the host of apsarases is dancing. 16.6.
Both Tumburu and Nārada sing beautifully upon their lutes;
all the sages stand outside the gate to offer service.
The morning rays spread forth, and even the lotuses have blossomed;
the bees wander within the hearts of the lotuses for the sake of the nectar.
The flocks of ruddy geese experience the state of householders;
the best of the twice-born attend upon you with mantras that say, "Arise! (9)
"Arise, arise, O Govinda! Arise, O Supreme Person!
Having thus awakened the Lord of Gods, even as the lamps were blazing—
One should cause garlands, perfumes, and other offerings to be presented to the deity Viṣvaksena,
and one should wash the vessels suitable for worship according to the prescribed rule.
Having placed the ritual strainers (pavitra) in his hands, wearing the vertical sectarian mark (urdhvapuṇḍra), and well-adorned,
while all musical instruments resound and the sound of the Veda is proclaimed— || 16.12 ||
Having meditated upon the Ghaṇṭā as consisting of the Śabdabrahman, the Preceptor should ring it with his hand;
then, with the Astra-mantra, he should bind the ten directions.
Then, with the root mantra, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma):
exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and likewise exhalation again.
Thus, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is described as being endowed with four types [of practice], or likewise with seven, or even with twice that number, or again with four times that number. || 16.15 ||
The number of the root mantra has been declared by those most learned in the scriptures as being equal to the number of syllables in the initial [mantra].
The knower of yoga should dissolve the earth, together with its fragrance, into water.
That [subtle element] together with taste [is dissolved] into fire; that into air along with the quality of form;
that into ether accompanied by touch; and that into the mind along with sound.

One should dissolve that ego-sense into the intellect, the intellect into the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle into the individual soul (jīva); one should dissolve that soul into the eternal Brahman.
Having established [the disciple], the Guru should meditate on the body as burnt by the seed-syllable of fire (vahnibīja);
he should then remember it as born again, sprinkled with the very seed-syllable of water (vāruṇabīja).
Having recollected the individual soul (jīva) as it emerged from Brahman, the supreme teacher [then recollected] the Great One (mahat),
and from that, the intellect (buddhi), and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) born from the intellect.
One should meditate on the mind as arising from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); from that, the ether through sound;
from the ether, the wind through touch; and from the wind, fire through form.

One should contemplate water as joined with fire and taste; from these two, one should likewise remember the earth together with smell. Having thus purified his body, the self-possessed practitioner [proceeds].
One should assign the eight syllables of the root mantra to the limbs in their proper order;
one should place the Praṇava at the navel and the letter *na* at the genitals.
One should place the syllable *mo* on the pair of knees, the syllable *nā* on the two feet,
the syllable *rā* on the head, and the syllable *ya* on the two eyes.
Having thus placed the syllable *ṇa* upon the lotus of the face and the syllable *ya* in the lotus of the heart,
and having meditated upon that Supreme Person after arranging those phonemes in this manner.
One should worship the God with the mind through various successive rites,
such as the offering of water for the guest (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the bath (snāna), and the garment and sacred thread (vastra-upavīta).
Incense, flowers, as well as incense smoke, lamps, and a handful of flowers; likewise, various kinds of food offerings, betel leaf, and mouth-fresheners.
One should perform [the rites] with the mind alone by means of the root mantra;
thereafter, one should recite the root mantra at least one hundred and eight times.
In front of the deity, one should place five vessels upon a supporting base;
these vessels should also be perfectly pure and made of pure metal.
One should place another vessel called the Āvāhana-vessel;
it should be filled with water that has dripped [from the other vessels] and consecrated with the syllable *praṇava*.
One should perform drying and flooding with the syllables of fire and nectar;
one should display the Surabhi mudrā with [the mantra] ending in "namaḥ" in the dative case.

The water for washing the feet (pādya) is in the center; the water for the guest-offering (arghya) is on the right; the water for sipping (ācamana) is on the left; the water for bathing (snānīya) is in the corner dedicated to Śaṅkara; and the pure water (śuddhodaka) is elsewhere.
Touching each [vessel] with his right hand while recollecting their respective names,
the twice-born should utter "I prepare" (kalpayāmi) and take water from the arghya vessel.
The best of the twice-born should pour a little [water] from another vessel, level with the nose, having consecrated it seven times with the root mantra. (16.34)
The supreme guru should sprinkle the five vessels and all the materials for worship without exception upon the footstool of the deity’s primary image (mūlabera). || 16.35 ||
One should fashion the yoga-pīṭha with the mantra beginning "āyāntv ādya. First is the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), followed by the tortoise (kūrma) and the fire of time (kālānala).
Then Ananta, and after him Mahīpa; and above, in ascending order, Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya, each in their respective order. (16.37)
In the directions starting from the east, there are, in order, the four beginning with Adharma;
in the corners starting from the southeast, and in their center, is Sadāśiva.
These have been declared to be the feet of the Lord of Kamalā’s couch;
the four Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, are the four wooden legs of the couch. (16.39)
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhautika—these are the threefold [evolutes].
Likewise, the qualities such as Sattva and the others are said to possess preceding and succeeding attributes. (16.40)
The vertical and horizontal threads are the mattress; above that is the five-layered bedspread, the individual soul (jīvātman); and above that, the lotus seat (padmāsana) is prescribed.
On both sides, Parameṣṭhin and Trilocana are to be depicted;
behind [the deity] are the three: Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sananda.

One who knows the true meaning of the principles of the Tantric scriptures should worship these [deities] by extracting their mantras, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), in the dative case, and ending with *namaḥ*. 16.43.
Then, having beheld the deity face-to-face and having prayed for eternal abiding,
the placement of the mantra-syllables should be performed according to the previous method.
Having duly prepared the Yoga-pīṭha upon the Sahaja-pīṭha of the Karmārcā,
one should take water in a vessel for the purpose of the Arghya during the invocation.
Having raised [the deity] up to the forehead with the root mantra, one should bring it forth with the *cañcu* mantra;
one should invoke from the primary image and sprinkle [water] upon the head for the sake of the ritual action.

Having closed the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) with the syllable Om, and having offered a welcome and a face-to-face greeting to the Lord of Kamala, he assumes the posture maintained at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the mantra upon the *pārṣva*, one should worship them in sequence with the *arghya* and other offerings.
One should offer the *arghya* with the *Sāvitrī* verse and the *pādya* with the verse beginning "trīṇi padā. (16.48)

One should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācāma*) with the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, "That Viṣṇu..."; the cleaning of the teeth with the mantra "Tad viṣṇo..."; and the scraping of the tongue with the verse "Tad viprāso...", in reverse order.
With the Vedic mantra "Ṛtaṃ satyam," one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth;
then, with the "Puruṣasūkta" alone, one should bathe Puruṣottama. (16.50)
With the verse "yuvā suvāsāḥ," he should offer two garments that are washed and stainless;
with the "yajñopavīta" mantra, he should provide the sacred thread (brahmasūtra). || 16.51 ||
One should anoint Hari with fragrant paste using the mantra "Gandhadvārā," and one should adorn him with flowers while reciting the Vedic hymn "Viṣṇornuka."
One should adorn her with all ornaments using the mantra "jitanta";
with the mantra "irāvatī," one should offer unbroken grains (akṣata) at her feet.
One should offer incense made from black aloe-wood and other such substances while reciting the mantra "dhūr asi";
then, having kindled the lamps with the mantra "uddīpyasva," one should display them.
Having gratified the four deities and displaying dance and song,
one should worship Hari with various flowers and many names.
Various sacrificial offerings, well-cooked and prepared in the kitchen,
were properly sprinkled with clarified butter and accompanied by side dishes and drinks.
Having brought these items as appropriate and arranged them on a seat in front,
one should sprinkle them with the Astra-mantra and consecrate them by sprinkling around with the Varma-mantra.
Reciting the mantra "devasya tvā," he should offer it to the deity three, five, or seven times, while displaying the *grāsamudrā* (the gesture of taking a morsel). || 16.58 ||
Having thus offered [the food] according to the rules, together with water and side dishes,
one should also offer betel-leaf with fragrant substances and say, "This for the feet."
Then, having emerged from his dwelling, he should complete the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma),
offer the bali-oblation to the spirits, and perform the daily festival.
Then, having entered the temple and performed the *nīrājana* rite with the "final" [lamp], the supreme guru should dismiss [the deity] from the *mūlabera*, as before. (16.61)
Having recited the eight-syllable mantra according to his capacity and having prostrated,
he should accept the water from the [teacher's] feet and drink it three times with his head bowed.
One should also carry sandals and likewise bring Tulasī and other offerings for the sake of serving even those ascetics and learned men who have arrived.
The preceptor should offer water for the feet and other honors to the other devotees of Viṣṇu;
having himself partaken of the food and other offerings presented to Viṣṇu, he should then accept them for his own self.
One should cause all those who have come for the sake of service to receive [food];
the household deities are to be worshipped with food offered to Viṣṇu.
One should eat the food offered to Viṣṇu, that which has been presented to the goddesses, and that food which has been presented to the retinue beginning with Caṇḍa. (16.66)
A person should not eat that which has been cast into water or fire;
by that, his ancestors cross over, being satisfied—of this there is no doubt.
This worship of Viṣṇu has been described to you in brief.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Seventeen
Having worshipped the two deities stationed at the side of the entrance, Śrī Rāma entered the fire-chamber and,
having smeared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with cow-dung and water, [he stood] in the west.
Having sat upon the seat facing east,
one should place flowers on one's right side and other ritual substances on the left.

Having restrained the breath and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should place darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon the northern ground of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and then deposit [the ritual items] upon them in sequence.

Then [he should prepare] the vessel for clarified butter, the pot for the sacrificial rice (caru), the vessel for sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī), as well as the praṇītā water, fuel-sticks, darbha grass, rice grains, and the three enclosing sticks (paridhi). || 17.4 ||

The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles endowed with the proper characteristics, the *darvī* spoon, the fan, the stirring-stick, the wooden block, the bell, unbroken grains, fragrant substances, and other items [should be prepared]. (17.5)

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) within the space between the sacrificial pits, one should draw three lines each, oriented toward the east and extending northward, individually with the syllable Om.
Having set aside the writing board and the brush, and having washed his hands with water,
he should sprinkle the fire with water using two bundles of darbha grass and then establish it.
Having swept around with water and strewn the fire with kuśa grass using ten blades each, which have tips and are pointed toward the east with their ends facing north.

One should place the full *praṇītā* vessel, filled with water, between the *dravya* and the fire; having fashioned a *kūrca* with a pair of *darbha* blades containing unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should set it down.
There, one should invoke and worship the eternal Lord Vāsudeva;
one should seat Him upon a throne in the south-eastern corner of the fire.

Having covered the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with three purified *darbha* blades, he should place it in front of himself; there, he should set down the *praṇītā* water along with the *kūrca* grass and the *ānaka* vessels.
Having filled and purified the vessels with water, the preceptor should turn them face upwards and sprinkle them with the water used for sprinkling;
then he should bring the vessel for the clarified butter (ājya).
Having placed that *kūrca* upon it, and upon that *kūrca* which serves as a seat composed of that [deity],
one should worship the four-faced god to the south of the fire.
Having filled that vessel of clarified butter with the very butter that has been strained,
one should place it to the north of the fire and set the vessel containing the clarified butter upon it.
One should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) for it with a blazing sacrificial grass (barhis);
having placed two tips of darbha grass upon it, one should again perform the circumambulation with fire. || 17.15 ||
Having lifted that vessel out [of the water], one should place the fire within the fire;
one should cook it in the sacrificial fire using the heart and other limbs [as mantras] in the vessel containing the sacrificial porridge (caru).
The vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru) should be placed to the north of the fire in due order;
having placed the vessel of clarified butter (ājya) in front, the supreme preceptor purifies it three times.
Having untied the tuft-knot and touched it with water, he should place it in the fire;
having shown the cow of Surabhi, he should contemplate that ghee as nectar.
One should worship Indra and the others in sequence around the fire-pit;
then the preceptor should wash the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with very hot water.
Having wiped [the two blades] with a bundle of five *darbha* grasses at their root, middle, and tip,
and having heated them over the fire, one should place them toward the north.
Having untied the knot of the *kūrca* and touched water, one should place it in the fire;
one should sprinkle clarified butter once with the *sruva* ladle over each of the items for the oblation.
The enclosing sticks (paridhi) should be placed with their tips pointing upward in the west;
likewise, one should place them with their tips pointing eastward in the south and in the northern direction.
One should place both the supporting fuel-sticks (adhāra-samit) in the southeast and northeast;
then one should perform the sprinkling of water (pariṣecana) with the mantras beginning with "O Aditi... and so forth.
Having sprinkled fifteen pieces of fuel wood with clarified butter once,
he should then mutter the eight-syllable mantra while meditating upon the Supreme Lord.
Having wrapped his hand with kuśa grass and secured it with his fist in the mudrā gesture, he should take up the vessel of clarified butter; thereafter, he should perform the Prājāpatya offering.
One should offer oblations into the fire for Indra, for Agni, and for Soma,
using the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively, in their proper order.
Then, having sprinkled water around the fire, one should meditate upon it with four horns;
"Oṃ agnaye namaḥ svāhā"—thus there shall be the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the fire.
Having two heads, seven arms, three feet, and seven tongues,
he grants boons, holds a spear in his hand, and likewise carries a *sruk* and a *sruva* ladle.
He holds a shield that grants fearlessness and a vessel of clarified butter in his left hand;
indeed, [his attendants] are Kālī, Karālī, Sumanā, Lohitā, and Dhūmrā.
Sphuliṅginī, Viśvarūpī, and the seven tongues are thus proclaimed.
Kālī’s station is in the middle, while Karālī’s occurs in the eastern direction.
Manojavā resides in the southeast, Lohitā in the west;
Sudhūmrā has Soma as her abode, and Sphuliṅginī rests in the northwest.
One should thus remember the locations in sequence: Visvarūpī is in the northeast;
on the tongue and in the right face, with Dhūmrā, [one performs] killing and other rites.
Subjugation is achieved with Lohitā; with Kālī, one performs rites of pacification (śāntika);
and all success is attained with Sphuliṅginī when the face is turned toward the left.
Karālikā bestows victory, Puṣṭidā bestows nourishment, and Manoharā is captivating;
their colors are blackness, redness, and dark green respectively.
Then there is the form of sparks, and the color resembling crystal;
that which resembles refined gold is said to appear on the tongue in successive order.
The perpetual fire (nityāgni) is said to be old; the festive fire (utsavāgni) is young;
and the fire for initiation, pacification, and consecration is designated as the child-fire (bālāgni).
The fire produced from the friction of the two kindling sticks (araṇīs) is called the "infant fire" (bālāgni);
that produced from the sun-crystal stone (sūryakānta) is proclaimed as the "youthful fire" (yauvanāgni). || 17.37 ||
The worldly fire is the "Vṛddha" fire; this is declared to be the threefold fire-seal.
The span of the fuel-sticks is one tāla, which is considered to be the measurement from the tip of the little finger to the elbow.
If it lacks leather, there will be destruction; if it is split, the lineage will perish. If it is damp, there will be the loss of kinsmen; if it is old, there will be the loss of sons.
For a carpenter, the death of his wife brings quarrels; for one who has children, it brings anxiety; if she is large, it brings distress, while if she is small, it causes obstacles.

A fuel-stick (samid) that is excessively long or produced by over-ripening should be discarded if it is possessed of defects. Peace is attained through [fuel] originating from sacrificial trees, and good fortune through flowers.
Through incense substances one always obtains health; through curd, nourishment; through pure milk, purity; through food, various desires; and through clarified butter, long-lived progeny.
A man desiring the glory of Brahman should offer oblations with white lotuses;
one desiring prosperity should offer oblations with Lakṣmī flowers, or else with those belonging to Varuṇa.
One desiring knowledge should offer lotuses or *bilva* fuel-sticks with clarified butter;
one desiring a daughter should offer parched grain (*lāja*), and one desiring cattle should again offer cow-dung.
One desiring long life should use dūrvā grass; one desiring land, soil; one desiring sensory power, barley; and one desiring to be dear to all people, sesame seeds.
But one who desires spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) [should sacrifice] with grains produced from the Brahma-tree, as well as with bamboo-seeds, barley, wild rice (nīvāra), and śāli-rice. || 17.46 ||
All desires are accomplished for the sacrificer by means of the seeds as prescribed;
all desires are accomplished by an oblation of parched grain (lāja), of this there is no doubt.
One desiring food should offer other kinds of food; one desiring a son, milk-rice (pāyasa); one seeking gold, nimba flowers; and all desires are fulfilled by means of clarified butter.
At home, streams of ghee, honey, and milk should be four finger-breadths wide;
the offering of curd should be a spoonful (śukti), and the offering of milk-rice and other foods should be a mouthful (grāsa).
The offering of edible food should be half of that amount, consisting of unbroken fruits and flowers;
the offering of incense substances should be the measure of a single *niṣpāva* seed.

The fuel-sticks should be eight finger-breadths long, or half of that; the dūrvā grass should be six finger-breadths long; and the offering of cow-dung is said to be the size of a grape or a jujube fruit.
O Lord of Sages, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) of clarified butter should be one kuḍava;
oblations for the gods and ancestors offered with a measure either less or more than this [are deficient]. || 17.52 ||
The Dānavas and Daityas consume it; it does not conduce to fruit.
Having sprinkled the fire with armor, one prepares the seat within the fire.
One should perform the invocation of Hari into the fire with the mantras beginning with *ādhāraśakti*,
and carry out all the ritual services (*upacāra*) as before, O Uṣarbudha.
With those various mantras ending in "svāhā," having offered ghee once with each,
he should likewise perform the rite up to the final offering for the sake of the retinue as well.
Having offered oblations with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra), one should perform the sprinkling as before;
this is the daily worship in the fire, to be performed immediately after the installation and other rites.
One should perform other rites, such as the fire-oblation (homa), according to the rules prescribed for each specific action.
In the daily rite, the Vītihotra fire is to be maintained; however, there is no Praṇītā water nor the Ātmabhū fire.
There shall be no casting of sacrificial fuel into the fire, nor the cooking of the *caru* oblation;
the worship of Viṣṇu in the fire shall consist solely of clarified butter, concluding with the recitation of prayers.
The Aghāra oblation need not be performed when the fire has been lost; however, this entire rite, beginning with the re-establishment [of the fire], should be carried out in all cases of expiation.
The best of those who know the tantras should not cause Brahmā and the others to depart at the conclusion of the rite;
rather, having offered the expiatory oblations, he should then perform the final full oblation.
Having placed the *sruva* ladle in front of himself, the *ājyasthālī* vessel to the south, and the *sruc* ladle to the north,
he should take up the consecrated *kuśa* grass with both hands.
One should place the root mantra in the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the middle mantra in the center, and the other mantra in the ladle (sruvī).
Having touched them in this manner three times, one should offer oblations into the fire; likewise, one should burn the darbha grasses.
The preceptor should first place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) around himself and then set down the praṇītā vessel;
having filled it with water from the prokṣaṇī vessels, he should sprinkle it in the directions starting from the east.
He should pour the remainder on the ground, sprinkle his own head,
dismiss Brahmā afterwards, and fill the sacrificial ladle with water.
Then, having sprinkled water around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should extract the deity from the fire;
one should apply a tilaka mark with the ashes remaining from the oblation that dispels all obstacles.
Having worshipped the fire with the mantra "Agnaye," he then [offered] into the fire whatever was prescribed for it, according to his ability and according to the rules, out of devotion.
"O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Lord, accept this propitiation"—
with these words, one should place the fruit of the oblation upon the lotus-feet of the God.
"I have heard from Agastya, the supreme abode, the sequence of worship for the fire; now,
tell me today how the ritual of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is to be performed."
Śrī Rāma should worship the deity with water for the guest-offering and other rites in the fire using ghee from cows;
the most excellent of teachers, having filled the ladle with clarified butter, [should do so] by a measure of one kuḍava.

Having worshipped the sacrificial ladle (sruk) with fragrances, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), the preceptor [honored it] as being joined with a blade of darbha grass, provided with a fuel-stick (samidh), and filled with fruit.
Then, having covered [the vessel] with the *sruva* ladle and drawing up [the water] as far as the tip of his nose,
he rose while sounds were now resounding everywhere.
Proclaiming the mantra "pūrṇāhuti" among the twice-born,
the Guru should offer oblations into the pure fire with the root mantra.
One should perform the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation with a sacrificial porridge (caru) the size of a hen’s egg,
drenched in ghee and accompanied by all kinds of side dishes.
Having placed sugar, honey, and *darbha* fuel-sticks into the large ladle (*sruc*),
having moistened them with clarified butter, and having covered them with the tip of the small dipping-spoon (*sruva*).
One should offer oblations with the root mantra.
Chapter Eighteen.
Śrī Rāma said: I shall describe the procedure for the daily festival; listen attentively as it truly is.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World in the fire, one should then perform the daily festival.
Having entered the dwelling, one should worship the image of Balarāma;
then, having placed the sacrificial materials upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, one should carry them away.
One should prepare for the offering a large quantity of food with side-dishes, accompanied by milk, curd, and ghee;
or otherwise, one may provide pure food for the sake of the bali-offering.
Carrying water for all purposes, known as pure water, along with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, and lamps, the attendants should proceed.
Singing and dancing, with cymbals and drums in their hands,
they should go before the Lord together with many lamps.
Taking the fan, the chowrie, the parasol, and all other items belonging to the festival, the officials should proceed in front of the deity. (18.6)
Beginning with Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, one should perform the offering of oblations (balidāna);
the name of each deity should be accompanied by the dative case ending and the word "namaḥ. (18.7)
Having uttered the Praṇava and other [mantras], one should perform the offering of the bali;
saying: "This is the arghya, this is the bali, and this is the water for you. (18.8)
One should offer water to the northeast, accompanied by the sounds of palm-clapping and dancing;
then likewise fragrance, flowers, a lamp, the arghya offering, and finally the bali.
And water must be offered in the courtyard during the ritual of bali-offering for all the gatekeepers, beginning with Caṇḍa; this is the bull-like sound [of the rite]. (18.10)
The dance of Vaijayantī is indeed called Mallatāla;
the dance of Khageśa is Viṣṇukrānta, and its rhythm is Gāruḍa.
The musical note for Viṣvaksena is said to be the middle (madhyama);
his dance is called the Svastika; and the rhythm is Balita with the Ṛṣabha note.
Likewise, the dance of Gaṇeśa is performed with the Bhadratāla rhythm and the fifth note (pañcama);
O son of Kumbha, the note for Durgā is the sixth note (dhaivata).
The dance of Sarvamaṅgala should be performed with the Bhadratāla meter; the Brahma-dance of Brahmā should be performed with the Brahmatāla meter. || 18.14 ||
The voice of that Śunāsīra is said to be the middle note (madhyama);
the playful dance is declared to be accompanied by the ṣaḍja note.
The equal time-measure (samatāla) of fire is said to be the Ṛṣabha note;
the dance performed with the bound descent-time-measure (baddhāvatāla) is proclaimed as Sarvatobhadra.
The dance of Yama’s shield is said to be in the Gāndhāra note;
for Nirṛti, the rhythm is called Śṛṅgiṇī and the note is Madhyama. || 18.17 ||
Likewise, the mallatāla rhythm, the dance, and the circular movement (cakramaṇḍala) have been described;
the note of Varuṇa is said to be the fifth, called Maṅgala.
Tāla is the dance of the forest; Maruta is the dhaivata note.
Jayatāla, however, is said to be the dance of the back-stamping.
For Soma, the auspiciousness is the palm, the dance is the binding of the waist, and the musical note is said to be Niṣāda; for Śaṅkara, however, it is Dhaivata.
The musical note is Ḍhakkarī, and the rhythm is dancing with the left knee raised.
The voice of other gods as well is held to be the fifth [note].
The Bhadratāla is said to be the dance of all auspiciousness;
it is the offering-balance (balitāla) for living beings, and its musical note is said to be Gāndhāra.
O Pot-born One, one should display the dance of all auspiciousness (sarvamaṅgalanṛtta),
having circumambulated that [deity] in due order up to the end of the third enclosure.
Having offered the bali-oblation together with various dances and other performances according to the prescribed rule,
one should deposit the bali-substances and the remnants of the bali upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
At the conclusion of the festival, the most excellent of gurus, having worshipped Hari there as was appropriate until the end of the procession, then helped him down from the vehicle.
Having led them into the interior of the temple, one should establish Śrī and the other goddesses, as well as Brahmā and the others, each in their proper place.
One should perform the worship of other retinues and dependents with their respective mantras, but the offering should be presented to the principal deities.
Bali likewise [performed worship] for the gatekeepers, as well as for Vidhi and Rudra,
for Indra and the other world-protectors, and for all those dwelling in the enclosures.
In this manner, one should offer the bali-oblation to the presiding deities of the seats (pīṭhas),
as well as to the goddesses who reside there, and also to Tārkṣya and Śeneśa.
And for those devotees who have taken refuge [in him], he provides worship until their final attainment.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Bhārgava-tantra.
The Nineteenth Chapter.
If, in the event of a deficiency in the temple's foundations or its decorative elements, as well as in its constituent parts and so forth,
it can be repaired, then one should perform the restoration.
When the abode and the image have been rendered empty and impossible [to sustain], one should abandon them and create again;
having joined the previous substance suitable for re-creation, one should fashion it anew. (19.2)
A wise person desiring prosperity should cast into unfathomable water that which is unfit or discarded; nor should one worship an image that is broken or cracked. (19.3)
When the restoration of the limbs is easily accomplished, one should install the Śakti in the Kumbha;
however, in the case of an image that is infinitely decayed or a child-image, one should worship Hari [directly].
One should not conceive of [the deity] elsewhere, having abandoned the abode or the image;
for if one does so conceive, there is great fault for both the preceptor and the patron.
But during the conjunction, one should invoke the power of the celestial chariot into the Pole Star (Dhruva).
In the case of a permanent image (dhruvabera), or when it is joined with a water-pot (kumbha) or a child-pleasing image (bālakautuka),
if there is a deficiency regarding the attendant deities (parivāra), their invocation should take place within the permanent image.
In the case of a fracture or a joint in a limb, one should likewise provide a surrounding support;
having thus carefully considered everything, one should carry out the restoration of what is decayed.
In the intermediate space between the cardinal and intermediate directions of Mādhava’s residence,
one should construct a dwelling for the child in a suitable and pleasant location.
With five cubits by the length of the arm, and seven when contracted at the hips,
one should fashion that charming, quadrangular dwelling for children.
In whichever direction the entrance was located in the previously constructed temple,
one should likewise arrange the birth-chamber for the child in that same direction.
Whether made of metal, wood, or stone, a beautiful image of the Child should be fashioned as it was in the ancient temple. (19.12)
The height of the child image increases by five finger-breadths for every increase of one cubit,
and it decreases by twenty finger-breadths for every decrease of one cubit.
One should fashion the image as previously described, and not otherwise, O Agastya;
having thus fashioned the image of the Child and the temple, the wise man [should proceed].
At this auspicious time, having worshipped the best of the twice-born, having caused them to pronounce blessings, and having given them sacrificial fees; 19.15.
Permitted by those Brahmins, he should first choose a preceptor;
having prostrated before him according to the scriptures, he should adorn and worship him.
Then, for the sake of pacifying any deficiency in the limbs [of the ritual], the teacher who is learned in the scriptures should perform one thousand oblations with *dūrvā* grass mixed with honey.

Afterwards, having offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* and the "five *upaniṣads*," one should perform the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); by that, there is no doubt that peace is attained. || 19.18 ||
Thereafter, one should offer the sprouts and, having tied the protective cord (pratisara),
perform the entire ritual— including the preliminary consecration in water— exactly as before.
Either in the center of a child's house, or in a divine place, or even in a human dwelling,
having constructed an altar one cubit high, one should install [the image] upon it.
One should not perform the ritual placement of gems according to the rules with the root mantra;
rather, one should sprinkle [the site] as before and then proceed to the primary temple. || 19.21 ||
Having propitiated the primary image and placed the pitcher before Hari,
one should invoke [the deity] there from that [image], resorting to the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
Having worshipped the pitcher with the *arghya* water and Vedic chants accompanied by musical instruments, the Preceptor, taking the pitcher along with other images, [proceeded]. (19.23)
Having entered the children's hall by circumambulating that temple,
one should install the ritual icons and other images in their respective places there.
Then one should project the power residing in the pitcher into the image of the child;
one should perform everything as before and then request the presence [of the deity].
O Blessed One, remain present here until the restoration of your abode and your body is completed.
Having thus prayed, one should then worship the God together with his limbs;
one should worship all the attendants, free from any deficiency.
One should offer the deficient deities at the lotus-feet of the Lord;
even for those seats that have been omitted, they are said to be included as part of the retinue.
But for those who are dependent [upon him], there is distinctness, like that of a retinue;
and for all the goddesses, Śrī and the others, it is likewise like a retinue.
One should perform the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites as before;
or else, there may be only the obligatory rite until the completion of the restoration of the dilapidated structure.
One should perform the great festival according to whatever is the ancient daily rite;
there should be an offering of oblations on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and upon the seat (pīṭha) at the time of the true path.
Having thus completed [the rites], the wise preceptor, having gone to the inner sanctum and taking up a golden plough, should release the binding of the pedestal.
One should wrap the image with kuśa grass, kāśa grass, other types of grass, and likewise with ropes made of cow-hair; thereafter, one should place it upon the chariot.
Having circumambulated the village, or the ocean, or a lake, or any water that is unfathomable and never dries up; (19.34)
Having gone there, one should either cast the image [into water] or even bury it in the ground;
then, having bathed according to the prescribed rule, [one may proceed] if the rite of re-consecration is to be performed.
For the sake of rejoining, the preceptor should provide an image of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow;
having had it fashioned, he should perform either a new creation or a rejoining according to the prescribed rite.

All the rites, beginning with the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa), should be performed again as before during a new creation; however, this is not required in the case of a mere reconnection (sandhāna).
One should perform the ritual sprinkling and install the power of the child (bāla-śakti);
having thus sprinkled it according to the rules, together with the ritual images (karmabimba).
One should worship the Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, as before.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Bhārgava-tantra.
The Twentieth Chapter
Śrī Rāma has proclaimed in many ways the ritual bathing of the God of gods;
therein lies a specific Brahma-rite which one should employ in all ritual actions.
Alternatively, O great sage, one should perform either the Vaiṣṇava bath or some other meritorious rite; these are of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
The Brāhma rite, however, should consist of twenty-five [vessels], while the middle one should consist of eight fewer;
this Vaiṣṇava rite is declared to be meritorious when performed with nine jars.
In the center of the ground of the bathing pavilion, the Guru should prepare an altar,
five cubits in length and breadth, which is pleasing to the eye.
One should lay down fourteen threads with their tips pointing east and north,
moistened with sandalwood paste, forming sixty-nine squares.
Therein, one should clear away the three spaces— the Brāhma, the Daiva, and the Mānuṣa— each separated by one [space], for the sake of the pathways.
In the Brahma-square, however, having set aside the central path, there are nine locations for the jars;
in the Daiva-square, eight jars are to be placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The remaining eight [parts] should likewise be wiped on the human [altar];
one should prepare a seat with grains for those remaining parts that are to be wiped.
Clarified butter, warm water, a gem, fruit, iron,
bathing water, scents, and unbroken grains of barley— these eight are placed in order from the center outward for the Brahma-pitcher.
Having established [the deity] upon the eight divine pedestals, one should then offer water for the feet and curd;
thereafter, one should place the water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, drinking water, and then the jar of honey.
The Guru should place a jar of scented water in the eastern direction of the human [mandala].
In the south, sugarcane juice; in the west, coconut water;
in the north, the water of pacification (śāntitoya); and in the southeast, auspicious water (maṅgalodaka).
One should place a jar containing the essence of all medicinal herbs in the Yātudhāna [direction];
one should place water with all perfumes in the Vāyu [direction], and root-herbs in the Raudra [direction].
One should cast in ruby, emerald, sapphire, diamond, topaz, coral, pearl, and likewise emerald.
One should place lapis lazuli and the nine gems into the water-jar containing precious stones,
together with plantain, bījapūra, mango, dhātrī, and bilva fruits.
Coconut, jackfruit, and the juice of citron fruit;
likewise gold, silver, copper, lead, and tin.
One who is learned in the Kalpa-tantras should place seven water-pots made of bell-metal, iron, and the other [metals], each weighing one niṣka, within the water.
The wise man should place in the bathing pitcher the night-blooming lotus (Cassia fistula),
the sun-plant (Calotropis gigantea), sahadevī, śirīṣa, sadābhadra, and the tips of kuśa grass.
These six cleansing substances, each weighing one handful,
are indeed sandalwood, agallochum, kuṣṭha, murā, māṃsī, and saffron.
One should place nine fragrant substances— namely, hrabera, uśīra, and girija— in that jar, each weighing one pala.
Wild rice, bamboo-seed rice, śāli rice, priyaṅgu, ṣāṣṭika rice, wheat, and paddy—these six unhusked grains were each the size of a handful. || 20.21 ||
Furthermore, one should place these three— rice, barley, and bamboo—
in a jar of barley-water, each measuring exactly one *kuḍava*.
Tulasī, lotus, dūrvā grass, śyāmāka grain, and likewise unbroken rice (akṣata), as well as viṣṇukrāntā and bilva leaves— one muṣṭi measure of each individually.
One should place one pala of sandalwood and eight items in the water for washing the feet:
tips of kuśa grass, unbroken grains of rice, white mustard seeds, sesame seeds, flowers, and fruits.
One should place eight substances in the arghya-pitcher: barley in separate handfuls, sandalwood weighing one pala, and a fruit that has borne fruit.
Cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, jasmine, camphor, campaka, sandalwood, and flowers—these eight [are placed] in the vessel for the ceremonial sipping (ācāma). 20.26.
One should place these— cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter— in equal measures of half a *pala* each within it.
One should place four palas of each of these substances into a jar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
and one should likewise deposit these same substances into a jar of decoction water.
Śamī, palāśa, khadira, bilva, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, udumbara, and nyagrodha—these eight are known as the barks. || 20.29 ||
One should place these six substances in the peace-pitcher (śāntikuṃbha): Tulasī, bamboo, wild rice (nīvāra), barley, white mustard seeds, and sesame seeds. || 20.30 ||
Each of these should be the size of a handful, as well as powdered bark;
likewise, sprouts of Indravalī, shoots of Aśvattha, and Kuśeśaya [lotus].
The single-petaled lotus, kuṣṭha, saffron, the rohiṇī tree,
the eight auspicious flowers, as well as yūthikā and mallikā.
One should place three blue lotuses, jasmine, campaka, and likewise ketaki,
as well as fifteen substances, into the auspicious water.
Māṃsī, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, campaka, mustā, vacā, and karpūra—one pala each of these. || 20.34 ||
Having consecrated all the medicinal herbs in water, one should cast these ten [substances] into it:
camphor, saffron, costus, spikenard, sandalwood, and *murā*.
Priyaṅgu, kesara, mustā, tamāla, nāgakesara, the two types of mūla, kaccora, surasa, pika, and kesara. (20.36)
Uśīra, tagara, lodhra, and likewise haricandana; agaru-scented kuṣṭha, kāleya, and granthipallava.
Having ground one *pala* each of the buds of the *campaka* tree,
one should place them there in the jar containing water with all the fragrant substances.
Vyāghrī, siṃhī, balā, agnimantha, śarapuṅkhā, śatāvarī, bilva root, vacā, śuṇṭhī, koraṇḍa, and śatamūlikā. || 20.39 ||
Each of these root-herbs, weighing one pala, should be ground and placed in a jar; these are declared to be used for the rite of bathing the deity.
Having brought one *droṇa* each of honey, curd, milk, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and clarified butter—or alternatively, one *āḍhaka* of each—of Śiva; 20.41.
One should prepare all the material jars of that same size;
one should fill the powder jar with night-lily (niśā) powders up to the level of the neck.

In a field of merit, on a riverbank, a mountain, a sandbank, or a lake; at a waterfall, a confluence, or in a place that does not dry up, as well as in a sacrificial enclosure or a plot of fertile soil. || 20.43 ||
In a field of śāli rice, in a pool dug by the gods, on the horn of a bull, on an elephant, on a boar, on an anthill, and likewise in the dwelling of a crab; || 20.44 ||
And nineteen [vessels] should be placed in the lotus pond and the oblong pool;
one should fill each separately with earth and water in the measure of a handful.
One should first offer the sprouts and place the protective thread (pratisara) on the hand;
this applies to a single image, the primary image, or when there is a multitude of images for the bathing and the festive rite.
If the image is to be laid on a bed while the other [materials] are for bathing,
the preceptor should raise it from the bed in the morning by means of a brush.
Having worshipped the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth as before,
one should cause study, dance, song, and instrumental music to proceed at the gates.
Thereafter, one should place the bathing image in the bathing pavilion;
then, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day recited and also sprinkle the ritual jars.
One should also prepare bathing substances and perform the installation of the water jars; the wrapping with threads should be done with the mantra beginning "indraṃ natvā. (20.50)
One should place the jars in their respective locations with the root-vidyā;
the filling of the jars with substances and water is performed with the "all-mantra. (20.51)
Just as the arrangement of sprouts with a tuft of grass is pleasing to the eye,
one should have those jars covered with shallow bowls while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Their auspicious adornment shall be made with coconut fruits;
one should wrap the jars in cloths and decorate them with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice.
And when the quarters of the sky have been made to resound with the sounds of the Vedas, lutes, and other instruments,
the most excellent of preceptors should perform the invocation of the deities into the jars.
Vāsudeva resides in a jar of ghee, Puruṣa in warm water; Satya would be in fruit-water, while Acyuta is declared to be present during the bath itself.
Keśava is in the infinite, unbroken jar containing jeweled water;
the god Nārāyaṇa is in the metal vessel, and Mādhava is in the fragrant water.
Govinda is proclaimed for the barley-water (yavodaka), Viṣṇu for the water for the feet (pādya); Madhuhantā for the arghya jar, and Trivikrama for the water for sipping (ācāma).
Vāmana is in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), Śrīdhara is in the vessel of curd;
Hṛṣīkeśa is in the jar of milk, and Padmanābha is also in the honey.
Having thus performed [this rite] in a decoction of astringent substances, Dāmodara becomes a boar;
and in a jar of molasses, he becomes Nṛsiṃha; and in sugarcane juice, he becomes a man-lion.
Śrīdhara is in Nālikera-uda; Hayāsya is in Śānti-vāri; Vāsudeva is in Maṅgala-uda; and Saṅkarṣaṇa is in Sarvauṣadhī.
Pradyumna is in all fragrant waters, and Aniruddha is in the root-herbs;
thus are the deities of the Brahma-pitchers proclaimed.
Lakṣmī resides in a jar of powdered substances, and the Earth in a jar of clay;
thus the wise man should perform the invocation, preceded by the yoga-pīṭha.
Having uttered the eightfold enclosure with each respective name in the dative case, joined with "namaḥ" and the syllable "oṃ," one should then perform the invocation.
Having worshipped him according to the rules with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with the *praṇava*, and having duly consecrated the fire and propitiated the Lord of Śrī therein; 20.64.
"Sweet are the winds," "Sweet by night," "May our food be sweet," "The Lord of the Forest";
"I know," "Of Viṣṇu indeed," and "The plants converse. || 20.65 ||
And likewise the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka, as well as "yā oṣadhīḥ," and immediately thereafter the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, "tad viṣṇoḥ. (20.66)
By the Śruti text "Not you are Viṣṇu," by the mantra "The deeds of Viṣṇu," by the Yajus formula "O Dadhikrāvan," and indeed by the Ṛk verse "Swell up! (20.67).
The preceptor [should recite] "madhuvātā," "oṣadhayastvam," "viṣṇuryā phalinī," "śanno devīḥ," the Sāvitrī, and "trātāram. (20.68)
After [reciting] the Mahāvyāhṛtis, immediately following "Gandhadvārām," they then poured the clarified butter of the Vasus, which flows in a hundred streams. || 20.69 ||
One should offer oblations with clarified butter using these mantras and collect the remnants of the offering;
one should also sprinkle them into the jars and dismiss the deity from the fire.
Accompanied by the officiating priests, the preceptor consecrates the jars with the five pacification mantras and the weapon mantra, and covers them with a cloth.
One should offer a tooth-stick, scented oil, and then an āmalaka fruit;
one should then cause the two rinses for the mouth and the sipping of water to be given to the deity, as well as the arghya and other offerings.
One should bathe Hari with water from jars while reciting the Pauruṣa Sūkta;
one should worship Him with garments, sacred threads, and so forth, up to the offering of food.
Having first sprinkled with the *kūrca*, one should subsequently perform the consecration with the water-pot (*kuṃbha*).
This constitutes the Brāhma bath; now listen as the Vaiṣṇava bath is described.
Having placed those jars for the Brahman and the Devas and invoked [the deities] as before,
one should offer sixteen oblations with the Vaiṣṇava hymn alone.
And having first offered oblations with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī while sprinkling the remnants of the offering, everything else is as before; there is no difference whatsoever.
Now I shall proclaim the merit of the ritual bathing of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, which,
having transcended both the divine and the human, is established in the Brahma-sphere within nine jars.
One should place the pitcher for Brahman filled with ghee in the east, and place the pitcher for the water for the feet (pādya) in the southeast;
the pitcher for the respectful offering (arghya) in the south, and the water for sipping (ācamana) in the west.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are in the north; a vessel of curd in the southeast;
a jar of milk in the southwest; and a vessel of honey in the northwest.
And in the northeast corner is Kaṣāya; the materials and deities are as before.
[One recites] "Born from the waters" and "I am the Veda, the Lord of Creatures. (20.80)
"He who [knows] the Ṛc for the gods, the Brāhmaṇa, and that which is beyond the Goddess of Speech... 'four with faith' and so forth. (20.81)
One should offer oblations into the fire with nine [mantras] and sprinkle it with the residual ghee;
O Agastya, everything else is as previously described.
The oblation (*homa*) during the rite of bathing with turmeric should be performed with the *Śrīsūkta*;
when there is a bath with clay, the offering should be made with the *Bhūmisūkta*.
Vāsudeva, Pārameṣṭhya, and Prājāpatya—
this threefold [rite] is the great ablution (mahāsnapana) for rites of expiation.
Eight jars of materials for the Brahmins should be placed on every side;
pure water-jars should also be set out, their total number being two hundred.
O Agastya, the worship of the material pitcher has been described previously;
Nārāyaṇa is traditionally held to be the deity of all pitchers containing pure water.
O Sage, one should place pearls or silver into all pure waters; the mantra for the oblation (homa), however, is that which was previously declared.

Having offered oblations with clarified butter by means of those [mantras], and subsequently having offered one thousand and eight oblations with the twelve-syllable vidyā, he should perform the *sampāta* oblation.
An expert in ritual action should perform everything else as previously described;
this bath known as Vāsudeva grants all desires.
Now I shall describe the Pārameṣṭhya [rite] correctly; listen attentively.
Around the Vaiṣṇava jars, there should be eight separate ones.
Having performed everything for these one hundred and thirty-six water-pots exactly as before, according to the procedure prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas. || 20.91 ||
One should perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa with the water in the jars using the root mantra alone,
and with the Vaiṣṇava Sūkta ending with the Gāyatrī, just as before.
Having offered eight thousand oblations with the root mantra, everything else is as before; now hear concerning the Prājāpatya rite.
The ritual of the meritorious ablution (puṇyasnāna) should be performed with eight [vessels] on each side;
when done in that manner, there are likewise seventy-two jars of water.
The invocation of Viṣṇu is performed with the six-syllabled Vaiṣṇava mantra; by means of that, there is a special worship consisting of one thousand and eight recitations.
Having consecrated them with those various jars of ritual substances and their accompanying waters,
and having bathed, adorned, and worshipped them according to the prescribed rite.
Having prostrated, circumambulated, and praised him in many ways with hymns,
he should afterwards lead the one adorned for the bath into the interior of the temple.
If the ritual for Ekabera is performed, the bathing takes place at the primary *kautuka*.
O Agastya, born from a jar, listen as I describe the bathing of Kaubera.
Ghee is in the center, curd in the southeast, nectar in the southwest quarter,
honey in the northwest quarter, and sugar in the northeast quarter.
Nṛsiṃha and Śarkarādeva [should be worshipped] as before for the others,
with the mantra "brahmajajñānam" and the knowledge-mantra "ayāścāgne."
With the verse "To him who does not press [the Soma]" and with the mantra "Come hither," and likewise with "Him, the Lord"— in this manner, everything else remains as before.
In this very manner, with the forty auspicious waters, the bath is declared to be auspicious; having recited the [mantras], there is the invocation of Hari.
One should offer that very substance into the fire one thousand and eight times;
with a single jar of ghee, the unsurpassed bath is accomplished.
O Lord of Sages, this [diagram] for Indra, joined with the eight Upakuṃbhas,
constitutes the oblation for Aparājita by means of the Aparājita mantra.
The god who deludes the three worlds [should perform] a fire-oblation of one thousand and eight [offerings] of pure water-pitchers dedicated to Indra, using the mantra of the three worlds.
Everything else should be performed as before by those skilled in ritual action.
Thus, O great sage, has the ceremonial bath been described to you in its various forms.
One who has bathed with the waters used for the bathing of the gods does not sink into hell;
he who protects that sacred site with devotion shall not undergo rebirth again.
Bearing the sandals upon his head, one becomes a servant of Vaikuṇṭha;
by placing the sacred powder upon his head, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
Having taken the powder from the sandals and the sacred bathing place, the supreme guide should cause it to be distributed to all the devotees who desire to serve him.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Twenty-One
O venerable Agastya, O Lord of the gods of gods, O son of Jamadagni, O treasury of compassion!
When there occurs a deficiency or excess in the performance of daily, occasional, and other such rites— || 21.1 ||

For all [castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who have entered the four stages of life (āśramas), what indeed is the solution in that regard? Tell me, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees! 21.2.
Having completed the supreme worship known as the Purifying Sacrifice (Pavitrayajana),
all those men were purified and their karmas dissolved. || 21.3 ||
It should take place in the month of Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada, or Āśvayuja;
on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and on a day celebrated as auspicious and joyful.
One should perform the auspicious rite of adorning the Lord of Kamalā with sacred ornaments on the days of Aśvinī,
Śravaṇa, Puṣya, Rohiṇī, or Punarvasu.

O Lord of Sages, one should perform the auspicious Pavitraka rite according to the prescribed rules during the three northern solstice months, or under the asterisms of Svāti, Mṛgaśiras, Anurādhā, or Revatī.
Then, having obtained threads— either those woven by Brahmin maidens,
or those purchased from the market, or silk— provided they were free from defects, according to his means.
Having taken [the seeds] and washed them with water, one should mix them with mung bean powder;
then, having tripled them, one should dry them thoroughly in the sun. (21.8)
Furthermore, having tripled the cord, the wise one should fix it upon the gnomon; he should then have the purifier (pavitra) fashioned according to the dimensions of the limbs.
One hundred and eight sūtras are proclaimed for all [the parts]; one should prepare them, reaching down to the navel, for the purpose of consecration and dwelling.
The head-ornament of the teacher, the venerable Padma, was his guru;
he composed thirty-two works, which for him were like a girdle of fire.
The measurement of the neck for both the *kuṃbha* and the *karakā* has been declared;
twenty-seven knots are prescribed for those two.
I shall now declare those ten images of the pavitra;
their dimensions, their designation as knots, and likewise their names as ornaments.

The [qualities] are superior, inferior, and middling; immediately following these are those called the crown (kirīṭa), the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, and the one called the forest garland (vanamālā)—these ten.
The authority [of the path] does not extend beyond the navel; it is joined with thirty-two knots.
That which is designated as "knots" extends to the heart, and there are twenty-five knots.
The ornament reaching to the ankles consists of thirty-two knots;
the superior one reaches the limit of the knees and has one hundred and eight knots.
The medium [length] should extend to the thighs with eighty knots;
for the inferior [length], it is proclaimed that there are sixty knots extending to the navel. (21.17)
The measurement of the crown for that name is said to have thirty-two knots;
the Śrīvatsa, bounded by the neck, has twenty-seven knots.
The Kaustubha gem should extend to the heart and be joined with thirty-two knots;
one should fashion the sacred garland of forest flowers (vanamālā) so that it reaches down to the feet.
This [system] consisting of many knots belongs to those who are independent;
it concerns the Bimba-mantras that are dependent, as well as the goddesses beginning with Uttamā.
The measurement of the fire-altar should be one cubit; it is traditionally taught that there are twelve knots for all the retinues, joined with thirty-two knots.
One should likewise conceive of the gatekeepers as extending to the navel;
one should then imagine the lotus pericarp, which is unlike the others, extending to the edge of the pedestal.
One should not imagine the navel to be accompanied by many knots, whether for one's gurus, officiating priests, or indeed for anyone else.
One should make it fragrant with perfumes and substances such as camphor,
or with gems, pearls, coral, gold, or even flowers.
One should fill the knots and adorn them with saffron and other substances;
one should prepare the sacred threads (pavitra) according to the extent of one's means.
On the tenth day at night, having offered the sprouts,
the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should bow down and circumambulate Hari while offering prayers.
For the sake of pacifying deficiencies in the ritual duties of the four castes and the stages of life,
and for the destruction of all defects, let those who attend the great festival observe it.
For the prosperity of all the worlds and for the destruction of famine,
for the attainment of health by the sick and for the accomplishment of the Lord’s desired aims.
"Today the great festival called Pavitrārohaṇa is being performed;
grant us permission, O Lord of Gods, and enjoin us to our duties."
Having thus made his request, the preceptor, having fasted, went from that temple into the interior of the pavilion, seated upon *darbha* grass facing east together with the officiating priests.
One should spend the entire night in the recitation of mantras and meditation on Hari;
when dawn has broken, one should commence the ritual of consecration (adhivāsana).
Having offered the oblation with a concentrated mind, one should perform the consecration at night;
the purificatory ornaments, the bath, and the marriage-thread ceremony should take place under the Dhruva constellation.
At one time, having performed all other auspicious rites,
he should then tie on the protective amulet (pratisara) and worship the door-arches.
He should station Brahmins learned in the four Vedas in the four directions,
amidst the resounding noise of musical instruments and within the pavilion over the heap of grain.
One should place the purifiers upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward;
having sprinkled them with water from the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) rite, one should dry them by means of drying and other such methods.
Having anointed it with fragrant substances and also perfumed it with incense,
one should scatter flowers and then wrap it in a new cloth.
Having displayed the wheel-mudrā, one should worship with the weapon-mantra;
then, starting from the northeast, one should encircle the pavilion with threads.
Having visualized a discus above, a lotus below, and maces at the eight doors,
as well as a conch in the cardinal directions of the pavilion, one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits.
May those beings who pierce through actions and create obstacles indeed go outside, having taken their share of the offering.
With this mantra, an offering (bali) of black gram food should be made to the spirits.
Then, having bathed the Lord of Gods, one should worship Him up to the end of the sacred thread (upavīta).
Having fashioned a mandala, one should install the deity within it and worship him;
then, having placed the mandala into the water-jar, one should worship Vāsudeva.
Having offered the Sudarśana vessel and the food according to the prescribed rite,
he then established the fire in the sacrificial pit and offered eight pieces of fuel-wood with the root mantra.
Then the preceptor should offer sixteen oblations with clarified butter using the *caru* and the *Nṛsūkta* by means of the *sruva* ladle,
and eight more oblations with the root mantra.
Having collected the dripping clarified butter (ājya), one should pour it onto the strainers;
the placing of the strainers (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed with the Vedic verse, "This is Viṣṇu. (21.44)
Having placed [the deity] in the auspicious water-pot, the small vessel, the fire, and the mandala,
one should likewise perform the rite for the primary image along with the auspicious ceremonies.
Having performed the same for all the images, one should then encircle the temple;
one should spend the night with recitations and other rites, using threads of five colors.
Then, having remained awake through the night, one should bathe the Teacher of the World residing within the maṇḍala at dawn, worship him thoroughly, and once again cause the wheel-lotus to revolve.
Having performed the worship of the doors and other parts, one should worship the lotus of the wheel;
having installed the deity therein, as well as the water-pot and the ritual vessel.
The wise man should worship as far as the edge of the lamp, and having offered the fourfold oblation,
he should sacrifice the fourfold oblation into the fire with the *Nṛsūkta*.
Barley, rice, bamboo, sesame, parched grain, and likewise *sumana* flowers, then aloe-wood and clarified butter, and finally fuel-sticks as the ninth, each separately. || 21.50 ||
During an auspicious moment, the Guru performs one hundred and eight oblations with purificatory materials;
he prepares the maṇḍala, the water-pot, the ritual jar, and the marriage-thread.
Having adorned the sacrificial pit, the fire, and the lotus-mandala,
and having circumambulated them, he then [performed the rite] for the permanent marriage-thread in the temple.
Having adorned them with purificatory rites, one should worship all other images and likewise those who are dependent on others, up to the conclusion of the oblation.

One should perform the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) for the goddesses, their retinues, and the sacred seats (pīṭhas) in due order, accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments, the Vedas, and other chants.
The offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) for all [the deities] is prescribed with the root mantra.
The preceptor, having entered the temple of Hari together with the image-keepers, [performs the rite]. (21.55)
Having prostrated and filled his joined palms with flowers, he should then offer praise;
he should scatter those flowers at the lotus-feet of the Deity.
Having placed all human goals as well as the purifiers belonging to Hari at his feet, and having praised and bowed down, one should accomplish one's own purpose.
Then, one should cause [the offerings] to be given to the chief worshippers, the officiating priests, the assistants, and to the others, such as the brahmins and the rest.
Having beheld the face of the god and touched the feet of the Teacher of the World, one should, with palms joined in reverence and full of humility, recite this verse.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, you who are saluted by all the worlds,
[pray] for the pacification of any deficiency or excess in the ritual services performed throughout the year.
This act of propitiation has been performed by us with devotion;
accept nothing from us here, O Mādhava, for my sovereignty remains mine.
Everything has been done at your command; you alone are our supreme refuge.
O Supreme Person, forgive whatever in this was deficient or excessive.
Thus one should pray to that God in the afternoon; likewise, one should devoutly perform the festival and the daily ritual bathing for the Lord of the World.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed during both periods— either nine, seven, or five times—
for three nights or one night, accompanied by the worship of the door and other [deities].
On the final day, the preceptor should perform a great festival;
he should perform the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) for Hari, either with the Puṃsūkta or with the Anuvāka.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this rite of the sacred ascent been described;
he who performs it with devotion attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Twenty-Two
O Blessed Lord, O Master, what atonement should there be for the deficiency or the omission of the daily, occasional, and other such forms of worship? (22.1)
Śrī Rāma said:
Listen, O son of Mitrāvaruṇa; I shall tell you everything in due order—those actions by which [the goal] is fulfilled and by which Hari becomes pleased. (22.2)

One who has not bathed, or one who has not been initiated, or one who is devoid of the sectarian mark (tilaka), wearing soiled clothing, having worn-out garments, and lacking purificatory items; || 22.3 ||
Without purifying the body through the sequence beginning with dissolution by means of samādhi,
and without performing the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), even when the Lord of the Universe has been worshipped—
A wise person should recite the eight-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times while performing worship,
provided they have not washed their feet and hands and have not sipped water for purification (ācamana).
Chanting the five Upaniṣads, naked with hair disheveled,
panting, laughing, or even angry, with limbs perspiring and though perhaps prattling on— (22.6)
One should worship the Lord of the gods and recite the weapon-mantra (astra-manu) one hundred times;
by merely touching hair, clods of earth, bones, hair, and so forth, one becomes ritually impure.
Having approached a woman without having first bathed, one should worship Puruṣottama;
one should bathe him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and mutter the five Upaniṣads.

Likewise, having touched the garment of a menstruating woman during the worship of a deity, one must bathe after touching a seller of the Vedas, a Caṇḍāla, a sacrificial post, a dog, or a menstruating woman. (22.9)

Having touched a crow, a heretic, one who has fallen from his caste, an outcaste, a donkey, or the like, or having touched a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), a funeral pyre, or anything else unfit for touch during worship; 22.10.
One should perform a bath with water from the five Vāruṇika mantras using kuśa grass;
one should bathe the deity with milk during worship that includes flowers along with their stalks.
If the Supreme Lord has been worshipped with impurities such as feces or urine,
