or if the image has been touched by women or those who have been led astray, one should perform [expiation].
One should perform a ceremonial bath with water infused with *kuśa* grass while reciting the *parameṣṭhin* mantra,
[even if one is] born of outcasts, *pulkasa*s, *caṇḍāla*s, or those born of inverse or natural order unions.
Food that has been touched by those who are untouchable, such as Śūdras and others, or by twice-born men devoid of proper conduct, or even by dogs, jackals, and donkeys, should not be offered.
Having prepared an oblation with unfit grains such as kodrava and offered it, he was bathed with ghee by mistake; thereafter, he was bathed with warm water.
If the oblation is too hot or too cold, or if it is offered without vegetables and the like,
one should recite the "Five Upaniṣads" a hundred times.
In a village defiled by corpses and the like, one should offer cooked food;
having performed a bath with milk, there should be the recitation of the "Five Upaniṣads."
But if one dies in the interval while the worship has already begun,
one should complete the entire rite according to the manual and conclude it before the God of gods.
In that [practice], there is no ritual of bathing and so forth, no fire sacrifice, no offering of oblations, and no great festival;
one should perform only the food offering—this is what is called its specific procedure.
One should again offer [the image], or if it has already been offered to another,
one should bathe it with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and perform ten thousand recitations (*ayuta*) of the root mantra.
If flowers offered to another deity, a chariot or other vehicle belonging to another, or likewise perfumes, garments, and so forth, have been employed in worship and similar rites; 22.21.
Having performed the auspicious bathing, one should recite the "root mantra" one hundred times over anything defiled by worms,
insects, and the like, or that which has been prepared for another deity.
If [the substance] has been used for worship and other rites, one should perform the bath with curd;
or else, with the remnants of what was eaten, or again, with the remnants of what was offered to Viṣṇu.
A wise person should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times during worship or even when bathing [the deity], provided the water has not become stale.
If [an image] has been worshipped with an object defiled by excrement, urine, or the like, one should perform an immersion in a jar of water mixed with *kuśa* grass for its pacification.
One should bathe [the deity] with Viṣṇu-vessels and again perform worship and other rites. All the water from a well defiled by a corpse or similar things should be removed.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle water at the end for the sake of purification;
however, if there is a breach in the prepared ritual services (*upacāra*), one should then cause them to be performed twice over.
For the sake of pacification, the wise one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
in the event of a deficiency in the worship of the God of gods, there should be double the worship.

When there is a deficiency in worship or a lapse in time, one should worship the Supreme Lord again with double the usual materials; indeed, at the conclusion of the rite of expiation, one should perform worship.
If there is a deficiency in the one-day worship, there should be a ritual bathing with water for pacification;
if the deficiency persists after one day has passed, it continues for three days.
The wise person should perform the ceremonial bathing with a pitcher of auspicious water.
Beyond this point, should there be any deficiency in the worship for twelve days, [the following should be done].
If there is a deficiency, one should bathe [the image] with all types of perfumes until the end of the fortnight;
if there is a lapse in worship for a month, the bathing should be performed with the root-herbs.
When the end of one year has arrived, one should cause the bath to be performed with the Brāhma-mantra;
if two years have elapsed, one should bathe [the image] with the Pārameṣṭhya-mantra.
The bathing of Vāsudeva should take place from then until the end of the year;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration (saṃprokṣaṇa) for up to three years, as in the case of a formal installation (pratiṣṭhā).
In all cases of expiation, one should provide a meal for Brahmins;
or, if [the offense] was not according to the scriptures, one should perform worship, an offering, or the rite of oblation.
The expiation for that [sin] is to perform a ceremonial bath with unhusked grain-water;
thus it is when many days have passed while worship has been performed contrary to the rules.

One should perform a ritual bath with that Vāsudeva-mantra; by that, peace shall be attained even in the event of touching the fire when it is untouchable, or when it is defiled by worms, hair, and the like.
One hundred and eight oblations with the Vyāhṛtis pacify [the defilement] caused by a Caṇḍāla, one in a state of birth-impurity, a menstruating woman, a corpse, or a Pulkasa.
Ten thousand oblations are prescribed with the Vyāhṛtis in the fire when the worship of the retinue has been omitted, or when there is a failure or omission in the offering of the bali.
At the appropriate time, having doubled those respective mantras, one should offer oblations into the fire for their pacification, using either sacrificial fuel-sticks or clarified butter.
If the offering substance falls, one should have it performed again by another;
for the sake of pacification, one should perform a ceremonial bath for Hari with coconut water.
Once the offering has been cast into the image, one should again place it upon the vehicle and so forth;
then, having completed the remainder of the offering, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava ablution.
If the image of the Lord of the World is touched by thieves whose caste is unknown,
one should perform a Prājāpatya penance and a ceremonial bathing for its propitiation.
If earthenware, a painted image, or an amulet— these three things—
are defiled by Caṇḍālas or others, one should discard them all and create new ones.
If the image is touched by outcasts (pātakins), one should perform a Brāhmaṇical ablution;
if it is touched by a Śūdra during the consecration (kautuka), one should bathe Hari with sacred water.
When the image of Parameṣṭhin has been touched by ordinary Brāhmaṇas,
its purification for that transgression shall be performed with a bath using water from kusa grass.
If [an image] is touched by wicked women, by those who are untouchable, or by *kuṇḍas* or *golakas*,
one should perform a meritorious ceremonial bath (*snapana*) of Hari for its pacification.
Upon entering the inner sanctum, those born of Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or Anuloma unions,
or women, should perform a sprinkling there with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If entry into the inner sanctum is made by Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, or others,
the auspicious clay and other materials must be discarded, and the area should be washed with cow-dung and water.
One should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
having created everything once more as before, all else is just as it was previously.
Upon touching images made of stone and other materials, one should perform the *brāhma* rite;
even upon entering [a place] where there is impurity, bathing is prescribed, as it is for a *caṇḍāla*.
Śūdras, Pulkasas, Caṇḍālas, Yavanas, those impure, and sinners—
whether authorized for ritual acts or not— are [excluded] whether through knowledge, ignorance, or even intentionally.
If they should perform the rites, they should then purify the temple;
afterwards, one should have the auspicious day (puṇyāha) proclaimed and cause the Vedas to be chanted by Brahmins.
One should bathe [the image] with the Vāsudeva mantra and provide a meal for the Brāhmaṇas;
[one must avoid contact] with Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, Svapnacas, jackals, those who are impure, and donkeys.
Listen to the expiation when one has entered the ground portion of the temple enclosure:
one should perform sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then have the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) recited.
Upon touching the images located there, or their retinue,
or the pedestals, one should perform an expiation just as was done previously.

If there is contact with the rain of fireflies during the journey, or if he is burned by fire, he should perform a meritorious ablution; for if he has been burnt, it must be done in every case thereafter.
Having fashioned [the image] again according to the rules, one should perform the rites as before;
at the conclusion of the installation, one should bathe the Lord of the World with the Vāsudeva mantra.
When the sacrificial hall had been established and the water-pot and the fire had been consecrated,
[it was defiled] by Caṇḍālas, those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), and other untouchables as well.
Having clearly abandoned the other [fire] and established [the new one], he should offer eight hundred oblations with the *mūla-mantra*,
and recite the mantras of each respective deity one hundred and eight times.
Whether during a ceremonial bath or a procession, if the image falls to the ground,
one should re-install that image and perform a meritorious ritual bathing.
If the water-pot has been touched by frogs, mice, or any such creatures, or by cats and the like, or if it has been overturned or destroyed, one should discard it.
Having established the [deities] within the pitchers, one should perform their respective invocations;
during the great festival beginning with the flag, one should mutter the mantras dedicated to those deities.
If any lapse should occur, it is pacified by the Flower Sacrifice;
in this abode where festivals are held constantly, no rite preceded by a banner is required.
The wise man should perform a festival for the sake of expiating that [transgression];
furthermore, he should propitiate the Supreme Lord with the Pārameṣṭhya bath.
When a great festival is underway and the banner has been lost for some reason,
one should prepare another banner and feed many Brahmins.
When the banner has fallen to the ground for whatever reason whatsoever,
one should raise it up again and afterwards provide abundant food for the Brahmins.
In cases where there are breaks, gaps, or the like, and where the omission of syllables or similar defects may occur,
one should join them as appropriate and sprinkle [the text] according to the prescribed ritual.
Having placed it back [on the funeral pyre], one should offer a satiation of food to Brahmins for its pacification;
just as when a Caṇḍāla or similar person enters, the interior of the jar becomes defiled.
In the same way, for earthen vessels such as the *pālikā* and others, it will certainly be so;
one should again offer sprouts for their pacification, followed by the feeding of Brahmins.
If the shoots are unfavorable, or if they are eaten by mice, cattle, or horses—
even when arising from anthills and the like— one should perform a rite for their pacification.
A peace-offering with the *vyāhṛti* syllables and the feeding of Brahmins;
in a dwelling devoid of a village or similar settlement, there is a circumambulation of that very house.
When a great festival is underway, if the village or other location becomes disturbed by rain, wind, fire, and so forth, one should later perform an expiation and hold the festival again.
If a festival is interrupted by divine circumstances or by human agency, the expiation shall be a ceremonial bath performed according to the rite prescribed for Prajāpati.
One should cast the bali offering in the temple, in the village, on the street, and in the four directions;
having thus restored all lost rites in their entirety, just as before.
One should perform all subsequent duties according to the path prescribed by the rules;
even if the offering of oblations has not been performed, one should perform what was previously omitted.

In the event of disturbances such as great winds and the like, one should perform other rites according to the rules; likewise, during the intervals between those [rites], one should offer oblations to Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and the spirits (bhūtas).
In the event of a minor pilgrimage, one should perform the ritual bathing originating from Vāsudeva;
if the image has been lost by thieves or other causes, one should perform the rite of worship with great festival.
But when the image has fallen on the street, one should place it back upon a vehicle,
perform a circumambulation of the street, and then observe the Prājāpatya penance.

If by falling one should render the image of the deity mutilated, the wise should perform a great rite of worship and, having joined it back together according to the rules, complete all other required tasks.
In the event of a breakdown of the vehicle, one should lead the deity by means of some other vehicle;
this applies to those authorized for the ritual, whether for the installation or for the sacrifice.
If that rite is obstructed by some cause, whether divine or human, one should complete it through other qualified persons who are similar [to the original performers]. 22.82.
To pacify any deficiency or excess in the sacrificial ladles adorned with purifiers, or in the mandala, one should recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times.
If a consecration is performed without the preliminary ritual of immersion in water (jalādhivāsa),
one should perform the ablution with the Pārameṣṭhya mantra and recite the "Root Mantra" one hundred times.
Hari will endure affliction for more than a month but less than twelve years;
beyond that, Vāsudeva does not tolerate dwelling in affliction.
When one has transcended the bounds of the afflictions (kleśa), one should perform the rite of the "Inner Abode of the Child" (bālālayāntara);
one should arrange for an expiation (prāyaścitta) consisting of a ritual bath for Vāsudeva.
If, however, there should arise a confusion of all the established doctrines (siddhāntas) or of the Tantras among one another, the supreme state (pārameṣṭhya) is the expiation.
Whether accompanied by a retinue or without them, it is worshipped;
this is called the *mantrasiddhānta*, for the form is indeed one and not otherwise.
Where the four emanations, Vāsudeva and the others, are worshipped as being devoid of a retinue, that is the Siddhānta Āgama.
Along with Vāsudeva and the others, there are Nārāyaṇa, Hayānana,
Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, and Sūkara— these are the nine forms.
And they, along with their retinues—Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, Kroḍa, Haṃsa, Vāgīśvara, and others—are honored [as expounders] of the Siddhānta known as Tantra. (22.91)
They are worshipped according to the difference in the speaker; likewise, they may have two, three, or more faces.
Even there, it is but a single form, whether with or without a retinue.
This tantra has been taught as distinct from other tantras; it is fourfold.
The confusion of established doctrines (siddhāntas) with the tantras leads to ruin.
Therefore, one should worship the Supreme Lord without any confusion of these traditions:
the Vaikhānasa, the Pāñcarātra, the Bhārgava, and likewise the Śaiva.
These four tantras are praised for the ritual of worship;
one should worship Puruṣottama, the Lord of Gods, without confusion [of these systems]. 22.95.
If confusion should arise during the rites of installation and festivals, or during worship, bathing, and so forth, there will be great ruin for the king and the kingdom. (22.96)
Therefore, one should perform the entire web of ritual actions according to the rules, without confusion and likewise without contact with those who hold other offices. 22.97

The ancient ritual procedure, beginning with the plowing of the ground and ending with the consecration, must be performed by that same person for the purpose of re-establishment; one should not conceive of it otherwise.
That image and that tantra, and he himself is once again the installer;
through this very re-conception, there occurs a reversal of the entire web of ritual actions. || 22.99 ||
When the ancient temple has been destroyed, or when the ancient image is lost, the presiding authority is no longer known; thus, a new creation proceeds according to one's will.
The qualified candidate was fully known; indigestion was a constant source of curiosity;
the temple was captivating; yet for a long time, the neglect of worship persisted. (22.101)
In accordance with the previous tantra, that qualified practitioner should perform all the rites; otherwise, there will be upheaval in the kingdom.
When the deity has departed due to affliction, whether in a village or even in a city,
one should not perform auspicious rites there until the karma has been eradicated from its very root.
How much more so, then, when there is a deficiency in the worship of the God of gods?
Therefore, having sprinkled [the deity] intensely with one's whole being, one should then perform the worship.
If there is an omission of worship to the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow due to any cause whatsoever,
and if one has not attained the qualification for the tantras, then the worship may be performed according to the wish of the patron.
Then, having performed the pacification of deficiencies and having sprinkled [the site] according to the rule,
the Lord Hari becomes pleased by the sacrifice performed through another tantra.
Whether in the Siddhānta, the Tantra, or the Śāstra, those who know the scriptures and especially those desiring prosperity must not commit a transgression when not in times of distress. (22.107)
In the event of an omission of worship for the domestic image, one should perform an ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
After a month has passed, or even up to six months, one should perform a meritorious ceremonial bath (puṇyasnāna).
The procedure for sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) shall take place within six months or one year;
beyond that, there shall be re-consecration (pratiṣṭhā) when the worship of the domestic image (gṛhārcā) comes to an end.
When there is a deficiency in the ritual offerings during the installation of deities such as those of the Thirty-three,
no other method is prescribed than a ceremonial bath performed solely with Puruṣa-sūktas.
If a deficiency occurs in the worship of a Śālagrāma stone or similar objects,
or if they are touched by one who is untouchable, one should wash them with water and then worship them again.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Twenty-Three
Śrī Rāma said: O great sage, all the expiations have been described;
among all of them, one should first perform the rite of the sprout and the auspicious thread.
And the ritual of formal acceptance (adhivāsa) should be performed as prescribed for the consecration ceremony;
on the following day, in the morning, the procedure for the placement of the ritual jars (kalaśa-sthāpana) shall take place.

Except for the Aparājita [consecration], for meritorious rites dedicated to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the ritual pitcher (kumbha) containing water must be established during the rite of expiation (prāyaścitta). || 23.3 ||
In the center, one should place the vessel of substances, and pure water all around it;
pearls or silver should also be placed within them, and they should be filled with water.
Having invoked the deity, worshipped him, and established the sacrificial fire,
the preceptor, having offered oblations according to the rules up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), [performed the rite].
Then, having bathed, recited prayers, and fed the best of the twice-born,
and having honored and bowed to his guru, he gave him a sacrificial fee.
Having bestowed the sacrificial fee upon the officiating priests, the assistants, and the Brahmins, the Guru should lead the deity into the interior ground of the temple. (23.7)
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall now describe in due order the procedure for ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa),
whether for the rejoining of broken limbs and so forth, or for the temple (dhāma) or the sacred image (kautuka).

Whether there has been a long-term neglect of worship, or [the image] is buried in the earth, or even in the event of death; or during birth, sexual intercourse, or at the site [of such acts]; or even when touched by an artisan during the making of a ritual object—[in these cases, purification is required].
In these and other such cases, sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) is prescribed;
one should first cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited while uttering the mantra "viṣṇornuka".
One should sprinkle the temple, the image, and so forth with water using mantras containing the word "water" (abliṅga), and likewise wash them;
thereafter, one should offer sprouts after having tied a protective cord (pratisara).
One should perform the ritual bathing of the limbs with the rite pertaining to Viṣṇu;
then, being self-possessed, one should lay the deity upon the bed just as in the ceremony of installation (pratiṣṭhā). || 23.12 ||
One should worship the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth, as previously described.
Upon the altar, on a pedestal of grain, one should place the great water-pot.
With all its limbs encircled by thread, accompanied by jewels and a consecrated image, enriched with a tuft of grass for a lid and provided with a pair of garments. || 23.14 ||
On its very right side, one should place a similar water-pot;
Vāsudeva in the great jar and Sudarśana in the water-pot.
Then, having invoked [the deity] according to the rule, one should worship him with offerings ending in the food-oblation (naivedya);
and having duly prepared the fire, one should invoke the Lord of the Universe therein.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations separately with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and parched grains, he performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma) as before.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having dismissed [the deity] residing in the fire,
and having likewise dismissed the other deities, one should cause the Lord to enter within.
One should sprinkle Puruṣottama with the water from the great pitcher using a bunch of kuśa grass, reciting the five Upaniṣads, the water-mantras (abliṅga), and other [mantras].
At the appointed time, the most excellent Brahmins should recite the peace-mantras;
having thus consecrated the Lord of Gods, one should worship him as before.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion; betel and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given.
One should then give a fee to the preceptor (ācārya) consisting of one hundred niṣkas or more.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
The Twenty-Fourth Chapter.
O Blessed One, Agastya, Lord of all the worlds, served by the hosts of all the sages:
you alone are the Blessed Viṣṇu; you are Brahmā; you are Maheśvara.
You are Āditya and you are Agni; you are Candra and you are Purandara.
You are Vāyu, the soul of all beings, and you are Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas.
Ananta, the lord of serpents, you are the creator of all embodied beings;
devoid of beginning, middle, and end, you move within all creatures.
You are the Puruṣa, the Supreme Brahman, the eternal seed of the universe;
apart from you, I see no Lord higher than the highest.
At the end of the eon, when the ocean is agitated, having withdrawn the entire world,
O Lord of Gods, you carry it within your belly upon the circle of Śeṣa as Śeṣa himself.
You go with the king of birds; you bear the goddess Śrī upon your chest;
this entire world is the remainder, and you, O Supreme Lord, are the one who remains.
Today I have been graced by you; having been looked upon with your side-glances, O Lord of Men, I am purified and have become someone who belongs to the world of merit.
O Lord, ocean of compassion, through your grace I have grasped the essence of the entire Pañcarātra; I have some service to perform for you. 24.8
That too must be taught today, even though it is a secret and difficult to obtain;
[I shall teach] the qualification for the recitation of the mantra known as the eight-syllabled one.
Śrī Rāma said: "O best of sages, you have asked well. I shall teach you the essence of everything in brief; that mantra for which you are qualified shall now be explained in detail."
He considers himself the subordinate and the Supreme Lord as the sovereign;
he feels compassion for all beings, and by them he too is compassionately regarded.
Free from desire in all undertakings, I am such that I regard even death as a friend in this triple world; yet he fears it.
Whether hungry or thirsty, always meditating on Hari,
he regarded rain, wind, and sun as equal to his own nature.
One should be exceedingly content even in hardships, humble in times of security and prosperity;
one should be like a eunuch toward women, and blind from birth when perceiving faults.
He was mute when the faults of others were spoken; he was deaf in the assemblies of those who know the Vedas during praise and blame; and he was bathed in tears of joy. (24.15)
A servant of the devotees of Hari, whose mind is solely intent on the service of Hari—such a person shall be qualified to receive this mantra. (24.16)
That lord of sages should resort to the two-fold division as "pure" and "mixed";
the first is the Ekāyana Veda, which sets forth Brahman alone.
Refined by that very [mantra], it is proclaimed as pure, mixed, or triple;
for the Traividyas it is eight syllables, while for the pure ones it is twelve syllables.

The uninterrupted performance of the five-fold daily rites (pañcakāla) with mantras such as the *balā* [mantra], and the purificatory rites beginning with impregnation (*niṣeka*) performed by means of the *balā* and other [mantras]—[these constitute the duties]. 24.19.
For them, the twelve-syllable mantra alone is their knowledge; not the triple Veda, nor the Sāvitrī, nor any other mantra for the rites of private study and recitation.
Free from desire for roots, all were meditators on the "twelve-syllable" mantra; devoid of contact with the dead or the newborn, they sought only liberation.
These [Śūdras] are not ordained as eligible for activities such as ploughing;
if they should perform them out of ignorance, they fall [from their status], of this there is no doubt. (24.22)
Having accepted an image installed by one initiated and established in the tenets of mantra, he should worship it for his own sake.
Having performed the consecration of that image using the twelve-syllable vidyā, which is devoid of seed-syllables, powers,
and limbs, one should cause it to be given to the owner of the original tree.
There is no initiation, nor indeed any purification of the body through cremation and so forth;
nor is any ritual such as the placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) desired in the upward path of Ekāyana.

Even for those who have entered the single path and possess the three types of knowledge, [the mantra] is likewise devoid of seed-syllables, powers, and limbs, and is stripped of seers and meters. (24.26)

The recitation of the mantra, which is the very essence of the acts of private study (*svādhyāya*), makes one fit for the worship of the gods; through initiation, the knower of the three Vedas becomes qualified. (24.27)
Initiation within the mandala of the wheel and lotus is proclaimed as his primary [method];
the secondary initiation would take place solely in the presence of the fire.
One who has been initiated should perform the rites of plowing and so forth for the God of gods;
however, that twice-born man who is devoid of initiation shall have no authority [to do so].
Therefore, one who desires to worship Hari should undergo initiation in the presence of Hari;
having invoked Hari into the water-pot, the mandala, and the fire, one should worship him.
Having pierced through the thread of illusion and being released from the binding of the eyes, the person becomes purified upon beholding the mandala of the lotus-wheel.
Having scattered golden flowers and received the mark called the *puṇḍra* from his guru,
he studied all the mantras, beginning with the eight-syllabled one.
Having been consecrated with the waters of the ritual jar, he was empowered with the knowledge consisting of the worship of Hari,
so that he might duly worship Viṣṇu and install him.
To perform great festivals and so forth, as well as daily and occasional rites, this shall be the primary initiation; now listen as I describe the secondary one.
One should worship a sacrificial mound, an image of Viṣṇu, a water-pot, and a flame;
or else, according to availability, one may worship the fire alone.
One who is marked on the root of the arm should offer oblations with the Hetirāja mantra, or together with the Pāñcajanya mantra; thereafter, one should proceed as before with the name and so forth.

Having received [this] from the Guru according to the scriptures, may he be proficient in the ritual of worship—whether it be the daily, the occasional, or the optional rites, such as the plowing and other agricultural activities. (24.37)
This second initiation, characterized by the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras), is [the one described];
these are declared to be the qualified candidates for the ritual of the worship of Vāsudeva.
For these [twelve] alone are authorized to recite the eight-syllable mantra or other mantras; no others have the right even to mention or remember them. (24.39)
I shall now declare the eight-syllable mantra; listen with an attentive mind.
First is the beginning of the meters, and immediately after that is Vighneśa.
The individual soul (jīvātman) with its subtle body (oṭadeha) is declared the third caste;
Vighneśa together with Viṣṇu is the fourth, O Pot-born One.
Then the fifth wind, Mahājvāla, bears Viṣṇu;
that Viṣṇu, who has a beautiful face, is declared to follow immediately after the sixth.
At the end, the vital breath (prāṇa) shines among the Maruts, always the sustainer of all beings.
This eight-syllabled mantra of yours has been correctly declared by me.
The sage is declared to be the divine Nārāyaṇa, and his deity is likewise [Nārāyaṇa];
the metre is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the seed-syllable is Viṣṇu with the bindu. (24.44)
Furthermore, O great sage, the six limbs have been described by means of three words in their collective sense; now I shall speak of them individually—listen to that.
Bharadvāja, Kauśika, Jamadagni,
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, and Agastya are declared to be the sages in their respective order.
For the second and subsequent [mantras] of Tāraka, Parameṣṭhin shall be the seer (ṛṣi);
for those beginning with the Praṇava, the meters (chandas) are Gāyatrī and the rest, and they are indeed unchanging.
And I shall state Virāṭ as the deity for these [elements] in order: Dharā, Dhruva, Soma, Āpas, Agni, and the sixth is said to be Varuṇa. (24.48)
Pratyūha and Prabhāta are the eight deities; they should be placed in order upon the ground locations starting from the navel and ending at the heart. 24.49.
The Lord has four arms and noble limbs, bearing the conch and the discus;
he resembles a dark cloud and has eyes like lotus petals.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, a girdle, and anklets; with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem upon his chest; and decorated with earrings and finger-rings.
He was clothed in yellow garments, adorned with a sacred sacrificial thread,
and bore an upright tilaka mark on his forehead made of white clay.
Constantly fanned by Śrī and Bhūmi with yak-tail whisks,
his face like a full-blown lotus, he possessed a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
by this, all the gods can be accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
The best of the twice-born should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with this mantra;
liberated from all sins, he will certainly become a great yogi.
The four Vedas with their constituent limbs, as well as various treatises—
all this is itself established within the eight-syllable mantra.
Constantly reciting this and meditating upon it, one is liberated from all evil.
What is the use of many other mantras? Everything is accomplished by this alone.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
Chapter Twenty-Five
Śrī Rāma,
having been thus initiated into the three Vedas and being devoted to recitation and meditation, should, with his mind fixed upon Hari, become intent upon the five daily observances.
In the morning he should seek knowledge and thereafter receive it;
following that, he should perform sacrifice, and then remain devoted to the study of the sacred texts.
The twice-born man should pass his time thus through yoga until the end;
having risen from bed in the morning, he should chant the names of Hari.
Then, having cleansed his body, beginning with the cleaning of his teeth,
he should plunge into the waters of a river or similar body of water while reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Then, clothed in two garments and anointed with sandalwood paste or clay,
one should bear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead and offer water for honor (arghya) to the Sun.

Having circumambulated three times with the Sāvitrī mantra and having gratified the deities, one should restrain the breaths, form a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and recite [the mantra] until the solar orb [is reached].

Having performed the ritual attendance upon the Sun, having beheld him, and having completed the remainder of the rite, [one should recite] either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.
Having offered oblations into the fire and bowed to the Lord of Gods as far as the top of his throne,
and having looked upon him, he circumambulated him three times together with his sons, wife, and attendants.
Having performed the requisite preparations consisting of the propitiation of those worthy of honor,
and having bathed and worshipped the Lord of the World as well as the ascetics and guests, [he departed].
Then, having satisfied [the guests], he himself should eat the remains of the sacrificial food (havis) left over by his guru;
thereafter, he should either recite the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, or study the scriptures, or even cause them to be recited.
Having bathed, completed the ritual objective, offered the water of honor (arghya), and attended upon the fire,
he should bow to the God of gods with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā.
Having offered praise and partaken of food, one should apply oneself to the practice of meditation upon one's own self;
becoming intent on breath control (prāṇāyāma), the knower of reality should employ the root mantra.
One should purify the *nāḍīs*, namely the *iḍā* and the *piṅgalā*, by means of the inhalation and exhalation;
and there, in each respective place, one should practice the retention of the vital air (*vāyu*) through yoga.
One should dissolve the earth into water, that [water] into fire, that [fire] into air, and that [air] into space;
one should dissolve that [space] into the individual soul (jīva), and that [soul] into the supreme, stainless Brahman.
Having bathed daily at the sacred ford during the clear midnight of the night, the wise man,
with a pure mind, sits properly upon his seat in a secluded place.
Thus, one initiated into the practice of yoga should meditate upon the Supreme Brahman—
the imperishable light of consciousness situated within the center of the lotus of the heart.
Shaped like a kadamba bud, eternally satisfied, free from ailment,
infinite, consisting of bliss, composed of consciousness, radiant, and all-pervading.
One who is proficient in the science of yoga should pass his time meditating thus: like a lamp in a windless place, with the radiance of an unartificial gem. 25.18.
At the conclusion of yoga, having again performed creation from the individual soul down to the earth by reversing the process of dissolution, one should satisfy the deity.
Then he should sleep upon a bed, either with a well-dressed woman or even without her;
passing his days in this manner, at the end he shall go to the god Hari.

Alternatively, being pure, one who desires liberation should recite the eight-syllable mantra according to his capacity; such a seeker of liberation attains liberation, and one desiring prosperity attains incomparable fortune.
Health, the prosperity of sons, the earth garlanded with crops,
incomparable royal splendor, and eternal royal fortune.
Longevity, incomparable knowledge, and proficiency in all undertakings—
whatever the reciters desire shall be in the palm of their hand.
O best of sages, this scripture is the eternal secret of all;
it should be given to a devotee of Viṣṇu who brings benefit to the worlds.
It should be given to those who perform meritorious deeds and to those who are fearful of evil;
it must never be given to an atheist nor to one who lacks devotion.
This scripture, which is this *Brahmasampuṭa*, is to be kept secret;
the Lord is pleased with whoever recites it with devotion. (25.26)
Liberation is in his palm; he is released from all sins. One desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring a wife quickly obtains a beautiful woman.
One desiring long life obtains a long lifespan; one who is ill is freed from disease; and one desiring prosperity attains incomparable fortune—of this there is no doubt. (25.28)
What need is there for much speaking here? Whatever one desires is obtained; this secret has been declared out of affection for you, O Lord of Sages.
"Released from all sin, go to your place," saying this,
I beheld that Parameṣṭhin, the Lord of the World.
As he looked on, the god Rāma, whose eyes were red at the corners, vanished;
I received this scripture along with its secret mysteries from the Lord of the World.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva, who possesses stainless and infinite power;
to the meritorious one, the one invoked by many, the Supreme Person, the Highest Self.
"O Agastya,
by this rite you must worship Adhokṣaja—
the God who removes all sins, the seed of the universe, and higher than the highest. (25.33)
That is the supreme goal, that is the supreme sacred ford, that is the supreme austerity, and that is great auspiciousness;
by means of that, everything comes into the palm of one's hand—of this there is no doubt.
For one who worships Vāsudeva, the eternal Lord of gods, what need is there for many sacred fords, what need for sacrifices, or even for vows? (25.35)
All that shall come into one's hands through the worship of Viṣṇu;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Vāsudeva.
Thus this great and divine scripture was received from the sage Bhārgava; the venerable ṛṣi Agastya taught it to the ascetics.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Bhārgavatantra.
